survey_angles: Poisoning attacks on online, continual, self-updating and drift-adaptive anomaly detectors and NIDS (2025-2026), covering gradual/frog-boiling poisoning, attacks on pseudo-labelling/self-training, and attacks on drift detectors

Defenses against data poisoning of online or continual learning that do not need peers: robust streaming estimators, certified or provable bounds for adaptive online poisoning, robust self-training, trusted-anchor methods, update validation before promotion (2025-2026)

Methods that tell benign concept drift apart from adversarial drift or poisoning in streaming data and NIDS, including drift explanation, drift attribution, and causal or directional analysis of drift (2024-2026)
On-device learning and continual learning on microcontrollers (TinyML training, ESP32, Cortex-M) with measured memory/latency/energy, and work on securing on-device learning (2025-2026)
Adaptive, continual or self-supervised intrusion detection for IoT/IIoT edge devices under concept drift (2025-2026), and whether they defend their adaptation against poisoning

Availability attacks on ML security systems: denial-of-service poisoning, attacks that force retraining or block adaptation, attacks on drift detectors (false alarms or stale models), alert fatigue and adversarial habituation (2024-2026). Relevance: our freeze attack.

Cross-device, peer-to-peer, gossip or neighbourhood-based verification among IoT devices for anomaly detection or poisoning resistance without a central server, plus behavioural baselines shared across similar devices (2024-2026)

Lightweight robust streaming statistics and certified robust mean/covariance estimation suitable for microcontrollers (median-of-means, trimmed estimators, robust sketching, robust PCA updates in streams), 2024-2026

Recent IoT and network-traffic datasets and benchmarks with real temporal drift or long time spans, and studies that measure how (IoT) traffic drifts over time (2024-2026, plus two direct foundations marked as background)

Emerging and unconventional directions for securing self-learning IoT anomaly detectors (2025-2026): LLM/foundation-model assistance, physical side-channel trust anchors, game-theoretic adaptation, conformal prediction under poisoning, honeypot-guided adaptation, hardware roots of trust for model updates
covered_vs_us:
What is NOT taken:

1. TOA (signature-direction split with a slow cumulative budget and a provable minimum time to compromise). Not in any paper. The nearest relatives restrict updates for other reasons, and a reviewer will raise each of them:
- 2606.29841 penalises protected eigendirections that come from the data covariance, has no cumulative budget, and freezes outright when lambda = infinity.
- OWAD's lambda3*Omega_i guards against forgetting, not attack.
- LID clamps to a static certified box rather than limiting a rate.
- EMA and beta-interpolation slow every direction equally.
We should name TOA 'threat-aware rate limiting' and contrast it with all four explicitly.

2. Freeze attack. Undescribed everywhere, yet many published defences have the vulnerable stop-start structure: T2T rollback, the DriftXpert and OWAD/NetSight gates, LID early stop, the RTTAD stopping rule, and EATA-style entropy filtering. The closest material is AHA's 'alert fatigue' and 'sensitization' vocabulary (abstract only) and WARDEN's 'dictionary starves' (harmless there because that channel adds no detection power). This is our most defensible first claim, pending a full read of 2609.23254 and the AHA text.

3. IoT, ESP32 and per-device lifecycle. No corpus paper covers an ESP32 or on-device poisoning defence, per-device self-learning with a safe bootstrap, or churn as an attack vector. Sensors 2024 shows the spawn hijack but gives no defence.

What IS taken, or must be conceded:

(a) Self-poisoning theory: the Polya urn, b acting as a reproduction number, and pi_c (WARDEN). We cannot claim to be first to theorise self-poisoning. Instead we should measure q(rho) for our detectors and show b >= 1 for the naive detector and b < 1 for ours.

(b) Open problem 1, poison inside drift. It is now a known impossibility for single-stream label-free learners (WARDEN Theorem 15; 2606.29841 Theorem 3.1). The 'attack hidden in drift beats our signature-free version' result therefore becomes a corollary, not a contribution. The contribution has to be the side information that escapes the theorem.

(c) Core/outer-ring rule. Its parts have cousins:
- DriftXpert's Outlier Ratio is our 'ring gets busier' test, used there as a retrain trigger.
- OWAD/NetSight's permutation-tested KL is a p-valued version of the same check.
- MCM's geometric-median/covariance approach gives bounded per-point influence but still has unbounded influence for mean shift and variance inflation.
- WARDEN cites Wang 2026 (2605.06204) to argue that trimming 'provably recovers little' under drift. We must answer this, either by showing the ring rule is not plain trimming or by conceding its theory is weak.

(d) Being 'gradual poisoning of a self-updating NIDS' is not novel by itself. AHA (CCS 2025), ANTIDOTE and Kloft and Laskov cover it.

(e) Adaptive-attacker evaluation is now expected: surrogate-by-query (Su et al.), window-blind schedules (ESANN 2025), learned pulsing (NDSS 2026), direction-diverse multi-agent attackers (SuSS 2026). Our hand-built 'hide in the core' attacker will not satisfy an A/A* reviewer.

(f) Dataset hygiene. The Computers & Security 2025 survey says no documented public concept-drift NID dataset existed through 2023. N-BaIoT captures are per-device and not concurrent, so any multi-device drift on N-BaIoT is synthesised and must be labelled as such.

Must-check before claiming novelty:
- 2609.23254 and Pasikhani TDSC 2026 (freeze and blind-set claims).
- For the peer idea: Byzantine-robust and personalised federated anomaly detection, DIoT (ICDCS 2019) and its poisoning follow-up by Nguyen et al. (DISS 2020), and Peer Group Analysis (Bolton and Hand 2001).
- For licensing: MUD-based anomaly detection.

lenses.lens: METHODS: which of our update mechanisms (TOA, the core/outer-ring rule) are already covered by 2024-2026 work, and what new mechanism could beat both them and the newest papers, especially on open problem 1 (an attack hidden inside strong genuine drift).
lenses.already_covered:
TOA (splitting each update into a part along the attack signature, rationed by a slow budget, and an orthogonal part applied in full, with a provable minimum time to compromise) is NOT covered by any paper in the corpus. The nearest relatives all restrict updates by direction or region, but none of them does it for a threat:
- "Theory of Continual Learning Against Data Poisoning Attacks" (arXiv 2606.29841): its robust feature defense puts a larger penalty on a protected set of eigendirections. Those directions come from the data covariance, not from an attack signature. It has no cumulative budget, and a penalty of infinity freezes a direction outright.
- OWAD (NDSS 2023): its λ3·Ω_i regularizer is importance-weighted consolidation. It protects against forgetting, not against an attacker.
- "Provably Safe Model Updates" (LID, SaTML 2026): projects updates into a fixed certified box around the starting parameters. That is a static region rather than a rate, and Algorithm 1 stops learning once the box intersection is empty.
- Su et al. (ICLR 2025): its EMA defense slows every direction equally. DriftXpert's β weight interpolation is a similar undirected anchor.
A reviewer will raise all of these, so the paper must say plainly: TOA is threat-aware rate-limiting, and these are forgetting-aware or static-region constraints.

The core/outer-ring rule is NOT covered as a mechanism, but its parts have close cousins, and one paper argues against its premise:
- DriftXpert (arXiv 2609.08623): its Outlier Ratio (recent outlier fraction divided by historical) is essentially our "outer ring really gets busier" test. It uses it to trigger supervised retraining, not to gate spread growth.
- OWAD and NetSight (arXiv 2508.15100): permutation-tested KL on score histograms, which is a p-valued version of the same kind of check.
- "Online robust covariance matrix estimation and outlier detection" (arXiv 2601.03957): bounded per-point influence through the geometric median and the median covariation matrix. Its own influence functions are unbounded for mean shift and variance inflation, which are exactly the moves a boiling-frog attacker makes.
- WARDEN/CDC (arXiv 2607.21673): deliberately avoids trimming and sample selection, and cites Wang 2026 (arXiv 2605.06204) for the claim that trimming "provably recovers little" under drift. That directly undercuts the theoretical case for our dense-core rule, so we must answer it.

Self-poisoning theory itself is now owned by the WARDEN paper: a Pólya-urn kernel q(ρ)=a+bρ, where b acts like a reproduction number and there is a critical contamination rate π_c. We cannot claim to be first here.

The freeze attack is not described anywhere. The closest material:
- WARDEN's "dictionary starves" under tail mimicry. It is harmless there only because the dictionary adds no detection power.
- T2T rollback in 2606.29841, which discards benign neighbouring tasks.
- LID's early stop, DriftXpert's OR>T gate, RTTAD's "stop when no samples remain" rule, and the "alert fatigue" framing in the CCS 2025 AHA poster (I only read its abstract).

Open problem 1 is now formally explained by two results:
- WARDEN Theorem 15: in a 1-D score space, without labels, genuine drift and tail-mimicking contamination are indistinguishable, so detection power is capped at κ=α/(π+α(1−π)).
- 2606.29841 Theorem 3.1: no regularization-family learner converges under frequent shifted poisoning. Its 1-D proof is literally an EMA mean dragged by a bias.
So the failure of our signature-free version is an instance of a theorem, not a bug. Any fix must bring in side information that a single label-free stream does not have.
lenses.open_gaps:
1. Side information without labels. No paper uses cross-device (peer) corroboration to decide whether a self-learning detector may accept an update. CB-RBM (NeurIPS 2026, arXiv 2610.16694) uses feature-context consistency, but only as a frozen scoring signal on graphs, and it never gates updates.
2. Certified admission that still tracks drift. WARDEN freezes its reference set forever. CDC pays 33-37% of oracle TPR, and by our own inference its Storey estimate can be inflated to blind it. LID freezes too. No certified method also has a guaranteed adaptation rate.
3. A signature-free, multi-direction rationed budget. TOA needs a known signature, which an omission-style attacker (Rapid Poison, ICML 2026) could shape. It also protects only one direction, which a contrastive multi-agent poisoner that spreads its push over several directions (AAAI SuSS 2026) could exploit.
4. A formal safety-plus-liveness contract. No paper states both "minimum time to compromise" and "maximum honest drift tracked with false alarms at most α", and the freeze attack is a liveness violation. No defense in the corpus has a liveness guarantee.
5. Adaptive attacks on our own gates are untested:
   - Window-blind poisoning: solving W_n v=0 (Hinder et al., ESANN 2025) against our outer-ring windows.
   - Pulsing timed to our budget refills: the NDSS 2026 heavy-hitter monitoring paper's learned attacker times on/off bursts to its monitor's eviction and refresh timescales.
6. No IDS or IoT evaluation of WARDEN/CDC, and no ESP32 numbers for anything.
7. Two papers must be read before we claim novelty on budgets and blind sets: "The Price of Self-Calibration" (arXiv 2609.23254, which talks about evidence budgets and manufactured blind sets) and Pasikhani et al. (TDSC 2026). Neither has been verified.

ideas.name: Peer-Corroborated Drift Decomposition (PCDD): common-mode drift applied in full, the device-specific remainder rationed
ideas.idea:
Each device keeps its own centroid detector, which also addresses open problem 2. Every cycle:
1. Device i proposes a centre shift Δc_i.
2. A gateway (or a broadcast of k-dimensional PCA vectors) supplies the shifts of peer devices of the same type. We take a robust common-mode estimate: the coordinate-wise median, or the geometric median, of the peer shifts. Call it m.
3. Split Δc_i into the part explained by peer agreement (its projection onto m, scaled by peer consensus) and an idiosyncratic residual r_i.
4. Apply the common-mode part in full. Pass r_i through a TOA-style slow cumulative budget B·t.
5. Apply the same split to spread growth.
The point is that genuine drift (firmware rollouts, seasonal or diurnal load, ISP changes) is largely shared across peers. A poisoner who controls traffic to fewer than half the peers cannot fake consensus, because the median's breakdown point is 50%.
Theory target. A multi-stream extension of WARDEN's Theorem 15: if honest drift has cross-device correlation of at least ρ and the attacker controls f < n/2 streams, the two-world construction fails. The power cap κ then lifts to something like 1−O(f/n), and time to compromise is at least D/B, the same bound TOA gives today but without a signature.
Cost. A new device joining starts at the peer centre instead of breaking a single detector. The price is that drift on one device only (a single device's firmware update) is tracked at budgeted speed, which we report as a bounded adaptation latency.
Evaluation. N-BaIoT's 9 devices were not captured at the same time, so concurrent common-mode drift must either be synthesised or taken from CESNET-TimeSeries24, where many IPs drift over the same calendar time. Measure false alarms after the attack and TPR against κ.
ESP32. Medians of about 9 ten-dimensional vectors per cycle is trivial.
ideas.why_new:
- WARDEN Theorem 15 and 2606.29841 Theorem 3.1 both prove that a single label-free stream cannot separate drift from poison. PCDD adds side information from other streams, which neither paper considers.
- CB-RBM's feature-context consistency is the nearest idea, but it is a frozen score on graph nodes, gates no updates, and leaves refresh-window poisoning open.
- No IoT or NIDS paper in the corpus uses peer consensus to accept updates: not AOC-IDS-style, ACORN-IDS, NetSight, OWAD or DriftXpert.
- It also turns the 2024 Sensors (ONLAD) warning, that the step creating a new instance can be hijacked, into a guarded mechanism: a new instance is initialised from peer context.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It reuses TOA's budget machinery and proof template, but swaps the known signature for 'not corroborated by peers'. It directly targets open problem 1 (attack hidden in genuine drift) and open problem 2 (new device, 34% false alarms), and it keeps the core/outer-ring rule as a local pre-filter before the proposed shift is sent to the gateway.

ideas.name: Rejected-Mode Subspace Budget (RMSB): a signature-free, multi-direction TOA
ideas.idea:
Replace TOA's single known signature with a threat subspace that the detector estimates online from what it rejects:
1. Keep a small memory, about 8 slots, of the modes of rejected traffic: an online k-means on alarmed points in PCA space.
2. A boiling-frog poisoner exists to make a persistently rejected target region (for example Mirai scan or ack traffic) acceptable, so that region shows up as a long-lived rejected mode.
3. Honest drift makes rejected mass migrate and then get absorbed. A mode is marked persistent if it stays rejected and does not move for longer than a time constant τ.
4. Ration the cumulative centre and spread movement projected onto the span of the persistent modes' directions with one shared budget, which defeats spreading the push across several directions. Apply the orthogonal part in full, as in TOA.
5. Add a global cap on cumulative displacement that neither consensus nor ring support explains, as a backstop against attackers who push along directions with no persistent mode.
Theory. A subspace version of the TOA bound: every trajectory that ends with the attack mode accepted must spend at least dist(c_0, attack mode)/B of budget. That gives a minimum time to compromise without any signature.
Attacks we must test against it:
- Su et al.-style and 2606.29841-style best responses that poison along the most sensitive direction orthogonal to the threat subspace.
- A contrastive multi-agent poisoner, in the style of the AAAI SuSS 2026 paper.
- A 'decoy mode' budget-exhaustion attack: the attacker plants fake persistent rejected modes to burn the shared budget. This is the freeze attack transplanted to RMSB, and it needs a per-mode cap.
ideas.why_new:
- TOA itself depends on a signature, and Rapid Poison (ICML 2026) shows an attacker can shape the captures a signature is learned from (the Omission Attack).
- 2606.29841's protected set comes from the data covariance, not from attack evidence, and is not a cumulative budget.
- The AAAI SuSS 2026 multi-agent poisoner shows that attackers spreading over diverse directions is realistic, and no defense in the corpus budgets a learned threat subspace.
- Using the detector's own rejection history as side information is absent from WARDEN, CDC, OWAD, RTTAD and ACORN-IDS.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It generalises TOA: one fixed direction becomes a learned subspace, and the existing minimum-time-to-compromise proof carries over with the projection operator changed. It closes the gap that TOA needs a known signature, and it partly answers open problem 1 whenever the attacker's goal region is a stable rejected mode, even when the push is hidden inside drift.

ideas.name: Budget-Ratcheted Conformal Reserve (BRCR): certified admission that cannot be frozen
ideas.idea:
Take WARDEN's certified admission (conformal p-values against a reserve, turned into e-values, then e-BH per batch) and remove its fatal design choice, the reserve that is never refreshed:
1. The reserve migrates. Each cycle, at most η·m reserve points can be replaced, and only by points that pass e-BH against the current reserve. Optionally they must also be in the peer-corroborated core, from the PCDD idea above.
2. This bounds how far the reserve can move per cycle in Wasserstein-1 distance, which gives two guarantees together:
   - Safety: WARDEN's per-batch bound on false admissions, combined with a minimum time to compromise the reserve of at least D/η.
   - Liveness: if honest drift moves at most η per cycle, the conformal FPR stays at or below α+ε for the whole stream.
3. Because there is no stop-learning switch, a freeze attack cannot work by construction. The worst an attacker can do is slow migration to the floor rate η, and that is bounded.
Paper experiments:
- Measure the admission kernel q(ρ) on N-BaIoT for naive, core/ring, TOA and BRCR, and show b ≥ 1 for naive (predicting the 10% attacker share at which it gets poisoned) and b < 1 for the others. This is the urn lens of the WARDEN paper applied to our detectors.
- Attack WARDEN and CDC as published defenses. Honest drift breaks the frozen WARDEN. Our own inference, untested: inflating CDC's Storey estimate π_up pushes its threshold toward +∞ and blinds the detector, which is the blinding counterpart of the freeze attack. This would be the first IDS evaluation of WARDEN/CDC.
ESP32: a reserve of 1500 points in 10 dimensions is about 60 KB of float32, and e-BH on batches of 64 is cheap.
ideas.why_new:
- WARDEN freezes its reference set and handles drift only through CDC, which costs 33-37% of oracle TPR.
- LID (SaTML 2026) freezes inside a fixed box.
- Robust conformal prediction sets (RPS, ICLR 2025) assume exchangeability and are offline.
- No paper in the corpus pairs a certified admission bound with a guaranteed rate of drift tracking, or treats the freeze attack as a liveness violation. WARDEN's own stated open problems, dependent windows and time-uniform guarantees via stopped e-BH, map directly onto bursty IoT traffic.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It turns the freeze-attack finding into a formal liveness property that our defense satisfies and published ones do not. It reuses TOA's rate-budget idea, applied to the reserve instead of the centre. It closes open problem 4 by attacking WARDEN/CDC, T2T rollback and LID as published baselines.

ideas.name: Randomised multi-timescale ring corroboration: hardening the gates against adaptive attacks
ideas.idea:
Harden the outer-ring and budget gates of all three mechanisms against the two adaptive attacks the corpus makes credible:
1. Window-blind poisoning. Hinder et al. (ESANN 2025) show that any windowed monitor has an exactly characterised blind set Adv(A), and that combining detectors shrinks it: Adv((A,B)) is a subset of Adv(A) ∩ Adv(B). So run the outer-ring and spread-growth tests over 2-3 window lengths that do not divide into each other (for example l, 1.37l and 7×24h aligned to the diurnal cycle). A centre shift is accepted only if every window agrees. Choose one window so that known diurnal periodicity falls in its blind set, which reduces false alarms from honest cyclic drift.
2. Pulsing timed to the budget refills (the NDSS 2026 attacker). Make the budget refill schedule and the subsampling of core and ring points secret and randomised per device, keyed by a device secret. This puts into practice the 'variability' defense suggested by the AHA poster (CCS 2025), so far only as an idea.
Evaluation:
- Build the provably window-blind poisoner with Hinder's Algorithm 2 (solve W_n v=0 for our windows), and a small PPO attacker over the history of accept and alarm feedback (NDSS 2026 style), with and without alarm observability.
- Report each defense's exploitability, meaning the best-response gain, and Wilson-CI sigmoid curves of detection threshold ε* (the Boiling Frog Threshold paper, arXiv 2603.08455), including its sinusoidal/zero-mean drift, which is invisible to that paper's prediction-error monitors.
ideas.why_new: No defense in the corpus has been tested against window-blind schedules or a learned pulsing attacker. Hinder et al. give the theory but no defense. HHNFM attacks fixed-parameter monitors, not learners. AHA proposes variability only conceptually, from the abstract. It is cheap, ESP32-friendly and stacks on top of the other three ideas.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It directly strengthens the signature-free core/outer-ring rule, which is the mechanism open problem 1 currently breaks. It replaces our hand-built 'hide in the core' attacker with principled adaptive attackers, raising the evaluation to A/A* standard.

lenses.lens: Threat model. Which attacks on self-updating, drift-tracking detectors the 2024-2026 corpus already covers, which it leaves unstudied, and which new attacks or evaluations would count as a contribution at the A/A* level. The focus is on attacks against the defense mechanism itself rather than against the base learner.
lenses.already_covered:
1) Gradual (boiling-frog) poisoning of a self-updating anomaly NIDS is named and claimed. Adversarial Habituation Attack (CCS 2025 poster; I have only the abstract) shows it against a VAE/Suricata NIDS and frames it as habituation, creeping normality and alert fatigue. Self-Poisoning/WARDEN (arXiv 2607.21673) owns the threshold theory of self-poisoning: Polya urn, slope b acting as a reproduction number, critical pi_c. Theory of CL Against Poisoning (arXiv 2606.29841, Thm 3.1) proves that no regularized learner converges under frequent shifted poison, and its 1-D proof is an EMA mean dragged by a bias, which is exactly our centroid. Neither paper is about IoT or networks, and neither studies a deliberate gradual attacker on a centre plus spread.
2) Deliberately inducing drift against an adaptive NIDS is covered by Contrastive Adversarial Agents (AAAI SuSS 2026). It uses RL evasion agents against a supervised XGBoost NIDS that is retrained, and it is not label-free self-labelling poisoning.
3) Attacks that hide drift from window-based monitors: Adversarial Attacks for Drift Detection (ESANN 2025) gives closed-form invisible schedules (periodic, W_n v = 0). Boiling Frog Threshold (arXiv 2603.08455) shows zero-mean sinusoidal drift is invisible to frozen prediction-error monitors. Empirical Evasion/Poisoning vs Malware Drift Detection (arXiv 2608.03642) attacks CADE and Transcendent with one-shot clean-label poison and finds that crowding near the centroid pushes poison outward.
4) Test-time adaptation poisoning by a grey-box surrogate attacker: Su et al. (ICLR 2025) match feature moments so poison looks clean, and find that EMA and entropy filtering defend well. Their attack is per batch, on images, and is not slow.
5) Poisoning the adaptation pipeline of a learned defense: Rapid Poison (ICML 2026). It includes poisoning that induces false positives (up to 100% FPR on a target domain) through shortcut learning, which is the closest published idea of "make the defender raise false alarms on purpose". Replay-buffer label flipping and backdoors in a continual IDS: ReplayIDS (arXiv 2608.04602), which assumes write access. That paper mentions eviction attacks in only one line.
6) Hijacking a drift-adaptation mechanism on an on-device learner: Sensors 2024 (ONLAD). An acoustic sensor injection makes the centroid drift trigger create a poison model instance. The attack is abrupt and physical, and the paper offers no defense.
7) Adaptive RL attackers against stateful network monitors: Heavy-Hitter games (NDSS 2026). The learned attacker times on/off pulses to the monitor's refresh and eviction windows, works zero-shot through a surrogate, and is studied with and without feedback. This is evasion of fixed-parameter monitors, not poisoning.
8) Certified point-count robustness: RPS (ICLR 2025) notes in passing that deleting calibration points is a DoS on set construction, and gives a two-sided reliability definition.
lenses.open_gaps:
(a) The freeze attack, where an attacker deliberately trips a suspicion, rollback or gating rule so the defender stops adapting and honest drift then floods false alarms, appears in no corpus paper. Several published defenses have the vulnerable structure but never treat it as an attack surface:
- T2T rollback discards the honest neighbouring task too (2606.29841).
- WARDEN's dictionary "starves" under tail mimicry (2607.21673). This is harmless there only because that channel adds no power.
- DriftXpert adapts only when OR > T (2609.08623).
- OWAD and NetSight adapt only on a permutation-test shift (NDSS 2023; 2508.15100).
- LID projection clamps updates and Algorithm 1 stops once the intersection is empty (SaTML 2026, 2512.01899).
- RTTAD stops "when no sufficient samples remain" (2605.10242).
- Entropy-threshold filtering (Su et al.) has the same structure.
Rapid Poison induces false positives through what is learned, not through stopping learning.
(b) Blinding the label-free calibrator is unstudied: inflating CDC's Storey contamination estimate until the threshold reaches +infinity (2607.21673), or inflating variance through spread or threshold refreshes (MCM 2601.03957 shows influence on variance inflation is unbounded; ACORN-IDS and DriftXpert use mean + k*SD; CB-RBM refreshes a 95th-percentile threshold).
(c) Churn attacks on networks are unstudied. Join-time (trust-on-first-use) poisoning of a new per-device detector, hiding poison inside the real shift caused by a device joining, and forced resets through identity churn have no network or IDS treatment. The only near case is the physical instance-spawn hijack in Sensors 2024.
(d) Adaptive attacks against direction-aware or evidence-gated defenses are unstudied: poisoning the signature channel (an Omission-style attack from Rapid Poison, applied to TOA's signature), direction-diverse poisoning (AAAI SuSS 2026, 2606.29841's top-singular-direction attacker), pulses timed to the budget refill (NDSS 2026), and schedules provably invisible to the outer-ring windows (ESANN 2025).
(e) No paper measures the robustness/plasticity trade-off as a two-sided attack surface. Su et al. never measure what EMA costs under honest drift, and Rapid Poison names a three-sided dilemma but only attacks one side.
Caveats: three items are not fully checked. The full text of AHA (which may discuss inducing alert fatigue) is unread. Pasikhani et al. 2026 TDSC (an RL wear-out attacker) is unverified. "The Price of Self-Calibration" (arXiv 2609.23254, which describes "manufactured blind sets" in adaptive monitoring) was checked only at the abstract level. All three must be read before claiming (a) or (b) as first.

ideas.name: Gate-Tripping (Freeze) Attacks on Published Drift-Gated Defenses, with a Both-Horns Theorem
ideas.idea:
Turn the freeze attack from a weakness of our own baselines into a general attack class with a formal definition, a small theorem and a cross-defense evaluation.

Definition. Treat any defense as an update u_t = g(S_t) * Delta_t. Here S_t is a suspicion statistic computed partly from traffic the attacker controls, and g is non-increasing in S_t (it covers rollback, gating, clamping, entropy filtering and stopping rules). Following RPS (ICLR 2025), split reliability into two sides. Detection reliability means the attacker cannot get attack traffic accepted. False-alarm reliability means the attacker cannot get honest traffic flagged.

Theorem sketch. Suppose honest drift has velocity v and the spread is s. Then an attacker who keeps S_t above the gate for a time tau, at a traffic cost c(tau), causes post-departure false alarms that grow with v*tau/s. Combine this with Theorem 15 of 2607.21673 (in 1-D, drift and contamination cannot be told apart without labels) and Theorem 3.1 of 2606.29841. The result is a 'both horns' statement: a label-free defense either absorbs, which leaves it open to boiling-frog poisoning, or refuses, which leaves it open to the freeze attack. An attacker can choose which horn to exploit.

Evaluation. Re-implement six published gating mechanisms on top of our PCA-centroid detector, on N-BaIoT plus real long-run drift (Kyoto/AnoShift as used by OWAD and NetSight, and CESNET-TimeSeries24):
- T2T rollback (2606.29841): d_t over centroid second differences, rolling back when it exceeds 2.5x the mean of the last 5 scores.
- The DriftXpert OR > T trigger (code is public).
- An OWAD permutation-test gate (MIT code ships a KitNET demo), in both human-labelled and self-labelled modes.
- An LID box projection (SaTML 2026), which is exact and cheap for (c, s).
- An RTTAD-style GMM-confidence selection and stopping rule.
- An EATA-style entropy-threshold filter (from Su et al.).
For each one, design the cheapest trip signal, such as sparse spikes, out-of-range bursts, or traffic that inflates outliers just above T. Report:
- the freeze duty cycle achieved per unit of attacker traffic;
- false alarms during and after the attacker leaves, and how long they persist;
- alerts per device per hour (citing the alert-fatigue survey ACM CSUR 2025 that AHA references);
- an intransigence metric in the ReplayIDS style.
TOA and the signature-free method form the contrast group, because they never stop adapting in the orthogonal direction.
ideas.why_new: The open_gaps list above checks every corpus paper with a stop-learning or rollback gate: none treats the gate as an attack surface. WARDEN's 'dictionary starves' and Phenomenon 2 (frozen calibration giving 1.94x FPR) come closest, but they are a harmless channel and natural staleness respectively. Rapid Poison induces false positives through shortcut learning, not by stopping adaptation. Su et al. never measure what their recommended EMA or entropy defenses cost under honest drift. This idea also directly closes our open problem 4: the freeze attack would be shown against 4-6 published defenses, not only our baselines.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It extends our measured freeze result (85-87% false alarms after the attacker leaves) and reuses our N-BaIoT pipeline, the modelled poisoner and the TOA and signature-free implementations as the defenses that survive.

ideas.name: Calibration-Blinding and Ring-Inflation Attacks (the dual of the freeze attack)
ideas.idea:
This is a second new attack class aimed at label-free threshold calibration and spread gates. The freeze attack stops learning. This attack makes the defense learn a looser boundary on purpose, using traffic that looks benign.

Three concrete instances:
(1) CDC blinding (2607.21673). CDC sets its threshold at quantile level 1 - alpha(1 - pi_up) + eps_n. Flood with benign-looking points that are slightly off-distribution, giving low conformal p-values with no attack payload. This inflates the Storey estimate pi_up until the level exceeds 1 and the threshold becomes +infinity. Measure how long CDC stays blind and at what attacker share.
(2) Ring-inflation against our own signature-free method. Our method allows spread growth only if the outer ring really gets busier. Feed isotropic or attack-orthogonal benign traffic into the outer ring so that spread growth is legitimately approved, then send the real attack inside the widened spread. This turns our evidence gate into a confused deputy. MCM (2601.03957) supports why this works: influence is unbounded for variance inflation.
(3) Variance and percentile refresh poisoning against mean + k*SD or quantile thresholds: ACORN-IDS (mean + 2SD), DriftXpert (mean + alpha*std), and CB-RBM's 95th-percentile label-free refresh.

Defense contribution. Extend TOA's budget from the centre to the spread. Ration growth of spread along the signature direction, or along a direction-weighted Mahalanobis radius, so that ring inflation only helps the attacker in directions that do not matter for detection. Prove a minimum time to blind that mirrors our minimum time to compromise. Report TPR against WARDEN's kappa ceiling, alpha/(pi + alpha(1-pi)), to show where direction information beats the label-free bound.
ideas.why_new: The CDC paper tests only feature-space tail mimicry, which starves its dictionary, never threshold inflation. ACORN-IDS, DriftXpert and CB-RBM analyse no poisoning of the refresh window (CB-RBM's contamination test covers only training time). The MCM paper derives unbounded variance influence but uses non-adaptive i.i.d. contamination. No corpus paper attacks a spread or variance gate with traffic that is benign in content. One novelty risk: arXiv 2609.23254 ('manufactured blind sets' in self-calibrating trackers) was read only at the abstract level and must be read in full first.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It stress-tests the third rule of our signature-free method (spread growth only if the outer ring gets busier). It extends TOA's direction budget from centre moves to spread moves. It reuses the N-BaIoT/Mirai setup and the adaptive core-hiding attacker as the starting point.

ideas.name: Churn-Exploiting Attacks: Join-Time Poisoning, Churn Camouflage, and Reset Flooding
ideas.idea:
We already found that a device joining breaks a single detector (34% false alarms), which points toward per-device detectors. Per-device detectors bring a new lifecycle attack surface, and we can define three attacks on it.
(1) Join-time (trust-on-first-use) poisoning. A compromised or spoofed device (MAC/IP) joins and sends poison-shaped 'normal' traffic during the warm-up of its new detector. The centroid starts out compromised, with no boiling needed. Measure the minimum warm-up poison share that makes later Mirai scan/ack/syn traffic be accepted.
(2) Churn camouflage. Time boiling-frog poison to coincide with legitimate joins, firmware updates or departures, when every defense must loosen. This is a concrete, measurable version of our open problem 1 (attack hidden inside genuine drift), with real join shifts taken from N-BaIoT's 9 devices.
(3) Reset or spawn flooding. Rotate identities, or trigger the 'new device' and 'new instance' rule repeatedly, so detectors keep re-initialising. This forces permanent warm-up (a freeze-like denial) or spawns poison instances, the network analogue of the ONLAD hijack (Sensors 2024).

Defenses to test:
- Peer-context bootstrap: a new device starts from the prior of its device type and must agree with the context of its peers, in the style of CB-RBM's feature-context consistency.
- A rate limit on instance creation.
- Applying TOA's signature budget and the outer-ring check to the initial centre of a new instance relative to that prior.
- The MS-PCA knockoff test (2605.25460) to flag a new mean-shift subpopulation before the PCA basis is refit.

Metrics: per-device versus bystander false alarms (blast radius, following Rapid Poison's targeted vs collateral reporting), and time from join to compromise.
ideas.why_new: The only corpus work that touches model-instance lifecycle is Sensors 2024. It uses abrupt, physical acoustic injection on a vibration sensor, has no defense, and has no network or IDS setting. OWAD's SCADA deployment uses per-device detectors but has no adversary. MS-PCA notes that a new subpopulation shows up as a spectral spike but has no attacker. The TinyML ODL survey (2605.31226) contains no security content at all. No corpus paper treats device churn (join, leave, identity rotation) as a poisoning or denial vector in IoT intrusion detection.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It turns our open problem 2 (34% false alarms on a device join) from a limitation into a threat class plus a defense. It reuses the per-device N-BaIoT captures and both of our update rules. It sets up the ESP32 story, where each node runs its own small detector.

ideas.name: Defense-Aware Adaptive Attacker Suite against TOA and the Signature-Free Method
ideas.idea:
A/A* reviewers will ask how our defenses hold up against an attacker who knows them. We should pre-empt that with a fixed suite of named adaptive attacks, each traced to a corpus paper, crossed with three levels of attacker knowledge.

Attacks:
(a) Signature-channel poisoning. Signatures are refreshed from captured attacks, so the attacker shapes what we capture (an Omission-style attack, Rapid Poison ICML 2026) until the learned signature direction is orthogonal to the true poison direction. Then TOA applies the poison in full as 'everything else'. Compare with the signature-free method, which should be immune.
(b) Direction-diverse poisoning. Several poisoners trained with the contrastive reward from AAAI SuSS 2026 spread their displacement across mutually dissimilar directions orthogonal to the signature. Also include an attacker along the top singular direction of the defender's sensitivity, from 2606.29841.
(c) Pulsing timed to the budget refill: on/off poison synchronised to TOA's slow-budget refill and to the outer-ring window, as the NDSS 2026 learned attacker did with eviction windows.
(d) Window-adversarial schedules. Solve W_n v = 0 over our update and ring windows (ESANN 2025, Algorithm 2), and add zero-mean sinusoidal spread ratcheting (2603.08455).
(e) Core-crowding and moment-matching: poison that matches the first two moments of clean traffic (Su et al.'s feature-consistency term), checked against the observation in 2608.03642 that a crowded core pushes poison outward.
(f) A timing-only (IAT) poison restricted to feature changes realisable by adding traffic (ReplayIDS; the add-only constraint from 2608.03642).

Knowledge levels: white-box; grey-box with a surrogate rebuilt from observed accept/alarm or drop feedback (Su et al.); and blind. Include an observability ablation as in NDSS 2026.

Also train one PPO attacker over (share, direction, magnitude, timing) as a learned worst case.

Report:
- exploitability per defense (best-response gain in cycles-to-compromise and in FPR, NDSS-style);
- a 'boiling-frog threshold' eps* sigmoid with Wilson CIs over a log-grid of poison rates, for naive, freezing, TOA and signature-free (2603.08455 protocol);
- detection TPR against WARDEN's kappa ceiling.
Where the minimum time to compromise breaks (likely under (a) and (b)), propose a subspace budget: the signature span plus attacker prototypes estimated online, and/or a cap on cumulative displacement that drift does not explain. Prove the new bound.
ideas.why_new: No corpus paper evaluates an attacker against a direction-budgeted or evidence-gated update rule, because no corpus paper proposes such a rule. 2606.29841's robust feature defense uses per-eigendirection penalties, and its attacker is matched to that defense, not to a signature split. Each attack primitive exists separately in a different domain (LLM safety, CICIDS evasion, heavy-hitter monitors, drift monitors, image TTA). Combining them into an adaptive evaluation of an on-device IoT poisoning defense is new, and attack (a) specifically targets TOA's assumption that the signature is trustworthy.
ideas.builds_on_our_work: It generalises our single adaptive attacker that hides poison in the core into a full threat matrix. It tests TOA's provable minimum time to compromise under conditions its proof does not currently cover. It produces the theory-versus-measurement figure the paper needs, using our existing N-BaIoT/Mirai harness and modelled poisoner.

lenses.lens: IoT structure servers lack. An IoT detector is never alone: it has a fleet of near-identical peers, a physical body (radio, power draw), firmware and provisioning events that are signed and observable, and very regular periodic behaviour. Every idea below uses one of these as a second witness, i.e. side information outside the single unlabelled stream. That is exactly what the corpus says a self-learner needs. Theorem 15 of the WARDEN/CDC paper (arXiv 2607.21673) proves that from one 1-D label-free stream, drift and contamination cannot be told apart. Theorem 3.1 of "Theory of Continual Learning Against Data Poisoning" (arXiv 2606.29841) proves that no regularised learner beats frequent shifted poison. Our open problem 1 (poison hidden in strong genuine drift) is very likely an instance of those theorems, so the way out is extra information, not a cleverer one-stream rule.
lenses.already_covered:
- **Self-poisoning theory and certified admission for one stream:** WARDEN/CDC (arXiv 2607.21673). It has a frozen reserve, e-BH admission, the Polya-urn threshold law, and the two-world impossibility. No IoT, and no gradual attacker shifting the reference.
- **Impossibility for frequent shifted poison; per-eigendirection damping; T2T rollback:** arXiv 2606.29841. This is the closest thing to TOA, but its directions come from covariance, not from a threat, and it has no time-to-compromise bound.
- **Neighbour feature-context consistency as a drift-invariant score:** CB-RBM (NeurIPS 2026, arXiv 2610.16694). It works on graph fraud with a frozen model and never analyses poisoning of the refresh step.
- **Hash-partitioned majority voting for certified poisoning robustness:** RPS (ICLR 2025). It is i.i.d., offline and supervised.
- **Per-device detectors in a real SCADA deployment:** OWAD (NDSS 2023). Each device detector is independent, with no cross-device evidence, and a human labels every round.
- **Physical attack on an on-device learner:** Sensors 2024 (s24196416). Acoustic injection hijacks ONLAD's drift-triggered instance spawning, and no defence is given.
- **Blind schedules for window-based drift monitors:** ESANN 2025 (arXiv 2411.16591). It also shows that combining windows shrinks the blind set.
- **Zero-mean oscillating drift is invisible to prediction-error monitors:** Boiling Frog Threshold (arXiv 2603.08455).
- **Drift-gated stop-start adapters:** DriftXpert (arXiv 2609.08623) and NetSight (arXiv 2508.15100). Both are freeze-attack targets.
- **No security at all for on-device learning:** the TinyML ODL survey (arXiv 2605.31226) covers about 70 MCU on-device-learning works, and none of them has a poisoning model or ESP32.
- **What nobody in the corpus does:** use peers, physical-layer signals, signed device events or device periodicity as evidence that decides what a self-learning detector may absorb.
lenses.open_gaps:
- **Problem (1), attack inside strong genuine drift:** no single-stream fix exists, by Theorem 15 of 2607.21673 and Theorem 3.1 of 2606.29841. Side information is required, and no paper supplies it for IoT.
- **Problem (2), a new device joining (34% false alarms):** OWAD runs per-device detectors but bootstraps each one alone. The Sensors 2024 paper shows that automatic instance spawning is itself a hijack vector. Nobody gives a safe bootstrap.
- **Problem (3), ESP32:** the ODL survey says no paper reports energy per learning event on ESP32-class hardware, and none reports the cost of a security mechanism. Both are open.
- **Problem (4), freeze attack only on our own baselines:** published stop-start or gated adapters (DriftXpert's OR>T trigger, NetSight's permutation-test gate, WARDEN's frozen reserve, the LID projection in "Provably Safe Model Updates" from SaTML 2026) have never been attacked with the freeze attack.
- **Cross-device and physical evidence as admission control for self-learning:** absent from the corpus. The neighbouring literatures (Byzantine-robust federated aggregation, RF and power fingerprinting, MUD profiles) are NOT in the corpus and must be checked before claiming novelty.

ideas.name: Fleet-Orthogonal Adaptation (FOA): peers as the drift witness, a signature-free TOA
ideas.idea:
Each device keeps its own centroid detector. Every cycle it gossips its proposed centre delta d_i, which is about 10 floats in PCA space, over ESP-NOW or through the gateway. Each device splits its update into two parts. The peer-corroborated component (projection onto the robust consensus of the peers' deltas, a coordinate-wise median or geometric median over n peers of the same model or role) is applied in full. The idiosyncratic remainder, which no peer backs, is rationed by TOA's slow cumulative budget. The rule mirrors TOA, with the known attack signature replaced by 'everything the fleet does not agree on'. Honest drift is mostly common-mode: a firmware or cloud-endpoint change, the time of day, a new router, a shift in network load. So honest drift flows through freely and nothing freezes. A boiling-frog poisoner that controls f < n/2 devices can only move a device through the budgeted channel. The guarantee is that time to compromise is at least (distance to signature) / (budget rate) unless the attacker controls a majority of the peer group, which gives a provable bound without a signature.

The same machinery fixes the new-device problem (open problem 2). A device that joins starts from the peer-median centroid and spread instead of from zero, and its first cycles run under the idiosyncratic budget.

Planned experiments:
- **(a) N-BaIoT same-model pairs:** Provision PT_737E/PT_838 and SimpleHome XCS7_1002/1003 (pairs from dataset knowledge, verify). Inject the same honest drift into both and the poison into one, sweep attacker share, and compare against TOA, the signature-free core/ring method and naive.
- **(b) ESP32 fleet:** 4-6 boards running identical telemetry firmware. A real OTA update or endpoint change gives true common-mode drift, while a laptop poisons one board.
- **(c) Adversary sweep:** f = 0..n compromised peers, plus a Sybil attacker that spoofs peer gossip. Mitigate the Sybil with gossip that carries per-device MAC tags keyed at provisioning.
- **(d) Honest idiosyncratic drift:** one device's usage changes alone. Report the extra false alarms it pays as the cost of the budget, using a Combined Score = TPR x stability as in CB-RBM.

Seven-week plan:
- **Weeks 1-2:** simulation and theory.
- **Weeks 3-4:** N-BaIoT experiments.
- **Weeks 5-6:** ESP32 fleet run.
- **Week 7:** write-up.
ideas.why_new:
- **Single-stream methods:** WARDEN/CDC (2607.21673) and CL-poisoning theory (2606.29841) prove these hit a ceiling. Neither uses a second stream. Peer streams are precisely the side information that breaks the two-world construction of Theorem 15: a drifted World A is common-mode, while a contaminated World B is not. A short corollary showing this is a candidate theorem for us.
- **CB-RBM (NeurIPS 2026):** uses neighbour context to make the score drift-invariant, then freezes the model. It never uses neighbours to gate updates, never studies poisoning, and works on graph fraud, not IoT.
- **RPS (ICLR 2025):** partitions offline i.i.d. data and votes.
- **OWAD:** runs per-device detectors with no cross-device evidence.
- **Arxiv 2606.29841:** damps covariance eigendirections, not peer-uncorroborated directions.
- **Nearest outside literature, which MUST be checked:** Byzantine-robust federated aggregation (Krum, trimmed mean, median) and federated IoT IDS such as DIoT (ICDCS 2019, from memory). The difference to argue: those aggregate a shared model, whereas FOA keeps per-device models and uses the fleet only as a witness to split each device's own update, with a time-to-compromise bound and a freeze-attack analysis.
ideas.builds_on_our_work:
- It directly generalises TOA: the same split-and-budget proof structure, with the signature subspace replaced by the peer-uncorroborated subspace.
- It answers open problem 1 by turning the impossibility result into a requirement for side information.
- It answers open problem 2 with the peer-prior bootstrap.
- It gives the ESP32 work (open problem 3) a real multi-board purpose.
- It reuses the existing sim_toa.py / nbaiot_check.py pipeline: add a second device stream and a median-of-deltas step.

ideas.name: Physical-witness admission: learn only from traffic whose radio and power signals vouch for it
ideas.idea:
A network-side poisoner has to put bytes on the air, and an IoT device's physical layer is cheap to observe from an ESP32, so self-labelling admission can use two physical witnesses.

- **W1, RF provenance:** an ESP32 sniffer in promiscuous mode (or the device itself, via ESP32 CSI) records RSSI and CSI per frame. A small per-source profile (median and MAD of RSSI, plus a few CSI amplitude bins) is learned at provisioning. A frame enters the training pool only if its physical fingerprint matches the claimed source. The detector still scores every frame; only learning is restricted. Spoofed-source poison sent from the attacker's own box is then never learned from.
- **W2, energy consistency:** an INA219 current sensor (about $3) sits on an ESP32 node acting as the IoT device. Radio TX energy per cycle must agree with bytes-out per cycle according to a calibrated linear model. Traffic the device did not actually emit, or emitted under a hidden extra workload, breaks the energy-bytes relation. A centre shift is accepted only if the energy channel shows a consistent change.

The novelty claim is not detection by power or RF, which already exists. It is provenance-gated self-learning: physical consistency decides what the learner may absorb, and the attacker must now forge two independent physical channels to poison.

Planned experiments:
- **(a) Spoofing poisoner:** a laptop or second ESP32 injects Kitsune-visible traffic with the victim's MAC from 1-5 m away. Measure the admission rate of poison against honest frames, and the resulting time to compromise against naive, TOA and core/ring.
- **(b) On-device poisoner:** malicious code on the node itself emits the boiling-frog traffic. Here RF provenance passes, so measure how far the energy witness alone constrains it.
- **(c) Honest physical drift:** move the device, open doors, add people. Measure how often the witness wrongly rejects honest traffic, because that is the freeze risk of this gate. If the RF profile itself follows drift slowly through the core/ring rule, report that it does.
- **(d) Run the freeze attack against the witness itself:** RF jamming that makes all frames fail the provenance check, to see whether learning stalls. The mitigation: when witness failures become widespread, fall back to the budgeted channel instead of freezing.
ideas.why_new:
- **The corpus has the reverse direction only:** the Sensors 2024 paper uses a physical attack (acoustic injection) to poison an on-device learner, and offers no defence. Nobody in the corpus uses physical signals to defend a self-learner.
- **Prior work treats admission as a statistical problem:** WARDEN admits by conformal p-values against a frozen reserve, and RTTAD (arXiv 2605.10242) and NetSight admit by score confidence. Both are inside the single stream that Theorem 15 limits.
- **The TinyML ODL survey (2605.31226)** contains no security mechanism of any kind.
- **Must be checked outside the corpus (from memory, unverified):** RSSI/CSI-based spoofing detection (e.g. Chen et al. 2007), power-side-channel malware detection for embedded devices (e.g. WattsUpDoc 2013), and RF fingerprinting for IoT authentication. The difference to argue: those papers detect; we use physical consistency to gate what a drifting self-learner absorbs, and we measure time to compromise and the freeze side effect.
ideas.builds_on_our_work:
- It is a third admission layer in front of the existing core/ring and TOA update rules, so the existing code stays and the new part is an admission mask.
- It uses exactly the hardware we have (ESP32, plus one INA219 and a second ESP32 as sniffer).
- It produces the ESP32 results (open problem 3) with the energy-per-learning-event reporting the ODL survey says is missing.
- It extends the freeze-attack finding to a new gate type, i.e. jamming as a freeze trigger.

ideas.name: Event-licensed adaptation: signed firmware and provisioning events unlock the learning budget
ideas.idea:
Most large, legitimate changes in IoT behaviour come from discrete, observable, authenticable events: an OTA firmware update (signed images and secure boot on the ESP32), a configuration push, a device joining through provisioning, or a MUD profile change (RFC 8520). Idea: adaptation has two rates.

- **Background rate:** the TOA or FOA slow budget, the default all the time.
- **Licensed rate:** a large, time-limited budget unlocked only by a cryptographically verified event token. Example: the OTA handler on the ESP32 emits a token signed with the firmware signing key, valid for K cycles. During the licence window the detector re-fits quickly on the core/ring-filtered traffic, scoped to the event's device.

The network attacker cannot mint licences, so the fast path is closed to it. Honest step drift then costs a few cycles of false alarms instead of a freeze. New devices (open problem 2) are spawned only by a provisioning licence. That closes the hijack in the Sensors 2024 paper, where any abrupt drift past a threshold spawns a new, poisoned model instance.

Planned experiments:
- **(a) ESP32 nodes doing real signed OTA updates** that change telemetry rate and endpoints. Compare false alarms after the update with and without a licence, and against freezing baselines.
- **(b) Attacks:** an attacker who mimics an update's traffic signature without a licence, i.e. creeping normality, should gain nothing beyond the background budget. An attacker who times poison inside a genuine licence window is bounded by the window length K times the licensed rate, and the attacker's achievable displacement should be reported as a function of K.
- **(c) Freeze attack on published stop-start adapters:** re-implement DriftXpert's OR>T trigger (its code is public) and the box-intersection LID from "Provably Safe Model Updates". Show that each freezes under honest step drift or can be tripped, and that licensing fixes the step-drift case. This addresses open problem 4.
ideas.why_new:
- **"Provably Safe Model Updates" (SaTML 2026)** needs a lookahead buffer, i.e. advance knowledge of which directions the next task must move in, to recover plasticity (Task-2 accuracy 0.20 to 0.73). A signed device event is a trustworthy, IoT-native source of that lookahead, which nobody in the corpus uses.
- **The corpus gates adaptation only on statistics:** DriftXpert and NetSight on drift tests, OWAD on a human labeller. Statistics are what the freeze attack trips and what blind schedules evade: ESANN 2025 shows that window-based monitors have provably invisible attack schedules.
- **The Sensors 2024 paper** exposes unauthenticated instance spawning and leaves the defence to future work.
- **Must be checked outside the corpus (from memory):** MUD-based IoT anomaly detection (e.g. Hamza et al. 2018) and any work that ties IDS retraining to firmware or update events. The difference to argue: we use events to license the rate of a self-learner, inside a time-to-compromise analysis.
ideas.builds_on_our_work:
- It reuses the TOA budget as the background rate, so the minimum-time-to-compromise proof carries over, with one added term for licence windows (K times the licensed rate).
- It turns the freeze-attack finding into a design rule: never stop learning on suspicion; instead, adapt fast only on authenticated evidence and slowly otherwise.
- It gives a clean way to test the freeze attack on published defences (DriftXpert, LID), closing open problem 4.
- The ESP32 OTA plus secure-boot work is standard ESP-IDF, so it is feasible in about 2 weeks.

ideas.name: Phase-locked self-learning for periodic devices (with multi-period blind-set shrinking)
ideas.idea:
IoT devices are extremely regular: heartbeats every T seconds, polling cycles, daily routines. The device estimates its dominant period on-device (autocorrelation of per-second packet and byte counts, which is cheap) and keeps P phase-bin centroids and spreads instead of one. Each self-learning update compares a bin only with the same phase in earlier periods, i.e. seasonal differencing. Honest periodic variation then stops looking like drift at all. That removes much of the honest-drift pressure that makes freezing costly and that poison hides inside (open problem 1).

Two results from the corpus set the attack surface:
- **ESANN 2025 (arXiv 2411.16591):** poison that is l-periodic in the window length is provably invisible to a sliding-window check. So the outer-ring check runs over two windows of incommensurate length (the device period and about 1.37 times it); the theorem says Adv(A,B) is a subset of Adv(A) ∩ Adv(B).
- **Boiling Frog Threshold (arXiv 2603.08455):** zero-mean oscillating drift is invisible. So we test an oscillating poisoner that ratchets the spread, against per-phase spread tracking.

All of this is a handful of P x 10-float centroids, which fits easily on an ESP32.

Planned experiments:
- **(a) CESNET-TimeSeries24:** 40 weeks of real periodic per-IP series (in our known prior work). Inject a boiling-frog ramp and the freeze attack, and compare a single centroid against phase-locked centroids, measuring false alarms after the freeze and time to compromise.
- **(b) ESP32 nodes with real periodic telemetry.**
- **(c) Adversarial schedules:** solve W_n v = 0 (ESANN Algorithm 2) against our own windows and report the blind set with single versus multi-period windows.
ideas.why_new:
- **ESANN 2025** gives the blind-schedule theory, but it covers monitors only, with no learner, no poisoning and no IoT. Its water-network example only picks one window to hide benign cycles.
- **The Boiling Frog Threshold paper** shows oscillation blindness for frozen detectors in MuJoCo and proposes no defence.
- **RTTAD and ACORN-IDS (arXiv 2602.07291)** use synthetic K-Means drift splits with no temporal periodicity.
- **The dataset survey (Computers & Security 2025)** says long-term cyclostationary NID datasets are missing and that no documented public concept-drift NID dataset existed through 2023.
- **No corpus paper** conditions a self-learner's updates on the device's own periodic phase, or uses multi-period windows to provably shrink the poisoner's blind set.
- **Risk:** seasonal per-phase anomaly baselines exist widely in operations monitoring, which is outside the corpus and must be checked. The novelty claim must rest on the adversarial blind-set analysis, not on the binning.
ideas.builds_on_our_work:
- It is a drop-in change to the centre + spread state (one per phase bin), so TOA and core/ring apply per bin unchanged.
- It gives a principled adaptive attacker (the W_n v = 0 solver) to stress-test our methods, answering a likely reviewer request.
- It moves evaluation onto CESNET-TimeSeries24, which we already list, adding a second real dataset with genuine long-term drift.
- Best treated as a lighter fourth contribution or ablation alongside FOA, not a separate paper.

candidates.name: Fleet-Orthogonal Adaptation (FOA): peers as the drift witness, a signature-free TOA
candidates.one_line: Each IoT device keeps its own centroid detector. The part of its update that a robust peer consensus backs is applied in full, and only the peer-unexplained remainder goes through TOA's slow budget. This escapes the single-stream impossibility results and fixes the new-device problem.
candidates.mechanism:
Setup. Device i keeps (c_i, s_i) in a fixed PCA-10 space, with the basis frozen after a clean warm-up. Every cycle t:

1. Local proposal. The existing core/outer-ring rule produces a filtered proposed shift Delta_i.
2. Gossip. Device i sends Delta_i (10 float32) plus an HMAC keyed at provisioning, over ESP-NOW or via the gateway.
3. Peer consensus. Compute m_t = geometric median (Weiszfeld, 10 iterations) of {Delta_j : j in P(i)}. The peer group P(i) is chosen to be VULNERABILITY-DIVERSE: devices sharing the network role and gateway but differing in vendor or firmware. Network-level drift (ISP, gateway, diurnal, campus calendar) is then common-mode, while a single-exploit botnet campaign is not.
4. Split. The common part is a_i = g_i * m_t, where g_i is a scalar per-device gain fitted during warm-up (devices see different traffic volumes). The residual is r_i = Delta_i - a_i.
5. Update. c_i += a_i + Budget(r_i). Budget enforces ||sum_{tau<=t} r_applied|| <= B0 + B*t, i.e. TOA's cumulative-budget code with the signature projector replaced by 'residual after consensus'. Spread growth is split the same way: the peer-median ring-occupancy ratio is applied in full, and the device-specific excess is budgeted.
6. Join. A new device starts from (median of peer c, median of peer s) and runs its first K cycles under the residual budget only. That bounds join-time poisoning to B0 + K*B, and addresses the 34% false-alarm result.

Theorem targets.
(T1) Safety. If the attacker controls at most f < |P|/2 peer streams plus the victim's stream, the geometric median has breakdown point 1/2, so ||m_t - m_t^honest|| <= C*sigma_idio. Time to compromise is then at least (d(c_0, A) - r_acc) / (B + g*C*sigma_idio). This is TOA's bound without a signature.
(T2) Escape from the impossibility. WARDEN's two-world construction fails with peers: World A drift is common-mode, while World B contamination appears on at most f streams. A peer-aware rule therefore reaches FPR <= alpha in A with TPR -> 1 in B as |P| grows, provided the honest idiosyncratic drift rate is below B. We state this as a corollary of their Theorem 15.
(T3) Liveness. Honest drift with common part mu_t and idiosyncratic rate <= B is tracked with lag <= C*sigma_idio/B.

Failure boundary, reported honestly: correlated compromise of a majority of the peer group, i.e. f >= |P|/2.
candidates.why_new:
- Both impossibility results in the corpus (WARDEN Theorem 15 and 2606.29841 Theorem 3.1) are single-stream. Neither considers a second, concurrently drifting stream as side information, and FOA is exactly that.
- CB-RBM (NeurIPS 2026) uses neighbour feature-context only as a frozen, drift-invariant score on graphs. It never gates updates and never studies poisoning of its refresh step.
- OWAD runs per-device detectors in SCADA but gives them no cross-device evidence and uses a human labeller.
- RPS partitions and votes offline over i.i.d. data.

candidates.name: Gate-Tripping and Calibration-Blinding: the two-horned attack class on drift-gated defences, with a safety-plus-liveness contract
candidates.one_line: Formalise the freeze attack and its dual (blinding a label-free calibrator) as attacks on any suspicion-gated self-learner, prove that no single-stream gate escapes both poisoning and freezing, and break six published defences on IoT traffic.
candidates.mechanism:
Model. Any adaptive defence is written as u_t = g(S_t) * Delta_t. S_t is a suspicion statistic partly computed from attacker-controlled traffic, and g is non-increasing; this covers rollback, gating, clamping, entropy filtering and stopping rules.

Two-sided contract (detection and false-alarm reliability in the sense of RPS):
- SAFETY(rho, T): at attacker share <= rho, attack traffic is not accepted before T cycles.
- LIVENESS(v, alpha, L): for honest drift of speed <= v, FPR <= alpha + eps, including within L cycles after any attacker leaves.

Theorem ('both horns'). Use WARDEN's Theorem 15 two-world construction on the 1-D score: the attacker synthesises a World-B stream whose gate statistics match honest World-A drift.
- If g absorbs that statistic, SAFETY fails (boiling frog).
- If g refuses it, the attacker can deliberately trip the refusal for tau cycles at traffic cost c(tau). Post-departure FPR is then about 1 - Phi(z_alpha - v*tau/s), so LIVENESS fails.

Corollary. A gate escapes both horns only if its refusal region is not reachable by honest drift. TOA's directional refusal (only the signature component is rationed) satisfies this whenever honest drift is orthogonal to the signature. This explains our 85-87% vs 0.3% result.

Dual (blinding):
- CDC's level 1 - alpha(1 - pi_up) + eps_n is pushed above 1 by benign-looking, slightly-off points that inflate Storey's pi_up, so the threshold goes to +infinity.
- Mean + k*SD and percentile refreshes (ACORN-IDS, DriftXpert, CB-RBM) are inflated the same way.
- Ring inflation against our own signature-free method: attack-orthogonal benign traffic legitimately fills the outer ring, the approved spread growth widens the boundary, and Mirai then lands inside it.

Fix for the dual: extend TOA's budget to spread growth along the signature direction (a direction-weighted radius budget), giving a minimum time to blind that mirrors the minimum time to compromise.

Attacks to build, each as the cheapest trip signal per defence:
- T2T rollback: a spike every k cycles makes the score exceed 2.5x the mean of the last 5 scores, forcing repeated w_t = w_{t-2}.
- DriftXpert OR > T: keep OR just under T while honest drift builds, or force triggers to flood the labelling queue (public code).
- OWAD permutation gate, in human and self-labelled modes (public KitNET demo).
- LID box: drive parameters to the box face.
- RTTAD: inflate scores so no confident-normal samples remain, triggering its stop rule.
- EATA-style entropy filter.
candidates.why_new:
- The corpus check finds no paper that treats a stop-learning, rollback or gate rule as an attack surface.

- Rapid Poison induces false positives through what the model learns, not by stopping learning.
- Su et al. never measure what EMA or entropy filtering cost under honest drift.
- CDC was only tested against tail mimicry, never against threshold inflation.
- No paper states a liveness property for adaptive detectors.
- The theorem turns two published impossibility results into a constructive dilemma, and the six-defence evaluation closes our open problem 4.
- Caveat: AHA's full text and 2609.23254 ('manufactured blind sets') must be read first; either could partly pre-empt the framing.

candidates.name: Rejected-Mode Subspace Budget (RMSB): TOA whose threat directions are learned from the detector's own alarms
candidates.one_line: Replace TOA's single known signature with a budgeted subspace spanned by persistent, stationary modes of rejected traffic plus any known signatures, so the boiling frog's destination is rationed even when the push is hidden in drift or spread across many directions.
candidates.mechanism:
Key observation. A boiling-frog poisoner always has a destination: a region that is currently rejected (Mirai scan, ack or syn traffic, whether sent by the attacker or present as internet background radiation). Honest drift does not converge on a stable, long-rejected region. Rejected mass from honest drift moves and then gets absorbed.

Rejection memory. Online k-means with K = 8 slots over alarmed points in PCA-10 space. Each slot j tracks:
- centroid mu_j and mass rate w_j (EWMA);
- age a_j;
- centroid speed ||d mu_j / dt||;
- margin ||mu_j - c|| - r_acc.

Persistence. A slot is PERSISTENT if a_j > tau, w_j > w_min, speed < v_max and margin > 0.

Threat subspace. U_t = orth(span{mu_j - c_t : j persistent} ∪ {known signatures, if any}), with rank capped at r_max (e.g. 3).

Update:
- Delta_c = P_U Delta_c + (I - P_U) Delta_c.
- The orthogonal part is applied in full.
- The projected part draws from ONE shared cumulative budget: sum ||P_U Delta_c applied|| <= B0 + B*t. Sharing the budget defeats contrastive multi-direction poisoners, whose pieces all project into the same span.
- Spread: growth of the directional radius s(u) = sqrt(u^T Sigma u) along each u in U is budgeted the same way.

Backstops:
(a) A global cap on cumulative displacement not corroborated by outer-ring support, which covers attackers whose target never shows up as a rejected mode (the omission case: the attacker withholds attack traffic until after compromise).
(b) Anti-decoy rules. Persistence requires margin AND stationarity. Budget is charged per mode, at most B/r_max each, so planting fake modes can only spend their own share. Honest drift orthogonal to U is never slowed, so decoys cannot freeze the detector, which would be the freeze attack transplanted to RMSB.

Theorem. For any target A that is a persistent rejected mode when the attack starts, time to compromise >= (d(c_0, A) - r_acc)/B, whatever the mix of directions or timing. This is TOA's proof with P_sig replaced by P_U, plus a lemma that the persistence test is stable under bounded honest drift.

Liveness. Honest drift toward a persistent rejected mode (a legitimate new service first flagged as anomalous) is absorbed with latency at most d/B. We report this as a bounded adaptation cost.
candidates.why_new:
- TOA needs a trusted signature, which Rapid Poison's Omission attack (ICML 2026) shows an attacker can shape.
- 2606.29841 protects covariance eigendirections, not directions inferred from attack evidence, and has no cumulative budget.
- No defence in the corpus uses the detector's rejection history as side information for gating updates: not WARDEN, CDC, OWAD, RTTAD or ACORN-IDS. ACORN-IDS even labels whole clusters normal if they contain a single clean sample.
- SuSS 2026 shows that direction-diverse multi-agent attackers are realistic. A shared subspace budget is the first defence designed against them.
- It partly answers open problem 1 inside a single stream: drift camouflage hides the path, not the destination.

candidates.name: Event-Licensed Adaptation: signed firmware and provisioning events unlock a time-boxed fast-learning budget
candidates.one_line: Never stop learning on suspicion. Learn slowly by default (TOA/FOA budget) and quickly only for K cycles after an authenticated device event (signed OTA, provisioning, config push), turning the freeze dilemma into a bound the attacker cannot mint its way out of.
candidates.mechanism:
Two rates:
- Background: the RMSB/FOA budget B, always on.
- Licensed: B_L >> B for K cycles, after the detector verifies a token tau = Sign_sk(device_id, event_type, fw_hash or config_hash, t_start, K, scope).

Keys and verification. sk is held by the vendor or site admin. The detector (gateway, or an ESP32 node whose detector code is protected by Secure Boot v2) verifies with Ed25519 or ECDSA-P256 via mbedTLS. The OTA path (esp_https_ota plus signed app images) emits the token only after image verification.

During a licence:
- The scoped device's detector refits quickly on core/ring-filtered traffic.
- Re-entry check: at licence end, compare c_post with c_pre along the threat subspace U (RMSB or signatures). If the move toward a threat mode exceeds beta, revert ONLY that component. This is a directional revert, never a full rollback, so there is no freeze surface.

Provisioning licences:
- They are the only way a new per-device detector instance is spawned. The new instance is initialised from the peer prior (FOA) and warms up under the licensed rate.
- Unlicensed abrupt drift NEVER spawns an instance. This closes the Sensors 2024 hijack and bounds join-time poisoning.

Bound. Attacker displacement toward A by time t is at most B*t + N_lic(t) * K * B_L * kappa_rev. kappa_rev < 1 is the residual left after the directional revert. N_lic(t) is set by the legitimate event rate, which the attacker cannot raise without the signing key.

Threat model. A network attacker without code execution inside the detector's trust boundary. A compromised device's application firmware cannot mint tokens because the private key never sits on the device. We discuss device compromise that fakes local 'OTA happened' signals, and the answer is that verification happens at the gateway.
candidates.why_new:

- Every corpus defence gates adaptation on statistics, which is exactly what the freeze attack trips and what blind schedules evade (ESANN 2025). Examples: DriftXpert, NetSight and OWAD use drift tests, and OWAD also relies on a human.
- Sensors 2024 leaves unauthenticated instance spawning undefended.
- Must check outside the corpus: MUD-based anomaly detection (e.g. Hamza et al. 2018) and change-management-aware AIOps alert suppression. The difference to argue is that we license the learning RATE of a poisonable self-learner inside a time-to-compromise bound; we do not suppress alerts or whitelist flows.
