hits.conclusion:
VERDICT: NOT KILLED, but three parts are already partly taken, and the paper has to cite them and narrow its claims.

(1) The 'both horns' theorem has a static ancestor. CAPTURE (arXiv 2609.02265, Sep 2026), Theorem 2, proves FUR + RRL >= 1 - delta_phi for any rule that reads only one statistic: it must accept poison or reject genuine drift. WARDEN's Theorem 15 (arXiv 2607.21673) gives the FPR-vs-power ceiling. What is new and still open: an attacker who deliberately drives the refusal side for tau cycles at cost c(tau), and the resulting post-departure FPR / liveness failure. No paper found models a freeze attack, a trip cost, or any safety-plus-liveness contract for self-updating detectors.

(2) The blinding dual against CDC is partly conceded by WARDEN itself. It says a level above 1 means tau=+inf, 'trivially valid', and treats adversarial suppression as a power loss. Its own mimicry attack already gets 'hiding' (TPR 0.615 to 0.004). The contribution must be the explicit Storey pi_up-inflation construction with benign-looking off points, a minimum time to blind, and the direction-weighted radius-budget fix. It must not be pitched as 'CDC can be blinded'.

(3) In prose, Korycki & Krawczyk (arXiv 2020 / MLJ 2023) already list 'impairing the adaptation process', up to 'complete nullification', and label-budget spending through fake-novel points. So 'freezing adaptation' and 'flooding the label queue' are not new concepts. The formal contract and the per-defence trip attacks are. Kloft & Laskov (2010) introduced the false-positive-triggered update switch-off gate and explicitly left availability ('red herring') attacks out of scope, which supports the gap.

Per-defence findings:
- T2T verified (Hu & Duan, ICML 2026): the rule is 2.5x the mean of the last 5 scores, with rollback to w_{t-2}. It never considers attacker-forced rollbacks, though it notes that rejection under pervasive poisoning means 'total loss of system utility'.
- OWAD (NDSS 2023) lists its own adversarial robustness as future work.
- RTTAD stops 'until no sufficient samples remain', with no adversary considered.
- EATA attacks so far only evade the entropy filter (poisoning horn; Su et al., ICLR 2025; MedBN). None freeze it.

No paper attacks any of the six target defences by tripping their gates.

Factual corrections to the idea:
- ACORN-IDS sets its threshold at mu+2sigma on a CLEAN held-out validation split per task, not on refreshed stream traffic. The inflation attack only applies if that split or the pseudo-labels can be influenced.
- DriftXpert (the OR > T rule and its public code), CB-RBM and the 'LID box' defence could not be verified as real papers in this run.
- 'Baiting AI' (Pasikhani et al.) is an arXiv-only evasion attack. Its TDSC venue is not verified, and it does not induce alarms or alert fatigue.

Coverage limits: the shared WebSearch budget ran out partway through, so these were not searched:
- the conformal-calibration poisoning literature (for example a possible ICML 2024 'Data Poisoning Attacks against Conformal Prediction', unverified);
- the ANTIDOTE / boiling-frog PCA work (Rubinstein et al. 2009);
- the classic alert-flooding / 'squealing' IDS work;
- direct freeze attacks on EATA-style filters.

These should be checked in a follow-up run before claiming novelty for the blinding dual.

novelty.name: Rejected-Mode Subspace Budget (RMSB): TOA whose threat directions are learned from the detector's own alarms

verdict.name: Rejected-Mode Subspace Budget (RMSB): TOA whose threat directions are learned from the detector's own alarms
verdict.reasoning:
Three independent prior-art searches found no paper that does the full RMSB combination. That combination has five parts: (1) cluster the detector's own alarmed traffic; (2) keep only persistent, stationary modes with positive margin; (3) build a rank-capped threat subspace from those modes; (4) split each centre/spread update into an in-span part, drawn from ONE shared cumulative budget charged per mode, and an orthogonal part that is always applied; (5) prove a time-to-compromise bound for any target that is already a persistent rejected mode. Every individual part does have prior art, though, and the headline claims as written are too broad:

- "No defence uses the detector's rejection history to gate updates" is false as stated. Kloft & Laskov (JMLR 2012; AISTATS 2010) use the alarm/false-positive rate as a measure of attack progress and freeze or reset the online centroid learner. They also prove linear displacement bounds along a known attack direction. Only the narrower claim "the geometry of the rejections, not their rate" holds up.
- The rejection memory (k-means over rejected/unknown points, with size and cohesion tests for persistence) is MINAS (DMKD 2016) / OLINDDA. Those methods use persistence to ABSORB a cluster, which is the opposite of RMSB's use.
- Splitting updates into a protected-subspace part and an orthogonal part is standard. Examples are GPM (ICLR 2021), SafeGrad (2025, harm-direction gradient surgery), GuardSpace (2025), Gradient Immunity (2026) and RepShield (NIDS continual learning, 2026, not verified). RMSB differs in two ways: its subspace comes from alarms with no labels, and it rations the in-span part rather than zeroing it.
- The theorem follows directly from any per-step cap on displacement toward the target. It belongs to the same family as Nelson & Joseph (2006) and Kloft & Laskov (2012), so it is not a headline result. The only part with real technical content is the lemma that the persistence test stays stable under bounded honest drift.
- The key observation, that a boil leaves rejected mass that persists while honest drift is absorbed, is anticipated by the 2026 UMass Dartmouth MS thesis by H. H. Thompson. Its 'contrastive-loss concentration' and 'input-space directness' signals are used only for early warning.
- Decoy modes and allergy-style freezing are a known attack class against IDS that learn from their own suspicious-traffic pool: Perdisci et al. (S&P 2006), Paragraph and Allergy (RAID 2006). RMSB's anti-decoy rules therefore answer a known threat; they are not an unanticipated design point.

What is new is the combination: a threat subspace taken from the shape of the alarms, a shared per-mode budget that never freezes, and orthogonal drift that is never slowed, all in an unsupervised online IoT detector. Reviewers are likely to call it an incremental assembly of known parts unless the evaluation shows something none of the parts can do alone.

The searches have gaps. Federated-learning defenses that learn a malicious direction and then project (DnC from NDSS 2021, spectral signatures), the 'distributional quarantine' defense, SOUL, and Wasswa & Lynar (arXiv 2512.22488) were not searched. The full texts of RepShield and the Thompson thesis were not read. These gaps argue against a "novel" verdict.
verdict.closest: Kloft & Laskov, "Security Analysis of Online Centroid Anomaly Detection", JMLR 13 (2012), with the conference version at AISTATS 2010. It is the same detector family (online centroid) and also uses the detector's own alarms to protect the learner, through FPR monitoring followed by a freeze or reset. Its displacement bound along an attack direction has the same shape as RMSB's theorem. Runners-up are MINAS (DMKD 2016) for the rejection memory, the 2026 Thompson MS thesis for the key observation, and SafeGrad (2025) / GPM (ICLR 2021) for the projection primitive.
verdict.how_to_differentiate:
1. Narrow the novelty claim to "rejection geometry, not rejection rate". Directly against Kloft & Laskov, show that their FPR-triggered freeze/reset (a) falls to a freeze attack, where decoy alarms raise the FPR and stall honest adaptation, and (b) needs a clean hold-out set. Then show RMSB keeps adapting to orthogonal drift under the same attack. Implement Kloft & Laskov as a baseline next to TOA and Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025).
2. Present the rejection memory as an adversarial inversion of MINAS/OLINDDA: the same persistence test, but used to protect instead of absorb. Include a head-to-head showing that a MINAS-style absorber is what a boiling frog exploits.
3. Make the persistence-stability lemma the main technical contribution, not the by-construction bound. Stress-test it against Hinder et al.-style drift adversarials, including a target mode that moves slowly enough to fail the speed test and a destination that wanders.
4. Evaluate decoys explicitly using the Perdisci, Paragraph and Allergy threat model. Show that per-mode budget shares (B/r_max) cap decoy spend and that honest orthogonal drift is never slowed.
5. Evaluate the contrastive multi-direction attacker of Rivas & Piplai (AAAI-SS 2026) to back the shared-budget claim. Evaluate the omission case, where backstop (a) is the only protection, as its own guarantee.
6. Measure the d/B liveness cost on real benign drift, such as a new IoT service first flagged as anomalous, on N-BaIoT or a similar dataset.
7. Cite the Thompson thesis and contrast with it: it detects (early warning only), while RMSB rations with a guarantee.
8. Before writing the related-work section, finish the missing searches: FL malicious-subspace projection defenses such as DnC and spectral signatures, RepShield's full text, SOUL, and distributional quarantine.

hits.title: Security Analysis of Online Centroid Anomaly Detection (Kloft & Laskov), JMLR vol. 13; conference version: Online Anomaly Detection under Adversarial Impact, AISTATS 2010
hits.how_close: CLOSEST on the 'alarm history constrains the update' claim and on the theorem; it does not do the subspace part. I read the full PDF. Sec. 6 (Axiom 10) and Sec. 8.8 use the detector's own alarm statistics to protect the learner: if more than a fraction alpha of innocuous points is rejected, the centroid resets to a safe state. Sec. 8.8 says to treat the observed false-positive rate as a measure of the attack's progress and to turn online updates off when a critical rate is reached. The paper also proves linear displacement bounds along ONE known attack direction a. Differences: the alarm signal is a scalar rate and it never models where the rejected points sit; the response is freeze/reset, which is exactly the freeze-attack weakness; it needs a clean hold-out set to measure the rate; and the direction is given in advance, not learned. RMSB cannot claim to be the first to use alarms to protect an online centroid learner. It can only claim to be the first to use the geometry of the alarms. Must be cited and contrasted.

hits.title: MINAS: multiclass learning algorithm for novelty detection in data streams (Faria et al.; full author list not confirmed on a fetched page), Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery vol. 30; lineage includes OLINDDA (Spinosa et al., ~2007)
hits.year: 2016 (background; year and journal inferred from the indexed ISSN and volume, as the repository page did not render; OLINDDA not separately verified)
hits.how_close: CLOSE on RMSB's 'rejection memory + persistence test' component, with the opposite purpose. Examples the current model rejects ('unknown') go into a short-term memory. The memory is clustered with k-means / micro-clusters. Only clusters with enough examples (min_examples_cluster) become valid patterns. A distance threshold to the existing model decides 'extension of a known concept' (drift) versus 'novelty'. OLINDDA, as described in the search results, does the same with K-means over a short-term memory of unknown samples and labels new clusters drifted or novel by distance. So keeping K clusters over rejected points and testing them for persistence and cohesion is old. But these methods ABSORB persistent rejected clusters as new normal or novel classes, which is the behaviour a boiling-frog attacker wants. They have no adversary, no budget and no projection of updates. RMSB inverts their use: persistent rejected modes become protected directions. Cite as the origin of the rejection memory.

hits.title: Keeping up with dynamic attackers: Certifying robustness to adaptive online data poisoning (Bose, Lessard, Fazel, Dvijotham), AISTATS 2025
hits.how_close: Moderately close on the theorem side only. It gives certified bounds on the worst-case impact of an adaptive online poisoner, shown on mean estimation (essentially a centroid) and binary classification, and uses the certificates to design robust learners. From the abstract, it does not learn threat directions from rejected samples and does not budget movement per direction. Full text not checked for direction-specific budgets. A natural baseline or comparison for RMSB's time-to-compromise lower bound.

hits.title: Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning (Saha, Garg, Roy), ICLR 2021 oral
hits.how_close: Same mechanism, different goal. A protected subspace is built from data (SVD of activations from past tasks), and each update is split so the component inside that subspace is removed and only the orthogonal part is applied. RMSB's split Delta_c = P_U Delta_c + (I - P_U) Delta_c follows this pattern, but RMSB (a) builds U from rejected traffic, (b) rations the in-subspace part with a cumulative budget instead of zeroing it, which avoids freezing, and (c) has an adversary. A related item, Ru et al., Maintaining Adversarial Robustness in Continuous Learning (arXiv 2402.11196, 2024; seen only in search results, not fetched), projects updates to protect robustness, not against poisoning.

hits.title: SpectralKrum: A Spectral-Geometric Defense Against Byzantine Attacks in Federated Learning (Tripathi, Sharma, Mishra, Maiti)
hits.how_close: Moderate on the 'learn a subspace online and judge updates by projection' idea, inverted. It keeps a rolling buffer of past aggregates, runs rank-r PCA to estimate a BENIGN subspace, applies Krum in the projected coordinates, and drops updates whose residual outside the subspace exceeds a threshold. RMSB estimates a THREAT subspace from alarms and rations movement inside it. SpectralKrum has no movement budget inside the subspace, works across federated clients rather than on a single device's own history, and its authors say it gives little advantage when malicious updates are spectrally indistinguishable.

hits.title: AOC-IDS: Autonomous Online Framework with Contrastive Learning for Intrusion Detection (Zhang et al.)
hits.year: 2024 (arXiv page lists no venue; the user's literature review and an HKU repository record give IEEE INFOCOM 2024, not re-verified here)
hits.how_close: Moderate on 'the detector's own alarms shape the online update'. The online IDS pseudo-labels traffic from its own Gaussian decision module, both normal and anomalous, and periodically updates an autoencoder with a Cluster Repelling Contrastive loss, so self-flagged samples act as repelling negatives. It has no poisoning threat model, no persistence or stationarity test and no budget or bound, and it is itself exposed to boiling-frog poisoning. Its 2026 replication and extension (arXiv 2605.26166, Afzaal et al.) adds a 'PseudoFilter' for pseudo-label reliability, again without a poisoning model.

hits.title: MemStream: Memory-Based Streaming Anomaly Detection (Bhatia, Jain, Srivastava, Kawaguchi, Hooi), WWW 2022
hits.how_close: Low to moderate. I checked the full PDF. A streaming detector under drift whose memory is updated FIFO only when a record's anomaly score is within an update threshold beta. It names 'memory poisoning' and adds a discounting KNN self-correction. Rejected records are simply discarded and never mined for threat directions. No adversarial budget and no bound.

hits.title: Defending against Poisoning Attacks in Online Learning Settings (Collinge, Lupu, Munoz-Gonzalez), ESANN 2019
hits.how_close: Low. I checked the full text. It rejects incoming samples whose impact on the current online classifier is too large (if rejected, w_n = w_{n-1}) and combines learners with different learning rates to delay the attack. Rejected samples are not stored, clustered or used to constrain later updates. Supervised classification, not anomaly detection.

hits.title: Adversarial Concept Drift Detection under Poisoning Attacks for Robust Data Stream Mining (Korycki & Krawczyk), Machine Learning 112(10), DOI 10.1007/s10994-022-06177-w
hits.how_close: Low to moderate on RMSB's key observation that honest and adversarial drift can be told apart. It gives a taxonomy of adversarial concept drift and a robust RBM drift detector meant to separate real drift from poisoned 'fake drift'. It works at the detection level and does not budget updates or learn threat directions from rejected traffic. Already in the user's literature review.

hits.title: Adversarial Anomaly Detection (Radhika Bhargava), PhD thesis, Purdue / CERIAS TR 2019-4
hits.how_close: Low. It treats the concept drift that poison points cause as a signal that an attack is under way (DBSCAN, LOF, OC-SVM) and reports that detecting it degrades the detector. There is no rejected-mode subspace and no budget, and the implementation was not visible on the page.

hits.title: METANOIA: A Lifelong Intrusion Detection and Investigation System for Mitigating Concept Drift (Ying et al.)
hits.year: 2024 (arXiv Dec 2024; v2 Mar 2026; no venue listed)
hits.how_close: Low. A provenance-graph IDS with incremental learning that 'transfers suspicious states to avoid learning malicious behaviors', i.e. flagged items are kept out of the update. Not framed as a poisoning defense, with no subspace or budget. Mechanism details not verified beyond the abstract.

hits.title: Adversarial Attacks for Drift Detection (Hinder, Vaquet, Hammer), ESANN 2025
hits.how_close: Not prior art, but a direct threat to RMSB's persistence test. It constructs 'drift adversarials', streams that drift without being caught by common drift detectors. RMSB's lemma that the persistence test (age, mass, speed, margin) is stable under bounded honest drift should be checked against this kind of construction, for example an attacker whose target mode moves slowly enough to fail the stationarity test.

hits.title: Contrastive Adversarial Agents for Intentional Drift Induction in Network Intrusion Detection Systems (Rivas & Piplai), Proc. AAAI Symposium Series vol. 9, 2026 Summer Symposium, pp. 309-314
hits.how_close: Attack only, no defense. An ensemble of RL attackers trained contrastively to use non-redundant perturbation strategies, deployed in sequence or adaptively to destabilize retraining-based NIDS. This is close to the 'contrastive multi-direction poisoner' RMSB's shared budget is meant to defeat, so it is a good attack to evaluate against. Framed as drift induction rather than poisoning, and the authors call for diversity-aware defenses, which supports RMSB's motivation.

hits.title: Empirical Analysis of Evasion and Poisoning Against Malware Data Drift Detection (Yang, Lie, Papernot)
hits.how_close: Low. An empirical study of how evasion and poisoning affect a drift detector versus a malware classifier. From the abstract, there is no defense that uses rejected samples or constrains updates. Useful evidence that drift detectors themselves can be poisoned.

hits.title: The Boiling Frog Threshold: Criticality and Blindness in World Model-Based Anomaly Detection Under Gradual Drift (Zhe Hong)
hits.how_close: Low. It measures the drift-rate threshold below which gradual corruption is absorbed by z-score, variance and percentile detectors in RL world models. No poisoning adversary, no defense, and no use of alarms or rejected samples.

hits.title: ANTIDOTE: Understanding and Defending against Poisoning of Anomaly Detectors (Rubinstein et al.), ACM IMC
hits.how_close: Foundation for the boiling-frog threat on PCA-subspace detectors. Its defense is robust PCA (robust dispersion instead of variance), batch and server-side. No learned threat subspace from alarms and no per-direction budget. Already cited by the user.

hits.title: Can't Boil This Frog: Robustness of Online-Trained Autoencoder-Based Anomaly Detectors to Adversarial Poisoning Attacks (Kravchik, Biggio, Shabtai); journal version: Poisoning attacks on cyber attack detectors for ICS, Computers & Security 2022
hits.how_close: Attack only, on online-retrained autoencoders in ICS (interpolation and back-gradient poisoning). It proposes no defense of RMSB's kind. Already in the user's literature review.

hits.title: Frog-boiling attacks on network coordinate systems (Chan-Tin, Feldman, Hopper, Kim), SecureComm 2009; extended in ACM TISSEC 14(3), 2011
hits.year: 2009 (background; title and venue taken from search results and the author PDF https://www-users.cs.umn.edu/~hopper/frogBoiling.pdf, not fully re-read)
hits.how_close: Origin of the small-step 'frog-boiling' idea: each fake update stays under the outlier threshold. It shows per-step outlier rejection alone cannot stop it, which is why RMSB uses cumulative budgets. No rejected-mode subspace.

hits.title: Malicious Attack Defense in Human-to-Machine Applications Through Concept Drift Adaptation (Yu et al.), IEEE Internet of Things Journal vol. 12, pp. 53563-53573, DOI 10.1109/JIOT.2025.3616787
hits.how_close: Distant. An adaptive random forest with error-rate drift detection and haptic-mismatch relabeling, used to adapt to unseen attacks. No poisoning-of-adaptation model, no use of alarm geometry, no update budget.

hits.title: MORPH-IDS: A Context-Driven Multi-Agent RL Framework for Drift-Aware Moving Target Defense in Adversarial-Robust Intrusion Detection
hits.year: 2026 (lab news post dated 03/07/2026; authors and venue NOT stated, unverified)
hits.how_close: Distant. A drift embedding that includes undefined 'poisoning indicators' and RL switching between model ensembles. No alarm-derived subspace and no budget. Bibliographic details unverified.

hits.conclusion:
I could not kill RMSB. Nothing I found learns threat directions from persistent, stationary clusters of a detector's own rejected traffic and then caps the cumulative online update inside that span with a shared budget, while leaving orthogonal drift unrestricted. Every component, however, has prior art, and a reviewer will raise it:
(1) Using alarms to protect an online centroid learner is old. Kloft & Laskov (JMLR 2012, AISTATS 2010) treat the alarm (false-positive) rate as a measure of attack progress and reset or freeze the learner. They also prove a linear displacement bound along one known direction, which is what RMSB's theorem generalises. RMSB's claim must be narrowed to 'the geometry of the rejections, not their rate', and it should show that freeze/reset loses to the freeze attack.
(2) The rejection memory is old. OLINDDA (~2007) and MINAS (DMKD 2016) cluster rejected ('unknown') samples in a short-term memory, require cluster size and cohesion, and use a distance threshold to call each cluster drift or novelty. They do this to ABSORB the clusters, which is the reverse of RMSB. Cite them as the origin and present RMSB's persistence test (age + mass + low speed + positive margin) as an adversarial reinterpretation.
(3) Projecting updates onto a data-derived subspace is standard: GPM (ICLR 2021) in continual learning and SpectralKrum (2025) with a benign subspace in federated learning. RMSB's differences are that the subspace comes from alarms, the in-span part is budgeted rather than zeroed, and it runs on a single device's own history.
(4) The theory neighbour is Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025), certified bounds for adaptive online poisoning of mean estimation. It should be a baseline or compared result.
(5) Self-pseudo-labelled anomalies used as repelling negatives in online IDS updates exist in AOC-IDS (2024) and its 2026 follow-up, without a poisoning model.
Risks found in the literature: Hinder et al. (ESANN 2025) build drift streams that slip past detectors, so the stationarity test and its stability lemma need an adversarial check, for example an attacker who moves the target mode slowly enough to fail the speed test. Rivas & Piplai (AAAI-SS 2026) give a ready-made contrastive multi-direction drift attacker to test against. Defensible novelty: an alarm-geometry-derived threat subspace, a per-mode shared cumulative budget that stops the detector from freezing, and a time-to-compromise bound for any target that is already a persistent rejected mode.
Caveats: the shared web-search limit (200 calls per turn) ran out during this run, so planned searches on Newton (a frog-boiling defense that enforces physical laws on coordinate systems, not verified and not listed), on alert-correlation and darknet persistent-cluster work, and on more 2025-2026 FL work that removes malicious directions were not done. Unchecked details: the MINAS author list, DOI and year (taken from repository/ISSN metadata, not a rendered page); the OLINDDA details (from search summaries only); MORPH-IDS authors and venue; AOC-IDS as an INFOCOM 2024 paper (from the user's review and an HKU record, not the arXiv page). The UMass Dartmouth thesis-talk page ('Frog-boiling poisoning against drift-aware continual learners', Aug 2026), which the user's review lists as closest prior work, now returns 404 and its content could not be checked. A follow-up message can resume the remaining searches.

hits.title: Demonstrating and characterizing frog-boiling poisoning against drift-aware continual learners (M.S. thesis, Henry Heath Thompson, advisor Gokhan Kul, UMass Dartmouth)
hits.how_close: CLOSEST ON THE KEY OBSERVATION, but not the mechanism. The abstract was fetched from the repository (DOI 10.62791/20629). It runs a white-box frog-boiling attack on an autoencoder IDS whose buffer is managed by SSF, pushing the benign region toward a chosen attack class. With 5% injection it reports a 45-65% evasion rate. It proposes two DETECTION signals. (1) 'Input-space directness': a boil follows a sustained path, while natural drift wanders. (2) 'Contrastive-loss concentration': it tracks samples that fail to fold into the benign region, and these build up during a boil. Signal 2 is close to RMSB's 'rejected mass is persistent under attack, absorbed under honest drift' observation, so it must be cited and contrasted. It does NOT learn a threat subspace from alarm clusters, does NOT project or budget updates, has no time-to-compromise theorem, and offers early warning only. It is a thesis, not peer-reviewed. Its full text was not read, only the abstract.

hits.title: Security Analysis of Online Centroid Anomaly Detection (Kloft and Laskov, JMLR 13)
hits.how_close: DIRECT FOUNDATION FOR THE THEOREM. It covers centroid poisoning toward a known attack direction and bounds the attacker's gain under limited traffic share and a bounded false-positive rate, with experiments on HTTP and exploit traffic. RMSB's bound has the same shape: time to compromise >= (d - r_acc)/B. That bound follows by construction from any per-step cap on displacement toward the target. The theorem is therefore not a novelty claim by itself. No learned threat subspace and no projection.

hits.title: A 'Poisoning' Attack Against Online Anomaly Detection (Laskov and Kloft, workshop abstract; it restates Nelson and Joseph's bound)
hits.year: c. 2007 (background; venue and year are not printed on the PDF, and the figure metadata suggests a NIPS 2007 workshop)
hits.how_close: BACKGROUND. The PDF text was read. It restates Nelson et al.'s bound for an infinite-window centroid, T >= N(exp(D)-1) iterations to move the centre D radii. It shows that 'oldest-out' replacement makes the attack linear in D, and it studies 'nearest-out'. This is the classical time-to-compromise framing toward one known attack vector A. There is no rate budget, subspace or learned target.

hits.title: Bounding an Attack's Complexity for a Simple Learning Model (Nelson and Joseph, SysML workshop, Saint-Malo)
hits.how_close: BACKGROUND. This is the original hypersphere/centroid lower bound on the attacker's effort. The 2006 paper itself was not fetched. The URL is the related book chapter 'Attacking a Hypersphere Learner' by Joseph, Nelson, Rubinstein and Tygar, and I did not verify that the chapter is the same work. The citation was confirmed through a CV listing and the Laskov-Kloft abstract.

hits.title: ANTIDOTE: Understanding and Defending against Poisoning of Anomaly Detectors (Rubinstein, Nelson, Huang, Joseph et al., ACM IMC)
hits.how_close: BACKGROUND. It names the Boiling Frog attack on PCA-subspace detectors and defends with robust PCA. The detector is itself a subspace method, but the defense is robust estimation, not a budget on the threat-aligned component of updates. There is no rejection memory and no time-to-compromise guarantee. The project already cites it.

hits.title: Poster: Adversarial Habituation Attack: A Psychological Extension and Re-framing of Boiling Frog Attack (ACM CCS '25 poster, DOI 10.1145/3719027.3760741)
hits.how_close: ATTACK SIDE ONLY, DETAILS UNVERIFIED. The search snippet says it reframes boiling-frog attacks on anomaly-based IDS as gradual 'habituation'. The ACM page returned 403, so I could not verify the authors or any defense. It shows the threat is current at a top venue. No evidence of a subspace or budget defense.

hits.title: GuardSpace: A Guardrail for Safety Preservation: When Safety-Sensitive Subspace Meets Harmful-Resistant Null-Space (Zhang, Yang, Ren, Guo, Gu, Torr, Ghanem; arXiv 2510.14301)
hits.how_close: MECHANISM ANALOG IN ANOTHER DOMAIN (LLM fine-tuning). It builds a null-space projector so that adapter updates cannot change outputs on harmful prompts, and freezes a safety-relevant weight subspace. This is the same 'project updates out of a protected subspace' primitive. The subspace comes from weights and harmful prompts, not from a detector's own alarms. It is a hard projection with no cumulative budget, no never-freeze liveness, and no anomaly detection. A reviewer could call RMSB a 'null-space projection transplant', so frame the novelty around where U comes from and around the shared budget. Preprint; abstract only.

hits.title: Gradient Immunity: Null-Space Resistance to Malicious Fine-Tuning (Huang, Zeng, Zheng, Lu; arXiv 2608.05045)
hits.how_close: MECHANISM ANALOG. Its null-space layer suppresses or blocks gradients from harmful samples whose hidden states fall in a protected region calibrated on harmful data the defender holds. The 'protected region from known-bad data' idea parallels RMSB's known-signature part. It is not learned from a model's own alarms, does not budget over time, and is LLM-specific. Preprint; abstract only.

hits.title: RepShield: Robust knowledge representation in continual learning for network intrusion detection (Computer Networks, ScienceDirect pii S1389128626003208)
hits.year: 2026 (inferred from the pii; the page returned 403)
hits.how_close: MECHANISM ANALOG IN NIDS. Per the search snippet, it builds a historical feature subspace and projects new parameter updates onto its orthogonal complement (gradient-projection continual learning) to avoid forgetting under drift. Same projection primitive in an IDS, but the goal is preventing forgetting, not poisoning. No threat subspace, no budget, no adversary. The full text could not be fetched.

hits.title: MINAS: multiclass learning algorithm for novelty detection in data streams (de Faria, Carvalho, Gama; Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, DOI 10.1007/s10618-015-0433-y)
hits.how_close: PRIOR ART FOR THE 'REJECTION MEMORY' COMPONENT, with the opposite use. It groups examples marked unknown and promotes valid groups to novelty patterns that are ADDED to the model. RMSB clusters rejected points and RATIONS movement toward persistent ones. The idea of tracking persistent clusters of rejected stream data is not new; using them as a defense subspace appears to be new. The search summary could not confirm the exact buffering and clustering details.

hits.title: MemStream: Memory-Based Streaming Anomaly Detection (Bhatia et al., WWW 2022; arXiv 2106.03837)
hits.how_close: MODERATE. A streaming AD system that explicitly names 'memory poisoning'. It gates admission with a score threshold (beta) and FIFO replacement so flagged records do not enter normal memory, and it self-corrects. That is binary admission control. It keeps no memory of rejected modes, uses no directional subspace or budget, and does not model an adaptive boiling-frog attacker.

hits.title: Self-Poisoning in Adaptive Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Sharp-Threshold Theory and Certified Label-Free Calibration (Balachandran; arXiv 2607.21673)
hits.how_close: MODERATE on the theory and problem framing. Adaptive OOD detectors that update a memory bank from the stream can collapse through self-contamination: it uses a Polya-urn model with a threshold where the slope exceeds 1. The fix is a certified admission gate that reads only a frozen reserve, which the abstract says also holds 'even adversarially'. No direction or subspace decomposition, no rate budget, no use of rejected samples. Preprint; abstract only.

hits.title: Keeping up with dynamic attackers: Certifying robustness to adaptive online data poisoning (Bose, Lessard, Fazel, Dvijotham; AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258)
hits.how_close: MODERATE (theory). It certifies worst-case impact of adaptive online poisoning on online mean estimation, theta_{t+1} = (1-eta) theta_t + eta z_t + noise, which is close to a centroid detector. The defense optimises a shaped noise covariance S. There is no filtering, no rejected-point use, no projection or subspace budget, and no time-to-compromise. Read from the arXiv HTML. Already in the project's literature review.

hits.title: Adversarial concept drift detection under poisoning attacks for robust data stream mining (Korycki and Krawczyk, Machine Learning, DOI 10.1007/s10994-022-06177-w)
hits.how_close: LOW-MODERATE. RRBM-DD is a robust drift detector with per-feature truncated gradients and gating. It does not separate adversarial from real drift by direction or locality and does not cluster suspicious samples. No subspace budget.

hits.title: Can't Boil This Frog: Robustness of Online-Trained Autoencoder-Based Anomaly Detectors to Adversarial Poisoning Attacks (Kravchik and Shabtai; arXiv 2002.02741)
hits.how_close: ATTACK SIDE. Interpolation-based and back-gradient boiling-frog poisoning of online autoencoders in industrial control systems. It succeeds only for limited attacks, and SWaT resisted all ten. Its interpolation construction shows the poison heads for a destination, which supports RMSB's premise. No defense.

hits.title: An Investigation of Data Poisoning Defenses for Online Learning (Wang, Jha, Chaudhuri; arXiv 1905.12121)
hits.how_close: LOW-MODERATE. Analyses L2-norm, labeling-oracle, distance-to-centroid and slab defenses against online poisoning toward a target model, with geometric regimes for when poisoning is fast or slow. These are filtering defenses with no learned threat subspace or rationed projection.

hits.title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks (Steinhardt, Koh, Liang; NeurIPS 2017)
hits.how_close: LOW (geometry analog). The 'slab' defense projects points onto the line between class centroids and filters on that projection, a single learned threat direction used for filtering, not for budgeting updates. Attacks that rotate the slab by moving centroids are the analogue of attacking how U is estimated.

hits.title: Securing Virtual Coordinates by Enforcing Physical Laws ('Newton'; Seibert, Becker, Nita-Rotaru, State; ICDCS)
hits.how_close: LOW (cross-domain). It defends against the original frog-boiling attack on Vivaldi coordinates using safety invariants from Newton's laws instead of learned normality. The paper notes that learning-based defenses can be taught to accept malicious behaviour. It shows that invariant or rate-style constraints beat learned filters against frog-boiling, but it has nothing on subspaces or alarms.

hits.title: Theory of Continual Learning Against Data Poisoning Attacks (Hu and Duan; arXiv 2606.29841, ICML 2026 poster)
hits.how_close: LOW-MODERATE (theory). It frames continual-learning poisoning as an online zero-sum game, shows no defense works against linear-rate unbounded poisoning, and proposes task-to-task verification and sensitivity-minimising defenses. Not an anomaly detector, and no subspace budget. Abstract only.

hits.title: Adversarial Anomaly Detection (Radhika Bhargava, Purdue PhD thesis, CERIAS TR 2019-4)
hits.how_close: LOW-MODERATE. It estimates how many poison points DBSCAN, LOF and OC-SVM need and proposes a detection defense based on the concept drift the poison causes, at a cost in detector performance. Mechanism not described on the page. No projection or budget.

hits.title: Adversarial Attacks for Drift Detection (Hinder, Vaquet, Hammer; ESANN 2025; arXiv 2411.16591)
hits.how_close: LOW (supporting). It constructs streams whose drift goes undetected and gives necessary and sufficient conditions. This supports RMSB's choice to ration rather than detect, but it is not a defense. Search snippet only.

hits.title: A Framework for Drift Detection and Adaptation in AI-driven Anomaly and Threat Detection Systems (HDDAF; Lara-Gutierrez, Fernandez-Gago, Onieva; Int. J. Information Security vol. 24, DOI 10.1007/s10207-025-01118-9)
hits.how_close: LOW. A supervised pipeline combining Hoeffding drift detection, feature selection, adversarial training and incremental learning on CICIDS2017. It handles poisoning and drift together but has no learned threat subspace, budget or guarantee. Read from the PDF's first page.

hits.conclusion:
I could not kill the idea. I found no paper, from 2025-2026 or earlier, that does what RMSB does: learn threat directions from persistent, stationary clusters of the detector's own alarmed traffic, split each centre and spread update into a part inside that span and a part outside it, and cap the inside part with one shared cumulative budget while the outside part always goes through. The per-mode anti-decoy budgeting and the time-to-compromise bound for every persistent rejected mode also did not appear anywhere.

Each piece exists separately, though, and a reviewer will say so:

1. **The observation.** The closest work is the 2026 UMass Dartmouth MS thesis by Henry Heath Thompson. It finds that a boil shows up only in the shape of the drift over many rounds. One of its signals ('contrastive-loss concentration') tracks samples that fail to fold into the benign region, which is close to RMSB's 'rejected mass persists under attack' premise. It uses this only for early warning, with no projection, budget or guarantee. It must be cited and contrasted.
2. **The projection.** Projecting updates out of a protected subspace learned from harmful data already exists in LLM fine-tuning: GuardSpace (arXiv 2510.14301, 2025) and Gradient Immunity (arXiv 2608.05045, 2026). Orthogonal-complement gradient projection also exists in continual-learning NIDS, RepShield (Computer Networks, 2026), but there it prevents forgetting, not poisoning. RMSB's novelty rests on where U comes from (the detector's own rejected modes, no labels) and on the shared, never-freezing budget. 'We project updates' alone is not new.
3. **The rejection memory.** Grouping persistent rejected or unknown stream points is old: MINAS (2016) promotes them to novelty classes. RMSB uses them the opposite way, which is new.
4. **The theorem.** It is a by-construction consequence of the budget, of the same family as Nelson and Joseph (2006) and Kloft and Laskov (JMLR 2012). Present it as a property, not a headline result. The proposed lemma that the persistence test is stable under bounded honest drift is the part that carries real technical content.
5. **Other nearby work.** Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025) certify adaptive online poisoning of mean estimation using shaped noise. The 2026 self-poisoning OOD paper (arXiv 2607.21673) uses a certified admission gate from a frozen reserve. MemStream (WWW 2022) uses binary admission control. None of them uses alarm-derived directions or a directional budget.

Verdict: novel as a combination, but expect a reviewer to call it an incremental mix of these pieces.

**Limits of this search:**
- The web-search budget ran out before I could search federated-learning defenses that estimate a malicious direction from flagged updates and then project or filter (DnC from NDSS 2021, spectral signatures and similar), so that area is not covered. Federated defenses are cross-client, but a temporal variant could exist.
- I could not open the CCS '25 poster page (403) or RepShield's full text, and I read only the abstracts of GuardSpace, Gradient Immunity, the self-poisoning OOD paper and the Thompson thesis.
- Before claiming novelty, run one more targeted check covering federated-learning 'malicious subspace memory' projection defenses and the full text of the Thompson thesis.

hits.title: SafeGrad: Gradient Surgery for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning (Yi, Li, Zhang, Nie, Li, Huang, Liu)
hits.how_close: Closest analogue of the update mechanism, but in a different field. It splits each update into a part along a harm direction and the orthogonal rest, then deletes the harmful part (it projects the task gradient onto the plane orthogonal to the alignment gradient). Differences from RMSB: (1) it works on LLM fine-tuning, not intrusion detection; (2) the harm direction comes from a curated safety dataset, not from clusters of the detector's own rejected traffic; (3) it is a single direction, not a rank-capped subspace; (4) it removes the harmful part completely at each step, with no shared cumulative budget, no spread budget and no bound on time to compromise. Verified on the arXiv abstract page. Whether it has any budget is not stated there.

hits.title: Learning Only What Valid Adapters Can Express: Subspace-Constrained Adaptation Against Fine-Tuning Poisoning (Fabien Polly)
hits.how_close: Related subspace defense against poisoning, but the mirror image of RMSB. Updates are confined to an ALLOWED subspace estimated from a trusted pool of 196 LoRA adapters, rather than rationed inside a FORBIDDEN subspace learned from alarms. There is no cumulative budget and no time-to-compromise theorem, and the author calls the protection empirical. LLM adapters, not IDS. Verified on arXiv. The page does not say how the subspace is estimated.

hits.title: Keeping up with dynamic attackers: Certifying robustness to adaptive online data poisoning (Bose, Lessard, Fazel, Dvijotham), AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258
hits.how_close: Closest work on certificates. It gives certified bounds on what an adaptive online poisoner can do, for mean estimation and binary classification, and uses them to design robust learners. It does not learn threat directions from alarms, does not use a subspace projection, and does not separate honest drift from poisoning. RMSB's theorem is narrower but structured differently: a time-to-compromise bound per persistent mode, under any mix of directions. Verified on arXiv and PMLR. The page does not say whether the defense is a projection or a rate limit.

hits.title: MINAS: multiclass learning algorithm for novelty detection in data streams (de Faria, de Leon Ferreira Carvalho, Gama), Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
hits.how_close: Direct precedent for RMSB's rejection memory. Unknown (rejected) stream examples go into a short-term memory and are clustered. Cohesive, persistent clusters are validated as a novelty or an extension of a known concept. Crucially, MINAS uses persistence to ADOPT a rejected cluster as a new concept, which is exactly the absorption a poisoner wants. RMSB inverts this, using persistence to RATION movement toward the cluster. No adversary model and no budget. DOI 10.1007/s10618-015-0433-y. The exact threshold rules were not read.

hits.title: Misleading Worm Signature Generators Using Deliberate Noise Injection (Perdisci, Dagon, Lee, Fogla, Sharif), IEEE S&P
hits.how_close: Not a defense, but it attacks RMSB's core assumption. It shows an attacker can deliberately pollute the pool of suspicious flows that an IDS hands to a learner and mislead it, at noise levels near 50%. RMSB learns its threat subspace from exactly such a pool (its own alarms), so this is direct evidence that decoy modes are realistic. Verified from the PDF's first page.

hits.title: Paragraph: Thwarting Signature Learning by Training Maliciously (Newsome, Karp, Song), RAID 2006; and Allergy Attack Against Automatic Signature Generation (Chung, Mok), RAID 2006
hits.how_close: Classic attacks on learning from an IDS's suspicious pool. Paragraph's red-herring attacks delay or prevent learning an accurate signature. The Allergy attack (Springer DOI 10.1007/11856214_4, seen in search results only) makes the generator emit signatures of benign traffic, causing denial of service. Allergy is the ancestor of the 'decoys freeze the detector' attack that RMSB's anti-decoy rules (b) must defeat. Neither paper adapts a baseline under drift. Titles and venues were verified via search results and the Springer listing. The full texts were not read in this session.

hits.title: Securing Virtual Coordinates by Enforcing Physical Laws (Seibert, Becker, Nita-Rotaru, State), IEEE ICDCS
hits.how_close: A frog-boiling defense from the domain where the term originated (network coordinates). It replaces 'learn what is good over time' with fixed safety invariants derived from Newton's laws. The paper explicitly argues that defenses which learn good behaviour can be made to learn bad behaviour, and its invariants are meant to stop slowly accumulated lies. It uses no learned threat directions and no per-direction budget. Verified from the PDF text. (Frog-boiling origin: Chan-Tin et al., SecureComm 2009 / ACM TISSEC 2011, seen in search results only.)

hits.title: Security Analysis of Online Centroid Anomaly Detection (Kloft, Laskov), JMLR 13
hits.how_close: The same detector family as TOA/RMSB (online centroid). It bounds attacker displacement by the attacker's traffic share and the false-positive rate. Its proposed protection is to watch the FPR and switch off updates, which is a freeze, the very failure mode RMSB is designed to avoid. It has no direction-specific rationing and no learned threat subspace.

hits.title: ANTIDOTE: Understanding and Defending against Poisoning of Anomaly Detectors (Rubinstein, Nelson, Huang, Joseph, Lau, Rao, Taft, Tygar), ACM IMC
hits.how_close: Boiling-frog poisoning of a PCA-subspace detector, defended with robust PCA (robust dispersion). Note the inversion: ANTIDOTE robustifies the NORMAL subspace, while RMSB learns a THREAT subspace from rejected traffic and budgets movement into it. No online drift tracking, no budget, no time-to-compromise bound.

hits.title: MemStream: Memory-Based Streaming Anomaly Detection (Bhatia, Jain, Srivastava, Kawaguchi, Hooi), WWW 2022
hits.how_close: Streaming anomaly detector under drift that names memory poisoning and defends against it with two design choices: keep anomalous samples out of memory, and let the memory self-correct. This is plain alarm gating, which boiling-frog attacks are built to beat (they stay just inside the boundary). No rejected-mode memory, no directions, no budget. Verified on arXiv. The page does not describe the gating details.

hits.title: When Normality Shifts: Risk-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Unsupervised Tabular Anomaly Detection (RTTAD; Huang, Qiao, Zhang, Ye, Shang, Fu)
hits.how_close: Recent unsupervised anomaly-detection adaptation that tries not to absorb anomalies: it updates only on high-confidence pseudo-normal samples and 'constrains' suspected anomalies. The threat is accidental contamination, not an adaptive poisoner. No learned threat subspace, cumulative budget or guarantee. The abstract does not say how anomalies are constrained.

hits.title: Adversarial Concept Drift Detection under Poisoning Attacks for Robust Data Stream Mining (Korycki, Krawczyk), Machine Learning (Springer)
hits.how_close: Same problem framing: real versus adversarial drift in streams, where a poisoner fakes drift to trigger bad adaptation. Defense: a robust drift detector based on a restricted Boltzmann machine, plus a Relative Loss of Robustness metric. It decides at the level of a drift detector, not through direction-wise rationing of updates, and uses no persistence of rejected regions as far as the abstract shows. The paper's two drift types were not read.

hits.title: Adversarial Attacks for Drift Detection (Hinder, Vaquet, Hammer), ESANN 2025
hits.how_close: Attack-side support for RMSB's premise. It builds 'drift adversarials', drifting streams that common drift detectors miss, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for them. This argues against defenses that wait for a drift detector, and so favours always-on rationing like RMSB's. No defense is proposed.

hits.title: Empirical Analysis of Evasion and Poisoning Against Malware Data Drift Detection (Mingyue Yang, David Lie, Nicolas Papernot)
hits.how_close: Very recent, same theme (poisoning plus drift detection), but for malware classification. It is empirical attack analysis with no defense mentioned in the abstract. It is a sign the area is active and a likely reviewer reference, not a scoop.

hits.title: Anomaly Detection in the Open World: Normality Shift Detection, Explanation, and Adaptation (OWAD; Han et al.), NDSS
hits.how_close: The main security-venue framework for adapting a zero-positive anomaly detector to normality shift. Checked in the full text: its limitations section leaves the robustness of OWAD itself against adversarial attacks to future work. It has no poisoning defense. This is the gap RMSB targets.

hits.title: CADE: Detecting and Explaining Concept Drift Samples for Security Applications (Yang, Guo, Hao, Ciptadi, Ahmadzadeh, Xing, Wang), USENIX Security
hits.how_close: Uses contrastive learning to build a distance space for spotting and explaining drifting samples. This is the 'contrastive' part of the query, but it is used for drift detection, not for poisoning defense or budgeted adaptation.

hits.title: Learn to Adapt: Robust Drift Detection in Security Domain (Kuppa, Le-Khac)
hits.how_close: A drift detector for security data that claims robustness to attacker-induced drift and discovers new classes online (NIDS 2018 and APT C2 data). Clustering new classes overlaps loosely with RMSB's rejected modes, but there is no update rationing, budget or guarantee. Its mechanism was not described on the abstract page.

hits.title: Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning (Saha, Garg, Roy), ICLR
hits.how_close: Structural precedent for the linear algebra: it learns a low-rank subspace from data online via SVD of activations and restricts updates to the orthogonal complement. Its purpose is to prevent forgetting, not to defend against poisoning. No budget, no adversary. A Computer Networks paper, 'RepShield', reportedly applies orthogonal projection to continual-learning NIDS (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1389128626003208). It could NOT be verified (HTTP 403), and the search summary did not mention poisoning.

hits.title: Practical Evaluation of Poisoning Attacks on Online Anomaly Detectors in Industrial Control Systems (Kravchik, Demetrio, Biggio, Shabtai), Computers & Security
hits.how_close: Attack paper (with the earlier arXiv 'Can't Boil This Frog', https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02741). The attacker poisons online-retrained detectors while only non-alerting data enters retraining, which is the boiling-frog threat model RMSB assumes. No direction-budget defense.

hits.title: Exploring Model Dynamics for Accumulative Poisoning Discovery (Zhu, Guo, Yao, Du, He, Yuan, Liu, Wang, Han), ICML
hits.how_close: A defense against accumulative online poisoning (Pang et al., NeurIPS 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09993) that spots poisoned samples through a 'memorization discrepancy' in model behaviour. It detects samples rather than rationing directions. Not IDS.

hits.title: Adaptive Intrusion Detection System using Transformer-Based Neural Networks and Continual Learning Approach with Adversarial Investigation (Ariffin, Haris, Zaki, Hanif, Anuar)
hits.how_close: Continual-learning IDS shown to be fragile under replay-buffer poisoning (label flipping, backdoor). It proposes no defense, only noting that buffer integrity is required. Useful as motivation, not prior art.

hits.title: Online AutoML: Evaluating Poisoning Attacks on Cost-Utility Adversarial Training Defence Strategy for IoT Networks (Nwokoye, El-Khatib, Li Yang)
hits.how_close: Streaming IoT detectors under label-flip and noise-injection poisoning, defended by adversarial training and checked with ADWIN, DDM and EDDM. The setting overlaps (IoT, streaming), but the mechanism does not: no unsupervised baseline, no threat subspace, no budget. Whether the poisoning is gradual is not confirmed.

hits.title: ADAPT: A Pseudo-labeling Approach to Combat Concept Drift in Malware Detection (Alam, Piplai, Rastogi)
hits.how_close: Self-training under drift for security, where a self-labelling loop is the attack surface RMSB protects. The abstract states no adversarial threat model and no direction-wise rationing. Distant.

hits.conclusion:
The idea survived the attempt to kill it, with caveats. No paper found does what RMSB does: learn a threat subspace from persistent, stationary clusters of the detector's own rejected traffic, then ration the part of each update that falls in that subspace under one shared cumulative budget (center and spread), with a bound on time to compromise, while always applying the orthogonal part. The search covered 2024-2026 arXiv, IEEE, ACM, NDSS, USENIX, Springer and Elsevier.

Each piece has precedent:
1. **Rejection memory.** Clustering rejected examples and testing whether they persist is MINAS-style novelty detection (DMKD 2016). MINAS uses persistence to adopt a cluster as a new class; RMSB inverts that and uses persistence to protect against the cluster.
2. **Update decomposition.** Removing the part of an update that lies along a harm direction is SafeGrad (arXiv 2025, LLM fine-tuning). Its direction comes from curated safety data, it removes that part entirely rather than budgeting it, and it gives no guarantee. Polly (arXiv 2026) and GPM (ICLR 2021) project onto or away from a subspace learned from data, but for other goals.
3. **Bounding cumulative displacement.** Kloft and Laskov (JMLR 2012) bound displacement, but their remedy is a freeze. Newton (ICDCS 2012) uses fixed physical invariants. Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025) give certified bounds against adaptive online poisoners for mean estimation and classification.
4. **Security-venue drift adaptation.** OWAD (NDSS 2023) explicitly leaves adversarial robustness to future work. Korycki and Krawczyk (Machine Learning 2023), Hinder et al. (ESANN 2025), and Yang, Lie and Papernot (arXiv 2026) treat adversarial drift at the level of drift detectors. None rations updates by direction.

So the honest novelty claim is the combination plus the theorem, in the setting of a continuously adapting, unsupervised, low-traffic IoT detector. It is not any single ingredient.

The biggest threats from prior work:
- **The alarm pool is attackable.** Perdisci et al. (S&P 2006), Paragraph (RAID 2006) and Allergy (RAID 2006) show an attacker can pollute the suspicious pool that a learner reads from the IDS. That makes decoy modes and allergy-style freezing a known attack class. RMSB must show that rules (b), per-mode budget shares and the stationarity requirement, defeat it, and should cite these papers as the decoy threat model.
- **The omission case.** When the attacker sends no traffic to the target until after compromise, no rejected mode exists. Then only backstop (a) protects the detector, so that guarantee must be stated and evaluated on its own.
- **Write up the inversion.** Persistent rejected modes are exactly what novelty detectors such as MINAS, Kuppa and Le-Khac, and OWAD-style adaptation are built to absorb. A legitimate new service is therefore indistinguishable from an attack target at first. The d/B liveness cost is the price, and reviewers will ask for it to be measured on real drift.
- **Unverified items.** RepShield (Computer Networks, projection-based continual-learning NIDS) could not be verified (HTTP 403). It should be re-checked for any poisoning claim.

The web-search budget for this turn ran out, so several planned searches did not run:
- the 'distributional quarantine' defense mentioned on a Lacuna overview page;
- Sybil or multi-direction poisoning defenses in federated learning that use a shared cumulative budget;
- Wasswa and Lynar (arXiv 2512.22488);
- SOUL, a continual-learning NIDS that uses gradient projection memory.

Re-run these in a follow-up before claiming novelty in writing. All years and URLs above come from pages fetched or listed in this session; details marked as not read or unverified should be checked against the full texts.

novelty.name: Event-Licensed Adaptation: signed firmware and provisioning events unlock a time-boxed fast-learning budget

verdict.name: Event-Licensed Adaptation: signed firmware and provisioning events unlock a time-boxed fast-learning budget
verdict.closest: Cisco US Patent US9923911B2, "Anomaly detection supporting new application deployments" (Vasseur, Dasgupta, Mermoud; filed 2015, granted 2018). An NMS-originated NEW-APP message, which carries a schedule and a deployment scope, puts the detector into a "fast learning mode" that "increase[s] its learning rate temporarily". Claim 10 recites increasing the training rate. The old model can keep running in parallel, and an observation mode suppresses alerts. Runner-up: HADES-IoT (Breitenbacher et al., 2019). Signed one-time-signature owner commands with a replay counter disable the detector, re-profile it after a firmware update, and re-enable it. Operational precedent: Microsoft Defender for IoT gives newly discovered devices a 7-day learning window and lets an admin set a per-alert learning window in hours.
verdict.reasoning:
The headline idea is already published, so it cannot be claimed as new. That idea is: an external device or deployment event temporarily raises the detector's learning rate inside a scoped, time-boxed window. Three sources cover it from different sides:
- Cisco US9923911B2 has the event-triggered temporary learning-rate increase, with scope, a schedule and a parallel old model.
- HADES-IoT has a cryptographically signed firmware-update command that unlocks re-profiling, with replay protection.
- Defender for IoT has scoped, time-boxed relearning windows in a shipping product.

Close variants exist too:
- DIoT (ICDCS 2019) re-learns after firmware updates, triggered by fleet-wide alarm correlation plus a human.
- Sivanathan's thesis retrains after an operator confirms the upgrade.
- MUD (RFC 8520) and the MUD acceptable-URLs draft already give the gateway a signer-pinned, firmware-driven statement of normal behaviour, but use it for policy, not learning.

So "signed event, then faster learning" is an obvious combination of Cisco and HADES-IoT, and a reviewer would say so.

None of the three searches found the following parts, and the patent and HADES-IoT do not cover them:
- (a) The token is cryptographically bound to the gateway's own check of the OTA image or provisioning, and carries device_id, fw_hash, t_start, K and scope. Cisco's message is not described as authenticated. HADES-IoT's command is manual, host-based, and fully disables the detector.
- (b) A two-rate design that never freezes, with an explicit displacement bound B*t + N_lic*K*B_L*kappa_rev, where N_lic is tied to the signing key. This extends the bounds in Kloft and Laskov (JMLR 2012) and Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025) with a licensed term.
- (c) A directional revert at licence end that removes only the threat-subspace component of the update, instead of a full rollback, a freeze or alert suppression.
- (d) New per-device instances spawn only under a provisioning licence and start from a peer prior. This directly answers the Ino et al. (Sensors 2024) drift-spawn hijack, which offers no countermeasure.

Coverage caveats. Web-search budgets ran out in all three searches, so 2025-2026 coverage is thin. ESP32/TinyML signed-OTA IDS work and selective-rollback work were never searched. Whether the Cisco patent authenticates its message was not confirmed from the full text.

Feasibility errors in the mechanism text that need fixing:
- Mbed TLS has no Ed25519 support (issue #2452 is still open). Use ECDSA-P256.
- Secure Boot V2 on the original ESP32 is RSA-PSS-3072 only.
- Signed-app OTA without hardware Secure Boot does not stop an attacker with flash write access.

Threats that weaken the bound:
- Downgrade or replay of a validly signed old image or token. This needs monotonic versions or counters, plus gateway attestation that the device actually runs fw_hash.
- A window-timed attacker who puts all the poison inside predictable OTA windows, as in Kravchik and Shabtai's threat model.
- Attacker-induced legitimate events, such as forcing a factory reset so an admin re-provisions the device. That inflates N_lic.
- kappa_rev < 1 holds only along the known threat subspace U. Movement toward unknown attacks during a licence is unbounded.
verdict.how_to_differentiate:
Present the paper as "authenticated change-management for poisonable self-learning detectors", not as "event-triggered fast adaptation". Cite Cisco US9923911B2, HADES-IoT, DIoT, Defender for IoT and MUD/RFC 8520 as prior art for the trigger idea.

Claim four contributions as new:
1. A provable bound on attacker displacement, B*t + N_lic*K*B_L*kappa_rev. The attacker cannot raise N_lic without the signing key. Build it on Kloft and Laskov (JMLR 2012) and Bose et al. (AISTATS 2025), and state assumptions explicitly: replay protection, anti-rollback, and what happens to kappa_rev outside the subspace U.
2. The directional threat-subspace revert, as an alternative to freezing, full rollback, or alert suppression.
3. The licence-only spawn rule with a peer-prior start, evaluated directly against the Ino et al. (Sensors 2024) instance hijack.
4. A token construction that the gateway can verify, bound to verified OTA, SUIT (RFC 9019) or MUD events. It should include a nonce or monotonic counter and an anti-downgrade check.

Evaluate against these baselines:
- Cisco-style unsigned fast-learning mode
- HADES-style disable and re-profile
- DIoT-style fleet-correlated relearning
- An inferred-event baseline (Andrews et al., ACM TOIT 2026, firmware-change detection from traffic)
- Drift-test-gated adaptation (OWAD/DriftXpert-style)
- Always-on slow learning only

Include these adversaries:
- A boiling-frog attacker
- An attacker who times poison to licence windows
- A token-replay or downgrade attacker
- An attacker who induces re-provisioning

Show that the measured displacement stays under the bound, and that false-positive recovery after a real OTA matches the fast-learning baselines.

Fix the feasibility claims: use ECDSA-P256 in mbedTLS, and use Secure Boot V2 with RSA-PSS on the original ESP32 or ECDSA on S3/C6-class parts.

Before finalising, run the 2025-2026 searches that never completed. Topics: ESP32/TinyML IDS with signed OTA; selective or directional rollback of poisoned updates; attestation-gated retraining; and OTA-aware continual NIDS.

hits.title: Anomaly detection supporting new application deployments (US Patent US9923911B2, Cisco Technology Inc.)
hits.year: Priority 2015-10-08, granted 2018-03-20 (background, but the closest prior art)
hits.how_close: CLOSEST. This patent already describes the core 'event unlocks a temporary fast-learning mode' idea. A supervisory device (the NMS) sends a NEW-APP message to the supervisory agent, which tells the distributed learning agents about a planned deployment. An agent can then (a) enter a 'fast learning mode' and 'increase its learning rate temporarily' (claim 10 recites 'increasing a training rate for the merged anomaly detection model'), (b) keep its previous model running in parallel in case a real anomaly happens during the deployment, and (c) enter an 'observation mode' that suppresses alerts and sends a summary instead. MISSING compared with your idea: the message is not cryptographically signed (the text I read does not mention authentication). The duration is just 'temporarily', with no K-cycle budget. There is no scoping to one device or firmware hash. There is no slow background budget B or bound on attacker displacement. There is no directional revert along a threat subspace. And the event is not the only way to spawn a model. This patent removes any claim that 'event-triggered temporary learning-rate boost' is new; what is left is the security formalisation.

hits.title: DÏoT: A Federated Self-learning Anomaly Detection System for IoT (Nguyen, Marchal, Miettinen, Fereidooni, Asokan, Sadeghi), IEEE ICDCS 2019
hits.how_close: Close on the problem, different trigger. Sec. 'Evolution of IoT Device Behavior' (I checked the PDF text) says firmware updates cause false alarms. If many Security Gateways raise alarms for the same device type in a short time, the system 'can cancel the alarm and trigger re-learning' of the device-identification and anomaly models, and a human expert may confirm the cancellation so a malware outbreak is not mistaken for an update. So the update is inferred from fleet-wide alarm correlation plus a human; there is no signed token. Re-learning is a full relearn, not a rate-limited, time-boxed window. There is no bound and no directional revert. An attacker who causes synchronised alarms could in principle trigger re-learning, which is the gap your token closes.

hits.title: Data Poisoning Attack against Neural Network-Based On-Device Learning Anomaly Detector by Physical Attacks on Sensors (Ino, Yoshida, Matsutani, Fujino), Sensors 24(19):6416
hits.how_close: This is the 'Sensors 2024 hijack' your idea cites; it is an attack, not prior art for the defense. Confirmed: the detector watches the data centroid, and when drift passes a threshold it automatically spawns a new model instance trained on current data. Acoustic injection into a MEMS accelerometer makes the detector spawn a poisoned instance that later reconstructs real abnormal vibration as normal. The paper proposes no countermeasure and says one is needed. This supports your rule that only a licensed provisioning event may spawn an instance, and shows that rule is not yet published as a defense.

hits.title: Authorized update to MUD URLs (draft-ietf-opsawg-mud-acceptable-urls-11; Richardson, Pan, Lear)
hits.year: 2024 (Internet-Draft, 1 Mar 2024; expired and replaced by draft-ietf-iotops-mud-acceptable-urls; RFC status not verified)
hits.how_close: Gives an authenticated firmware-update signal to the gateway or controller, but uses it for policy, not learning. 'MUD URLs can only be updated by shipping a new firmware.' A new MUD URL is accepted only if it shares the base URI and its MUD file is signed by the same pinned signer, and the controller tracks old URLs against rollback. It explicitly notes a false-positive problem when firmware and policy drift apart. It does not mention anomaly detection, learning rates or retraining. It is a ready-made standards hook for your token (or an alternative to it), and you should cite it as such. The draft itself says the DHCP/LLDP channels that carry the URL are unsigned and malware could change them.

hits.title: Cold start mechanism to prevent compromise of automatic anomaly detection systems (US9838409B2 / continuation US10182066B2, Cisco)
hits.how_close: Partial. It guards against poisoning during initial learning: a supervised model trained offline first checks that the network is not already compromised. Unsupervised training starts only if no anomaly is found, and it can be suspended (indefinitely or for a set period) when the supervised model fires. This is gating learning on a check, close to your 'join-time poisoning' concern for provisioning. It is not an authenticated device event, there is no rate budget or bound, and suspending on detection is exactly the 'freeze on suspicion' behaviour your idea rejects. Second US number from Google Patents (US10182066B2 is a continuation of application 14/878,145); I could not confirm that the parent is US9838409.

hits.title: IoT Behavioral Monitoring via Network Traffic Analysis (Arunan Sivanathan, thesis, arXiv:2001.10632)
hits.how_close: Partial. Per-device models that 'dynamically accommodate ... updates to existing' devices. According to the search snippet of the PDF (I did not read the full text myself), an operator confirms a firmware upgrade after the engine flags anomalies, then the device model is retrained on about two weeks of post-upgrade data. It also says automatic update detection was not evaluated because labels were lacking. The trigger is a manual human confirmation, not a signed token, and there is no bound or revert.

hits.title: IoT Firmware Version Identification Using Transfer Learning with Twin Neural Networks (Andrews, Oikonomou, Armour, Thomas, Cattermole), ACM TOIT 2026

Useful as a baseline: an inferred event can be spoofed or missed, while a signed one cannot be minted.

hits.title: Methodology for intelligent pattern detection and anomaly detection in machine to machine communication network (US12375508B2, Aeris Communications)
hits.how_close: Weak. It infers an OTA firmware update from a high-download-then-high-upload pattern and cross-device correlation, then alerts. There is no authenticated signal and no change to how the detector learns.

There is no signed event or token, no varying learning-rate budget, and no poisoning analysis.

hits.how_close: Weak. It names firmware updates as a cause of concept drift on an IoT testbed of 10 devices, but retraining is triggered by drift detection only. It does not use update events, the learning rate is fixed at Adam's default, and it does not analyse poisoning during retraining.
