corpus.title: Self-Poisoning in Adaptive Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Sharp-Threshold Theory and Certified Label-Free Calibration (methods named WARDEN and CDC)
corpus.authors: Vishnu Bindu Balachandran, sole author, listed as "Independent Researcher" (outlook.com email). No institution.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2607.21673, v1 submitted 23 July 2026. Primary category cs.LG, cross-listed to cs.AI, cs.CR, cs.CV and stat.ML. 28 pages, 5 figures, CC BY 4.0. No venue is listed, so it is not peer-reviewed. The author mentions a companion manuscript under review on spectral OOD detection from a single batch and says the two papers share no theorems.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21673 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.21673v1, PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.21673, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2607.21673)
corpus.problem: Test-time adaptive OOD detectors update a memory from the unlabelled stream using pseudo-labels. AdaODD-style detectors (Zhang et al., arXiv 2311.16420) add the most normal-looking points to an ID bank. OODD-style detectors (Yang et al., CVPR 2025) add the most OOD-looking points to an OOD dictionary. Every point wrongly admitted makes the next wrong admission more likely. The paper calls this self-poisoning and claims it behaves like a phase transition, not gradual degradation. A second problem is that a detector calibrated once at training time goes stale under drift. With nominal alpha = 0.10 it actually gives FPR 0.194, about 1.94 times nominal. The paper asks whether false positives can be controlled without labels while still adapting.
corpus.method:
(1) Theory. Impurity rho_t is the share of wrongly admitted points in the bank. It is modelled as a generalized Polya urn in stochastic-approximation form: rho_t = rho_{t-1} + gamma_t[h(rho_{t-1}) + noise], where h(rho) = q(rho) - rho and q is the admission kernel (the chance that the next admitted point is wrong). The paper proves almost-sure convergence to the zeros of h. For an affine kernel q(rho) = min{a + b*rho, 1}, the slope b works like a reproduction number. If b < 1, impurity settles at a benign level a/(1-b). If b >= 1, impurity goes to 1 (full poisoning). Saturating kernels add a fold bifurcation with hysteresis. Results are also given for capped banks with uniform eviction. Literal FIFO eviction leads to a delay equation that the paper does not pursue. pi_c is the critical contamination rate.
(2) WARDEN (certified admission). It holds a frozen reserve of held-out ID points (m = 1500) that is never refreshed. Each candidate gets a conformal p-value against the reserve, computed with the frozen base scorer (kNN-to-bank), never with the dictionary. These p-values become e-values e_i = a*p_i^(a-1), and e-BH at level delta gates admission per batch (K = 64). Admitted points go into the OOD dictionary. The dictionary feeds only a second decision channel and never the admission evidence, which cuts the feedback loop. Lemma 8 and Theorem 9 bound wrong admissions independently of rho, so there is no supercritical branch. Corollary 10 extends this to an adversary who knows everything, under the assumption that true-ID points are exchangeable with the reserve. Decisions come from two conformal channels at alpha/2 each. Ranking uses the frozen base score, so AUROC equals the frozen baseline by construction.
(3) CDC (certified decontaminated calibration). It takes conformal p-values of an unlabelled window (n around 4000) against the stale training reserve. It estimates contamination with Storey's method (lambda = 1/2) plus a Hoeffding slack to get pi_up. The threshold is the window quantile at level 1 - alpha(1 - pi_up) + eps_n (DKW slack); if that level exceeds 1, the threshold becomes +infinity. Each window decides first and updates after. In the paper's words, it "corrects the quantile level instead of the sample", so there is no sample selection or trimming.
(4) Theorem 15, two-world impossibility. World A has ID drift that inflates the tail, with no contamination. World B has no drift but a share pi of tail-mimicking contamination. Both produce the same unlabelled stream. So any label-free threshold rule that keeps FPR <= alpha in World A has TPR <= kappa = alpha/(pi + alpha(1-pi)) in World B. Remark 16 gives kappa = 0.917, 0.690 and 0.526 at pi = 0.01, 0.05 and 0.10. A labelled oracle escapes this ceiling.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Data: no IoT or network data at all. Vision uses ResNet-18 and ViT trained with OpenOOD, with CIFAR-10/100 as ID and MNIST, SVHN, DTD, TIN, Places and CIFAR cross-pairs as OOD. Frozen foundation encoders are DINOv2 and CLIP. Text uses RoBERTa on SST-2 with 20News, AGNews and MNLI as OOD. Documents use LayoutLMv3 on Tobacco (intra and cross) and finance. There are 96 settings across four encoder families. The paper also cites 9,264 streaming cells in the main campaigns, plus 4,800, 6,960 and 3,840 cells in different places; these counts are never reconciled.
Stream: each point is OOD with probability pi in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5}. Arrival is i.i.d. or bursty (contiguous OOD blocks). Drift is a per-dimension variance change in whitened feature space; no magnitude is given in what I read. Settings: alpha = delta = 0.10, five exploration seeds, then a one-shot held-out replication on five new seeds with pre-registered hard gates.
Hardware: none stated. All experiments run on cached features, and end-to-end retraining is out of scope. No GPU, edge device, runtime, memory or energy numbers are reported. Code and artifacts are promised only "upon acceptance", and no repository is linked.
corpus.results:
Phenomenon 1: on bursty streams with pi <= 0.1, the ungated OOD dictionary loses 0.163 mean AUROC against its own frozen baseline. Single families lose up to 0.28, near-OOD pairs fall below chance, and impurity exceeds 0.9. The ungated ID bank loses only 0.026. At pi = 0.01 bursty, all 96 settings are harmed, by up to 0.41 AUROC.
Threshold law: the fitted kernel is q(rho) = a + b*rho with R^2 of 0.996-0.997 in each family, b around 0.944-0.947 and a around 0.05. That is just below the threshold, yet it predicts rho* near 1. The predicted pi_c falls within tolerance on 96/96 knee settings.
WARDEN: impurity is <= 0.111 in every standard cell, mean FPR is 0.056 (worst cell 0.121), and AUROC change is 0.000 by construction.
CDC: static FPR is 0.194; CDC certifies 100% of the drift-affected cells it was tested on, with mean FPR 0.042 (0.043 on held-out seeds). Median TPR retention against the oracle is 0.665 (0.632 held-out). The paper calls the power loss real: about 33-37% of oracle TPR.
Held-out replication: collapse reproduces (AUROC loss 0.114, 84% of cells harmed). The paper calls the collapse size seed-sensitive (0.11-0.16).
Gray-box tail-mimicry attack (App. D.2): outliers are moved toward their nearest reserve neighbour, eps in {0, ..., 0.9}, over 360 cells. Certificates hold with no failures, and FPR falls from 0.058 to 0.045. The dictionary gets no admissions ("the dictionary starves"), and TPR falls from 0.615 to 0.004. The ungated dictionary stays above 0.91 impurity.
App. D.1: the dictionary channel adds essentially no detection power (+0.000 to +0.008 TPR). The paper makes no state-of-the-art AUROC claim, and says adaptation "buys no AUROC" on well-whitened features.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the author: (i) the 1-D impurity state and affine reduction are "a modelling step"; richer state such as cluster structure is future work. (ii) The validity theorem assumes an exchangeable window, and the extension to dependent windows is loose; the author calls a tight dependent-window certificate "the principal open theoretical problem". (iii) CDC loses real power, about 33-37% of oracle TPR at pi <= 0.1. (iv) Guarantees are per batch, not time-uniform; an anytime version via stopped e-BH is open. (v) Adaptation gives no AUROC gain. (vi) Only feature-space tail mimicry was tested; "gradient-based input-space poisoning in the style of Su et al. (2025) ... is untested". (vii) Transaction fraud, intrusion detection and clinical monitoring are "in scope of the theory but untested here", and kernel coefficients must be re-measured for each domain. (viii) Results use cached features only.
Not stated but true, from my reading: the reserve is frozen and never refreshed, so ID-side adaptation is given up entirely and drift is handled only by re-quantiling. There are no compute, memory or edge results. There is no gradual boiling-frog attacker that shifts the reference over time. The cell counts are inconsistent. It is a single-author preprint with no peer review and no code yet.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Moderate on framing, low on our mechanisms.
(a) Self-poisoning of a self-labelling detector: same root phenomenon as ours. The paper now owns the threshold-theory version (Polya urn, b like a reproduction number, critical pi_c, July 2026). It cites Kloft and Laskov 2012 and calls WARDEN a "conformal completion" of that program. It does not cite ANTIDOTE or use the term "boiling frog". Its contamination is mostly natural OOD plus one corollary about adversaries, not a deliberate gradual drift attack on the centre. We must cite it and must not claim to be first to theorize self-poisoning.
(b) TOA-like direction budgeting: no. There is no splitting of updates into directions or subspaces, no attack-signature direction, no slow budget on movement toward an attack, and no minimum time to compromise. Its only "budget" caps the number of wrong admissions per batch through e-BH (about 0.62 per batch, Lemma 8).
(c) Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. The paper deliberately avoids sample selection and trimming. It cites Wang 2026 to say trimming "provably recovers little" under drift. Admission is judged against a frozen external reserve, not the current model's dense core, and nothing is backed up by the outer ring.
(d) Freeze-type attack: not described. Two points come close. First, WARDEN is itself a permanently frozen-reference design (frozen scorer and reserve), and Phenomenon 2 shows frozen calibration under honest drift inflates FPR to 1.94 times nominal. That is the mechanism our freeze attack exploits, but the paper treats it as natural staleness, not something an attacker triggers, and patches it with CDC. Second, under tail mimicry "the dictionary starves", meaning the attacker shuts off adaptation. That is harmless here only because the dictionary adds no power. No attacker is shown driving false alarms up by tripping the gate.
(e) Biggest direct overlap with our open problem 1 (attack hidden inside strong genuine drift beats our signature-free method): Theorem 15 proves that, in 1-D score space and without labels, drift and contamination cannot be told apart, and caps power at kappa. Our failure is likely an instance of this theorem, not a fixable bug.
(f) No IoT, no network traffic, no Kitsune or N-BaIoT, no ESP32 or on-device evaluation, no centroid detector, and no per-device detectors.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. The urn/threshold lens. Measure the admission kernel q(rho) for our naive centroid self-labeller on N-BaIoT, and check whether b >= 1 and whether the predicted pi_c matches the 10% attacker share we observed. Then show that TOA and the core/ring update keep b < 1. That gives our empirical results a theory figure in the same style as theirs.
2. A published baseline for open problem 4. Re-implement WARDEN (conformal p-values, e-values, e-BH, frozen reserve) and CDC, which should be quick because both are simple, and attack them on N-BaIoT/Kitsune. The paper says intrusion detection is untested, so this would be the first IDS evaluation. Our inference, not in the paper: CDC's threshold level is 1 - alpha(1 - pi_up) + eps_n. An attacker who sends many slightly-off but benign-looking points can inflate the Storey estimate pi_up and push the threshold toward +infinity, which blinds the detector. That is a blinding counterpart to our freeze attack that we could demonstrate. Also test boiling-frog drift, since WARDEN's frozen ID side cannot follow honest drift and relies on CDC at a 33-37% power cost.
3. Theorem 15 as positioning. Label-free methods hit a provable power ceiling kappa = alpha/(pi + alpha(1-pi)). TOA's attack signature is exactly the side information or separation assumption the theorem says is needed. Multi-dimensional direction information may also break the 1-D two-world indistinguishability, which is a candidate theorem for us. Report our TPR against kappa.
4. A CDC-style label-free threshold correction (Storey estimate plus DKW slack) as a cheap FPR guard on top of our detector on ESP32. It needs one quantile over a window of scores. A 1500-point reserve at our PCA dimension (about 10) is around 60 KB in float32, which looks feasible in ESP32 SRAM (my estimate).
5. Evaluation rigour: many settings and seeds, pre-registered pass/fail gates, a one-shot held-out replication, and both bursty and i.i.d. arrival. This is the level an A/A* venue would expect.
6. Their open problems match IoT well: dependent and bursty windows (network traffic is autocorrelated), time-uniform guarantees via stopped e-BH (Wang, Dandapanthula, Ramdas, arXiv 2502.08539), state richer than 1-D or with cluster structure (which leads to per-device detectors, our open problem 2), and untested adaptive or gradient attackers (Su et al., ICLR 2025, arXiv 2410.04682).
7. Related citations worth pulling: Bashari, Sesia, Romano, "Robust conformal outlier detection under contaminated reference data" (ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.04807); Wang 2026 on trimming and contaminated calibration (arXiv 2605.06204); OODD (CVPR 2025, arXiv 2503.10468); RDumb (NeurIPS 2023).

I could not find the drift magnitude, any compute or hardware details, or a code repository, because the paper does not give them.

corpus.title: Theory of Continual Learning Against Data Poisoning Attacks
corpus.authors: Yiting Hu (Singapore University of Technology and Design; HKUST Guangzhou) and Lingjie Duan (HKUST Guangzhou, corresponding author). Affiliations are as printed in the arXiv HTML v1.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29841 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29841v1, PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.29841)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, cs.LG primary with cs.GT. v1 was submitted 29 June 2026 and is the only version. The paper uses the ICML template ("Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML") and has an Impact Statement. No proceedings, PMLR volume or acceptance note appears anywhere, so acceptance at ICML 2026 or any other venue is NOT verified. My web-search budget ran out before I could cross-check this.
corpus.problem: Data poisoning of regularization-based continual learning (CL). Tasks arrive one at a time and the model is updated by w_t = argmin [task-t loss + ||w - w_{t-1}||^2 weighted by a matrix H_t], so past data is discarded. Attacker and defender play an online zero-sum game. The defender picks H_t. The attacker knows the model state and data, and perturbs task data under a budget E||eta_t||^2 <= M. The theory assumes label-only poisoning in continual linear regression. Attacks are sorted along 3 axes: (1) frequency: frequent means K attacked tasks grows linearly with T, infrequent means K = O(1); (2) magnitude: unbounded means M = Omega(T), bounded means M = o(T); (3) pattern: shifted means the perturbation has a deterministic mean shift, non-shifted means zero-mean noise. The question is which regimes can be defended at all, and how.
corpus.method:
(a) Impossibility, Theorem 3.1. No method in the regularized family can guarantee convergence under (i) frequent shifted attacks or (ii) frequent, unbounded, non-shifted attacks. The proof uses a 1-D regression with a constant shift Delta. The mean error follows m_t = c_t*m_{t-1} + (1-c_t)*Delta, so the estimate converges to the attacker's shift. This is exactly an exponential-moving-average mean being dragged by a persistent bias, the same structure as our centroid boiling-frog.

(b) Task-to-task (T2T) verification, against infrequent unbounded shifted attacks. The detection score is d_t = ||D1_t(w_t - w_{t-1}) - D2_t(w_{t-1} - w_{t-2})||, a projected second difference of consecutive model updates. The projections D1 and D2 are built from Hessians and regularizers so that d_t depends only on tasks t-1 and t. The threshold theta_t is a high-probability bound on benign pairs (Lemma 4.3, tighter under sub-Gaussian noise). The heuristic used in experiments flags a pair when its score exceeds 2.5x the mean of the previous 5 scores. A flagged pair triggers a rollback, w_t = w_{t-2} and H_t = H_{t-2}, which throws away BOTH tasks because the method cannot tell which one was poisoned. Theorem 4.4 gives excess risk O(K^2/(eps*T)), assuming informative data. Storage is 3p^2 + 2p, or O(p) with diagonal Hessians.

(c) Robust feature defense, against frequent, bounded, non-shifted attacks. Here rejection is untenable because almost every task is poisoned. It assumes the task covariances commute (shared eigenbasis U, Assumption 5.1) and sets H_t = U*Lambda_t*U^T, solving the minimax per eigendirection in closed form (Prop. 5.2). The top-ranked directions form a protected set where the adversary concentrates its budget, and these get a larger penalty lambda_j. The other directions get lambda_j = sigma^2/(n_t*R_j). A direction with zero previous risk gets lambda_j = +infinity, which freezes it. Theorem 5.3 shows that spreading worst-case sensitivity beats the baseline's single worst direction (the Zhao et al. ICML 2024 regularizer). The attacker's best response lines up with the top singular direction of a sensitivity matrix.
corpus.data_and_hardware: CIFAR-100 with frozen ViT-B/16 features (768-dim) and a trained linear head (AdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 128, 10 epochs per task). CIFAR-10 with a small CNN trained from scratch (Adam, lr 2e-3), using a diagonal-Hessian version of the defense. Each dataset is split into 100 tasks of 500 examples, and the full clean test set is evaluated after each task. Shifted attack: 10 of 100 tasks get a constant +10 added to every feature coordinate. Non-shifted attack: every task is poisoned with budget M = 2000, using the inner maximization of their surrogate objective. Synthetic linear experiment: p=8, T=10, n_t=20, sigma^2=1, M=10, W=1, 500 Monte Carlo runs. Baselines are EWC, iCaRL (5 or 10 exemplars per class) and an attack-free run. Hardware and GPU are NOT stated anywhere I read. Nothing involves IoT, network traffic, edge or embedded devices, or unsupervised or anomaly-detection learners.
corpus.results: The visible text and figure captions report results only qualitatively. I found no numeric accuracy tables. Under infrequent shifted attacks, detection-score peaks line up with the truly attacked tasks on both CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 (Fig. 2). T2T keeps accuracy close to the attack-free run, while EWC and iCaRL converge more slowly. iCaRL beats EWC under shifted attacks because its clean exemplars limit drift, but it is much worse under frequent attacks. The robust feature defense speeds convergence and reduces accuracy loss under frequent bounded non-shifted attacks (Fig. 3). CIFAR-100, with pretrained features, is more stable than CIFAR-10. The synthetic log-excess-risk figure (Fig. 4) is described, but I could not see its values.
corpus.limitations: Stated: the theory needs continual linear regression or the NTK/lazy-training regime, commuting covariances (only relaxed in the synthetic test), sub-Gaussian noise for the tight bounds, a stationary regime for the protected-set rate, and approximate Hessians (K-FAC or Gauss-Newton) for both the attacker and CIFAR-10. Future work is extending to large networks and to replay-based CL. Not stated, but clearly present: supervised, task-segmented CL with known task boundaries; no streaming or unsupervised self-labeling; no real concept drift beyond task shifts; small-scale experiments with no numbers in the text; no hardware or cost report. No adaptive attacker targets the defense itself, and nobody analyzes gradual poisoning that stays under the threshold.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overall: medium on theory, low on system and setting. Point by point:

(1) TOA-like direction budgeting: PARTIAL, conceptually adjacent but not the same. The robust feature defense damps movement per eigendirection, with stronger penalties on a protected set of directions the attacker is expected to target. A reviewer will see this as related to TOA, so we must cite and contrast it. It does NOT split updates into a component along a known attack signature and an orthogonal component applied in full. It has no cumulative slow budget over time and no minimum-time-to-compromise guarantee (its guarantee is asymptotic excess-risk convergence). Its directions come from the data covariance, not from attack signatures. Soft penalties apply to all directions, and some directions are frozen outright (lambda = +infinity). TOA's specific construction and guarantee remain novel relative to this paper.

(2) Core/outer-ring robust updating: NO overlap. Nothing is density-based, there is no core/periphery logic, and spread is never gated. T2T is a consistency check on consecutive parameter updates plus rollback.

(3) Freeze-type attack: NOT described. But both defenses are freeze-vulnerable by design. T2T's rollback throws away the benign neighbouring task too (they call this an attribution problem). An attacker who triggers flags occasionally can therefore make the model discard honest updates repeatedly while real drift builds up, which is our freeze attack. The lambda = +infinity directions are a built-in freezing mechanism. The paper never treats either as an attack surface.

(4) Our open problem 1, an attack hidden inside genuine drift: Theorem 3.1 essentially formalizes it. Frequent shifted poisoning, which is what boiling-frog is, cannot be beaten by any regularization-based learner, and their 1-D proof is literally a moving-average mean dragged by a bias. That supports us rather than scooping us.

(5) Setting: no IoT, intrusion detection, unsupervised or self-labeling detectors, real network data, or on-device or ESP32 work. This is a theory paper on supervised CL with CIFAR images.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
(1) Their frequency x magnitude x pattern taxonomy can structure our threat model and evaluation grid. Boiling-frog is "frequent, bounded, shifted". The freeze attack is a new axis they lack: attacking the defender's own rejection rule.

(2) Cite Theorem 3.1 to turn open problem 1 into a principled negative result: a signature-free, regularization-style learner cannot separate frequent shifted poison from drift. Then position TOA's escape route as side information (signature direction) plus a time-to-compromise guarantee instead of convergence. Per-device or cross-device consensus is the other side-information route, which also fits open problem 2. We could prove a short corollary of their result for our EWMA centroid.

(3) Use T2T as the PUBLISHED defense for our freeze attack (closes open problem 4). The centroid version is simple: d_t = ||(c_t - c_{t-1}) - (c_{t-1} - c_{t-2})||, with rollback when the score exceeds 2.5x the mean of the last 5 scores. Then show that occasional spikes force repeated rollbacks, the model stalls during honest drift, and false alarms rise. Their robust feature defense's lambda = +infinity freezing is a second target.

(4) Our PCA space is an eigenbasis, so their shared-eigenbasis assumption roughly holds there. Their per-eigendirection lambda_j design can be implemented cheaply as a strong baseline against TOA's signature-direction budget, and their diagonal-Hessian O(p) memory variant suits ESP32.

(5) Their game-theoretic adversary moves along the top singular direction of the defender's sensitivity. We can reuse that to build a stronger adaptive attacker against TOA: poison along the most sensitive direction orthogonal to the signature, which tests TOA's weakest point.

(6) Report bounds in their style (excess risk vs number of attacked tasks K) next to our time-to-compromise bound for a crisper theory section.

Caveat: WebFetch returns a model summary of the page, not raw text, so equations and thresholds above are paraphrased, not copied exactly. I found no numeric result tables in the text (results are figure-only and described qualitatively), and hardware is not stated. I could not verify publication status beyond arXiv because the shared web-search budget ran out before I could cross-check the venue. corpus.title: Feature-Context Consistency: Unsupervised Adversarial Detection with Drift Stability on Attributed Graphs
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16694 (HTML full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.16694v1; PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16694; code: https://github.com/serval-uni-lu/CB-RBM, MIT license, Python/PyTorch, which I checked exists)
corpus.authors: Firas Bayram, Maxime Cordy. The arXiv page and README give no institution. The GitHub org name "serval-uni-lu" suggests the SERVAL group at the University of Luxembourg, but that is my guess and I have not checked it.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv v1 posted 12 Oct 2026 (cs.LG, cross-listed cs.AI). The arXiv journal-ref field says Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 39 (NeurIPS 2026), and the repo README also says NeurIPS 2026. I have not checked this against the official NeurIPS proceedings or OpenReview. Year: 2026.
corpus.problem: Finding adversarial or fraud nodes in an attributed graph that changes over time, with no labels (labels are scarce or arrive late) and while the distribution drifts and degrades trained models. The attacker adds nodes and edges it controls but cannot change existing nodes' features. Four attacks: (1) Isolated Injection: fraud features with random context. (2) Feature Camouflage: legitimate-looking features with random context. (3) Sybil: fraud features linked to a 50-node clique of near-legitimate decoys, which fakes context. (4) Relation Camouflage: fraud features linked to the 10 highest-degree legitimate nodes, giving partly genuine context. The paper says training-time poisoning (topology poisoning, backdoors) is out of scope. White-box PGD is only an appendix stress test.
corpus.method: Core idea, "feature-context consistency": a legitimate node's own attributes match the aggregated attributes of its neighbours, and an injected node's do not. Context = sign-corrected mean of neighbour features. The sign vector is estimated once from unlabeled training statistics and then fixed. The model, CB-RBM, is a Gaussian-Bernoulli RBM with a GLU-gated context pathway; with zero context it reduces to a plain RBM. Score: Context Boost (CB) = sum over hidden units of the softplus difference in free energy with and without context. Detection score s = -CB. Threshold = 95th percentile on a calibration slice of the assumed-legitimate pool (target FPR 5%). Training: one-class, CD-1, 100 epochs, no attack labels. IMPORTANT: there is NO online or self-labelled weight update. Weights and threshold stay frozen in the main drift experiments. The only unlabeled updates are an optional re-estimation of the sign vector, contexts and threshold on the current window (Algorithm 1, step 6), with the model kept frozen. Theory: Theorem 1 (separation) says, under five assumptions (positive feature-context cosine correlation rho0 on legitimate nodes, coherent hidden activation, bounded moments, adversarial context gap rho1 < rho0, coherent dominance margin gamma), the expected CB gap between legitimate and adversarial nodes is at least n_h * epsilon. Corollary 1 gives Chebyshev FPR/TPR bounds, which the authors admit can be vacuous. Theorem 2 (drift stability) says that if the correlation persists and the Wasserstein-1 distance between consecutive distributions is at most delta_drift, then |E[CB_t] - E[CB_0]| <= L * t * delta_drift. Corollary 2 extends this to score quantiles. Inference cost is O(n_h * n_v) per node.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Data: XBlock Ethereum phishing graph (about 153K wallet nodes, 0.7% phishing, 38 features, rho0 = 0.30) and Reddit banned users (about 11K users, 3.3% banned, 73 features, rho0 = 0.68). Tolokers and YelpChi in Appendix K. The main drift experiments are synthetic: a random walk in feature space with context recomputed each step, T = 20 steps. Variants: Gaussian, correlated, heavy-tailed Student-t, delayed, weakened and reversed drift, plus topology growth and rewiring. A real temporal check uses XBlock: train on 2017, test on four cumulative quarterly windows of 2018. Hardware: the paper says only "a single GPU" with no model, CPU or RAM named. CB-RBM trains in under 10 minutes per dataset. Model size is n_h = 256 hidden units (XBlock) and 128 (Reddit). No IoT, edge, MCU or network-intrusion data, and no on-device experiments.
corpus.results: No labels used. Static: AUROC >= 0.96 and TPR@5%FPR >= 88% on all four attacks on both main datasets (e.g. XBlock Isolated Injection 99.9/100, XBlock Relation Camouflage 97.6/96.8, Reddit Relation Camouflage 97.3/88.2). The best supervised GNN on Reddit (GAT) reaches only about 67% TPR on Sybil. Drift, T = 20, "Combined Score" = TPR x stability: CB-RBM 0.94 on XBlock and 0.88 on Reddit. Best baselines: GraphSAGE 0.84 and XGBGraph 0.81 (XGBGraph with 17.8% drift FPR) on XBlock, GAD-NR 0.63 on Reddit. Mean FPR under drift: CB-RBM 6.1% (XBlock) and 7.1% (Reddit). The frozen plain RBM rises to 89-100% FPR. Across drift variants CB-RBM stays at or below 16% FPR at T = 20 while the plain RBM goes above 55%. Real temporal XBlock with the model frozen: 100% TPR on held-out isolated injections and FPR falling from 5.0% to 3.1%. GAT gets about 84-89% and CoLA under 16%. Contamination test (fraud mixed into the training and calibration pool at about 0.8-1.9%, 5% and 10%): FPR stays at or below 5%, but XBlock Relation Camouflage TPR falls from 80.5% to 39.0% at 10%. Theorem 2's bound is about 526x (XBlock) and 4,540x (Reddit) looser than the drift actually observed. White-box PGD (l_inf, 50 steps): XBlock AUROC 0.90 to 0.66, Reddit AUROC 0.42 at eps = 0.1 and 0.07 at eps = 0.5. I got these numbers through a summarising fetch tool, not word for word. Check them against the PDF tables before quoting.
corpus.limitations: Stated by the authors: (1) needs rho0 > 0, which can fail in random or adversarially curated topologies. (2) Detection weakens as the gap rho0 - rho1 shrinks. On YelpChi the raw gap is negative and supervised baselines win. (3) An attacker that gets genuine hub connections (Relation Camouflage) can evade in the limit. (4) Large topology change breaks calibration at the frozen threshold and needs a label-free refresh. (5) White-box gradient attackers degrade it badly, especially on Reddit. The authors suggest pairing it with an adversarially trained or certified second stage. (6) The drift theory covers only smooth, natural drift. Abrupt or adversarial drift "may need other mechanisms." (7) The bounds are loose worst-case certificates. Not addressed (my reading): poisoning of the unlabeled refresh window is not analysed (the contamination test covers only the initial training and calibration pools). There is no strategic or adaptive drift adversary, no update budget or rate limit, no streaming self-learning, and nothing on IoT, edge, latency or memory.
corpus.overlap_with_us: LOW. Different domain (graph fraud: Ethereum and Reddit, not IoT network traffic). It is a different learner: a one-class RBM trained once and then FROZEN, not an online self-labelling centroid detector. On the three things you asked about: (a) TOA-like direction budgeting: NO. It never splits updates into threat-aligned and orthogonal components and has no rationed budget or minimum time-to-compromise guarantee. Its Theorem 2 bounds how far the score drifts under natural Wasserstein-bounded drift, which is a different guarantee from ours (adversarial time to compromise). (b) Core/outer-ring robust updating: NO. Its only update is a label-free refit of the sign vector and 95th-percentile threshold on the current window, with no trimming, core selection or outer-ring check. (c) Freeze-type attack: NO. It never describes an attacker who deliberately trips a defense into stopping learning. It actually goes the other way: it freezes on purpose and argues that a drift-invariant score makes freezing safe under smooth drift. Partial overlap: (i) Its frozen plain-RBM baseline reaches 89-100% FPR under drift, the same effect as our "frozen defenses give 85-87% false alarms," but from natural drift, not adversarial tripping. (ii) It reports a training-pool contamination test (up to 10%), a weak cousin of our poisoning experiments, done once at training time with no boiling-frog dynamics. (iii) It names adversarial or abrupt drift as an open limitation, which is roughly where our work sits. Net: it does not take our novelty. It can be cited as a 2026 NeurIPS example of "make the score drift-invariant and freeze" that leaves strategic drift and refresh-window poisoning open.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow: 1) Context-consistency as a drift-invariant signal, which bears on our open problems 1 and 2. In IoT, a device's "context" can be the aggregate features of its peers (same-type devices on the LAN or the gateway's other devices) or its own slower-timescale window. Genuine drift (firmware update, seasonal use, a new device on the network) tends to be common-mode across peers, so features and context move together. A poisoner's slow push is device-specific and breaks that consistency. A peer-corroboration gate could work like this: accept a centre shift only if the device's shift agrees with the peer context. That is a direct test for open problem 1 (an attack hidden inside strong genuine drift) and gives a principled answer to open problem 2 (a new device starts from peer context instead of breaking a single detector). 2) Theorem template: their Lipschitz-times-Wasserstein drift bound |E[s_t] - E[s_0]| <= L t delta could pair with our minimum time-to-compromise bound. That gives two guarantees: honest drift moves our false-alarm rate by at most X, and the attacker needs at least T cycles. 3) Evaluation protocol: TPR@fixed-FPR (5%), their "Combined Score = TPR x stability" over T steps, and their drift-stress suite (Gaussian, correlated, heavy-tailed, delayed, weakened, reversed drift). Adopting these would make our tables look like a top-venue paper. 4) A new target for open problem 4 (freeze attack against published defenses): their label-free threshold and sign refresh is an unguarded self-learning step. An attacker who seeds the refresh window can push the 95th-percentile threshold up boiling-frog style, or force refreshes that the authors admit are needed after topology change. Re-implementing the CB-RBM "frozen model + periodic label-free refresh" policy on N-BaIoT and showing either boiling-frog or freeze-style failure would be a published-defense baseline we break. 5) A tiny RBM scorer: inference is O(n_h * n_v). With about 10 PCA features and 16-32 hidden units that is a few hundred multiply-adds, easily ESP32-feasible as an alternative or second-stage scorer. 6) Their stated future work is a cheap first-line detector plus a robust second stage. That is the framing we could adopt for TOA plus the signature-free version on-device.

corpus.title: Contrastive Adversarial Agents for Intentional Drift Induction in Network Intrusion Detection Systems
corpus.authors: Emilia Rivas and Aritran Piplai, both in the Department of Computer Science, The University of Texas at El Paso. Funded by HRSA grant 226-141-478A.
corpus.venue_year: 2026. AAAI Summer Symposium Series (SuSS 2026), Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series Vol. 9 No. 1, pp. 309-314, published 2026-06-23. It appeared in the symposium "Human-Aware AI Agents for the Cyber Battlefield: From Human Models to Autonomous Defense" (full papers). DOI 10.1609/aaaiss.v9i1.42946. This is a 6-page symposium paper, not AAAI main track, so it is a weak venue next to the A/A* target. Code: https://github.com/EmiliaR8/Contrastive_Drift
corpus.url: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI-SS/article/view/42946 (PDF: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI-SS/article/download/42946/50506)
corpus.problem: Retraining-based and drift-adaptive NIDS work when attacks change slowly or predictably. They break when several coordinated attackers deliberately use different strategies, which creates abrupt, multi-modal "adversarial concept drift" and splits the defender's limited retraining and analyst-labelling effort. Most earlier work models a single adaptive adversary with one stable objective. The paper motivates the problem with client-server NIDS in high-stakes settings such as healthcare.
corpus.method:
The setup is a red-vs-blue reinforcement learning simulation with four parts.
(1) Target: a binary XGBoost NIDS (benign vs malicious) on single packets.
(2) Blue defender: an RL agent taken from their earlier work (Rivas et al. 2025). Its state is [accuracy, FPR, FNR, KL(P_seen||P_all), Wasserstein(P_seen,P_all), mean(all) - mean(seen)], with dimension 5+d. Its action picks one of four adaptation methods: online learning, active learning (labelled-query budget 15 and uncertainty threshold 0.15 in the code), continual learning (replay of KMeans representative/diverse samples), or pseudo-labelling (self-labels at confidence 0.9 or higher, top 7 per class in the code). Its reward is 10 if accuracy is above the target T, otherwise -10r + 50(Acc_t - Acc_{t-1}), where r is the fraction of training data used.
(3) Red attackers: N agents. Each one's state is one preprocessed CICIDS-2017 packet as a 1825-dimensional feature vector. The action is a bounded continuous perturbation in [-eps, eps]^d added to the normalised features, clipped to [0,1], for up to 25 steps per episode. The reward is 5*(P_benign - 0.5) - 0.3*||a||_2, plus 10 when the packet is misclassified as benign, plus the contrastive term. The paper does not name the RL algorithm; the code uses Stable-Baselines3 SAC with 200 timesteps per learn call.
(4) Contrastive Bank: holds one prototype per agent, an EMA (0.95) of the normalised cumulative perturbation vector. The contrastive reward is cos(own prototype, current) minus the mean cosine to other agents' prototypes, weighted by 0.5 in the code. This pushes each agent toward a consistent attack direction that differs from the other agents'.
Protocols: in Config 1, N agents attack one after another, one round each (attack, blue retrains, evaluate). In Config 2, each agent attacks for 3 consecutive rounds before the next agent takes over, to test whether the defender over-specialises.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Data: CICIDS-2017 (cited through Stiawan et al. 2020), turned into packet-level 1825-dimensional vectors by their own pcap preprocessing. The paper never says which days or attack types were used. The public code loads only Tuesday.csv, rows 4,800,000-4,829,999 (a code comment says most malicious samples are in 4.82M-4.83M), in balanced batches of 100 with binary labels. From general knowledge of CICIDS-2017, not stated in the paper: Tuesday traffic holds the FTP-Patator and SSH-Patator brute-force attacks, so in practice the evaluation probably covers one attack family.
Hardware: not reported. The code mentions a /mnt server path and torch.cuda cleanup, which suggests a GPU server, but this cannot be verified.
Not covered: IoT devices, IoT datasets (N-BaIoT, Kitsune, etc.), on-device or embedded deployment, and latency or memory measurements.
corpus.results:
Config 1, eps=0.1 (Table 2), four agents, accuracy after each attack: 89.11%, 34.64%, 7.40%, 3.84%. Accuracy after blue retraining: 96.21%, 86.09%, 98.70%, 99.07%.
Config 1, eps=0.25 (Table 1, mean +- std): post-attack 88.96+-0.46, 34.82+-5.95, 7.38+-2.43, 4.30+-0.65%. Retrain 98.48, 92.18, 88.03+-8.29, 92.38%.
Six agents at eps=0.25 (Table 6): post-attack falls as low as 0.00% (agent 5). Retrain recovers to 85-98%.
eps=0.001 (Table 4) and eps=0.01 (Table 7): weaker and less stable degradation.
Config 2 (Table 3, 3 agents x 3 rounds): post-attack accuracy drops to 4.76% after 3 rounds of agent 0. After each switch it stays low but unstable (0-31%). Retrain accuracy drifts down to 80-86% for some rounds. The authors read this as over-specialisation to the earlier attacker.
Headline claim: average post-attack accuracy of 35%, against about 68% in their earlier single-attacker work. This is a cross-paper comparison.
PCA plots (Figs 2 and 4) show the agents' perturbation prototypes stay separated, so the contrastive term prevents the policies from collapsing into one.
Overall pattern: accuracy starts high, falls sharply under each new agent, partly recovers on the merged data, and recovers after full retraining. The defence is purely reactive and no defence is proposed.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors (future work only, no limitations section): tie automated diversity detection more closely to human-guided retraining, and evaluate on real critical infrastructure (they name LLM hosting platforms and high-stakes communication channels).
From reading the paper and code:
(a) One dataset (CICIDS-2017). The code uses a single day and a 30k-row slice, most likely one brute-force attack family.
(b) Perturbations are applied in normalised feature space with only an L-inf box and an L2 penalty. There is no problem-space or protocol-validity constraint, so the evading packets may not be realisable.
(c) No defence is proposed. The paper only shows that existing adaptation fails.
(d) Small scale: 2-6 agents, 4-9 rounds. Standard deviations appear only in Table 1.
(e) Reporting is inconsistent. Tables 1, 3, 5, 6 and 8 all say eps=0.25 but have different agent and run layouts. Table 5 has no caption saying which configuration it is.
(f) The introduction says the setup studies "which ways of engaging human annotators are most effective", but the results never evaluate this.
(g) The RL algorithm, training budget and hardware are not reported in the paper.
(h) The 35% vs 68% comparison is across papers, not run in the same setup.
(i) The defender is supervised and gets true labels for active and online learning, which a label-free on-device IoT detector would not have.
(j) The threat is test-time evasion whose drift effect enters through retraining. It is not a training-set poisoning attack with a bound on attacker share.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overlap is low on mechanism and moderate on framing.
Shared framing: an adversary deliberately induces drift so that an adaptive, self-updating NIDS ends up learning the wrong thing, and fixed-attacker evaluations are too weak. This makes it a related-work citation and supporting evidence for our threat model, not a competitor.
Our three contributions, checked one by one:
(1) TOA-style direction budgeting: no. The paper proposes no defence. It has no projection of updates onto attack directions, no rationing budget, and no time-to-compromise bound. Their Contrastive Bank does keep per-attacker direction prototypes, an EMA of normalised cumulative perturbation, but only to reward diversity on the attacker side, never to constrain defender updates.
(2) Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. They have no robust or trimmed statistics, no dense-core learning and no support check from the outer ring. The defender is XGBoost refit on labelled or pseudo-labelled batches.
(3) Freeze attack: no. Nothing in the paper deliberately trips a suspicion gate so that the defender stops learning and then fails under honest drift. The closest result is Config 2: long exposure to one attacker makes retraining over-specialise and become unstable when the attacker changes. That is "steering what the defender learns", not "making the defender stop learning". Their blue agent never freezes, because it always picks one of the four update methods.
Other differences: they use a supervised classifier where we use an unsupervised centroid anomaly detector. Their attack is evasion of malicious packets where ours is poisoning of the self-labelled normal model. They use CICIDS-2017 packets where we use N-BaIoT/Kitsune IoT traffic. They have no attacker-share parameter, no IoT, no on-device or ESP32 work and no device-joining scenario.
One partial touchpoint: their pseudo-labelling action is a self-labelling path (confidence 0.9 or higher), the same weakness our boiling-frog attack exploits, but they never attack it with poisoning.
Bottom line: they do not anticipate our novelty. They do give us a stronger attacker model that we must test TOA against (see what_we_can_borrow).
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Most important: a direction-diverse poisoner as an adaptive attack on TOA. TOA rations only the part of each update that moves toward a known attack signature. An ensemble of poisoners trained with their contrastive reward (own-prototype cosine minus mean cosine to other prototypes) would spread its displacement over several mutually dissimilar directions, or directions orthogonal to the signature, each staying under budget. We should run this attack and report whether TOA's minimum-time-to-compromise still holds. A likely fix is to budget the projection onto a subspace (signature span plus online-estimated attacker prototypes built like their EMA bank) and/or put a global cap on cumulative displacement that drift does not explain. A version of TOA that survives a contrastive multi-direction poisoner would be a clear new contribution.
2. Their rotation protocols as an evaluation design. Config 1 runs N attackers in sequence, one round each. Config 2 has each attacker stay k rounds before switching. Both map onto our scenarios: an attacker that trips a freeze and then leaves, and rotating poisoners under honest drift.
3. Label-free drift telemetry from their blue-agent state: KL and Wasserstein between seen and recent windows, and the mean-shift vector. These could help tell honest drift from poisoning, which is our open problem 1 (an attack hidden in strong genuine drift), and they are cheap enough for an ESP32. Their acc/FPR/FNR features need labels and do not carry over.
4. The Pre / Post / Merged / Retrain accuracy-progression table is a clean format for reporting per-round results.
5. Freeze-attack targets for open problem 4. Their related work names published adaptive NIDS defences that our freeze attack could be tested against: SPIDER (INFOCOM 2024), Zhang et al. continual learning with strategic selection and forgetting (INFOCOM 2025), CADE drift detection (USENIX Security 2021, background), and ADAPT pseudo-labelling (arXiv 2507.08597, malware).
6. Two related papers to check. Their predecessor, Rivas et al., "Adapting Under Fire: Multi-Agent RL for Adversarial Drift in Network Security", arXiv 2506.06565, SECRYPT 2025 pp. 547-554. I verified it on arXiv: the blue agent raises accuracy by about 30% within 2-3 adaptation steps using 25-30 samples per step. Second, Pasikhani et al. 2026, IEEE TDSC, "Baiting AI: Deceptive adversary against AI-protected industrial infrastructures". The paper describes it as a multi-agent RL attacker doing stealthy long-horizon wear-out attacks that mimic benign behaviour, which sounds close to boiling-frog poisoning. I did not verify it because the web-search budget ran out. It must be checked before we claim novelty.
7. Their public SB3 SAC code could serve as an RL-poisoner baseline. I only read it and did not run it.

corpus.title: Poster: Adversarial Habituation Attack: A Psychological Extension and Re-framing of Boiling Frog Attack
corpus.authors: Tashi Stirewalt and Assefaw Hadish Gebremedhin, School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA. Names and affiliations confirmed via the Crossref and OpenAlex records for DOI 10.1145/3719027.3760741.
corpus.venue_year: ACM CCS 2025 (Proceedings of the 2025 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, Taipei, Taiwan), poster track, pages 4830-4832 (3 pages), published 19 Nov 2025. It is a poster or short paper, not a full CCS paper. DBLP key conf/ccs/StirewaltG25.
corpus.url: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3719027.3760741 (DOI 10.1145/3719027.3760741). The abstract was obtained from the Semantic Scholar API: https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1145/3719027.3760741
corpus.problem: Anomaly-based IDSs that use ML can be fooled by attacks that change slowly. In the 'boiling frog' pattern the attacker shifts the model step by step until anomalous patterns count as normal. The authors say the security literature has no shared vocabulary or framework for this kind of slow manipulation. They frame it as a concept-drift weakness and link it to how humans get used to things (cognitive habituation).
corpus.method:
From the abstract, the contribution is mainly a conceptual framework. It introduces the 'Adversarial Habituation Attack' (AHA), which recasts and extends boiling frog using four ideas from psychology:
- Habituation: a weakening response to a repeated stimulus.
- Sensitization: a stronger response.
- Creeping Normality.
- Alert Fatigue: the 'cry wolf' effect.

The stated aim is a common terminology that links cognitive habituation to adversarial ML. The only defence they suggest is that 'introducing variability to counteract habituation' could inspire more robust defences. There is no named defence algorithm, and no budget or bound.

The abstract does not say how the attack schedule was built, how variability would be put into practice, or whether any defence was tested. I could not read the full text, so those details are unverified.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
- Testbed: the attack is demonstrated on a virtual network of Ubuntu machines, protected by one centralized network IDS built from Suricata plus a Variational Autoencoder (VAE).
- Hardware: none mentioned. No IoT devices, no microcontrollers, nothing on-device.
- Datasets: the abstract names none. OpenAlex lists only 4 references, and one is UNSW-NB15 (MilCIS 2015), so UNSW-NB15 may have been used for training or for comparison. That is unverified.
- Not mentioned anywhere I could see: N-BaIoT, Kitsune, CICIoT or any other IoT dataset.
corpus.results: The abstract reports only a qualitative result: the AHA attack was demonstrated against the VAE-based Suricata NIDS. It gives no numbers I can check (no detection rate, false-alarm rate, time to compromise or attacker share). Its main takeaway is that ideas from psychology, such as adding variability to counter habituation, can help explain AHA and inspire stronger defences against concept-drift weaknesses. The only citing paper I found (Semantic Scholar) is 'The Fly That Stopped: Mushroom-Body-Inspired Habituation as a Reward-Free Scheduling Prior for Autonomous Penetration Testing' (2026, venue not listed). I did not check it further.
corpus.limitations:
I could not read the paper's own limitations section. The limits below are what I can infer from the abstract and metadata:
1. It is a 3-page poster. The work is mostly about terminology and framing, with one demonstration.
2. It uses a single centralized VAE NIDS in a virtual Ubuntu network: no IoT traffic, no constrained devices, no per-device models.
3. No quantitative evaluation or defence evaluation is visible. Defences are only suggested ('introducing variability').
4. There is no theory: no compromise-time bound, no attacker-share analysis.
5. The reference list is very short. OpenAlex lists 4 works:
   - Chan-Tin et al., 'The Frog-Boiling Attack', ACM TISSEC 2011, DOI 10.1145/2043621.2043627
   - UNSW-NB15, MilCIS 2015
   - 'Alert Fatigue in Security Operations Centres: Research Challenges and Opportunities', ACM CSUR 2025, DOI 10.1145/3723158
   - 'Adversarial Attacks on Anomaly Detection', Springer Encyclopedia of ML and Data Science, 2022

   Neither ANTIDOTE nor Kloft and Laskov appears in that list. The metadata may be incomplete.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overlap is low on methods. On the threat, overlap is moderate and only in framing.
- Threat: it is the same family as ours, slow boiling-frog normalisation of a self-updating anomaly NIDS, and it is the newest top-venue (CCS 2025) work that names this threat. We must cite it.
- TOA-like direction budgeting: no. Nothing in the abstract or metadata suggests it splits updates by direction, rations movement toward a signature, or bounds compromise time.
- Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. No robust or gated update rule is described. The only defence idea is the vague 'introduce variability'.
- Freeze-type attack: not described as an attack. This is the closest point of contact, so we should handle it carefully. AHA lists 'Sensitization' and 'Alert Fatigue (cry wolf)' as parts of its framework. Our freeze attack also ends in mass false alarms, which is alert fatigue. But the abstract does not describe an attacker deliberately tripping a defence's stop-learning or suspicion gate so that honest drift then floods false alarms after the attacker has left. In AHA, alert fatigue reads as the psychological or human-analyst effect. Our contribution is a concrete attack on the defence logic itself. The 3-page full text might discuss inducing alert fatigue as an attacker strategy; I could not verify this.
- Setting: no overlap. They use a centralized VAE plus Suricata on a virtual Ubuntu LAN, with no IoT, on-device or ESP32 work, no N-BaIoT or Kitsune, and no attacker-share analysis.
- Net: it does not take our novelty claims. It does confirm that the CCS community is interested in slow-poisoning, concept-drift attacks on NIDS.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Vocabulary and positioning. Map our threats onto their terms:
   - Boiling-frog drift of centre and spread = habituation.
   - Attack hidden inside strong genuine drift (our open problem 1) = creeping normality.
   - Freeze attack = an attacker-induced sensitization that leaves the detector in lasting alert fatigue once honest drift continues.

   Then claim the freeze attack as a mechanistic, measured attack on the gates of drift-robust defences, which their framework names only conceptually. Phrase this carefully, since we read only the abstract.
2. 'Variability' as a defence. Their only defence hint suggests randomised elements in our method:
   - a secret or randomised TOA budget schedule
   - random subsampling for estimating the dense core and the outer ring
   - jittered acceptance thresholds

   Each makes it harder for an adaptive attacker to hide poison in the core or in drift. These are our own extensions, not the poster's.
3. 'Dishabituation probes'. The psychology analogy suggests a small on-device store (it fits in ESP32 flash) of anchor samples: known-normal plus signature or attack exemplars. Replay them every few cycles to check whether the detector still reacts strongly. If the response has decayed (habituation), roll back. If the false alarms on the normal anchors keep rising (a sign of a freeze), force adaptation. This is our extrapolation, not something the poster describes.
4. Alert-fatigue metrics. Report alerts per device per hour, plus how long false alarms stay high after the attacker leaves, alongside FPR. Cite the alert-fatigue survey (ACM CSUR 2025, DOI 10.1145/3723158) to show the freeze attack's real operational cost.
5. A second target for open problem 4. Rebuild their style of detector, a VAE scoring Suricata (or Zeek) features on a Raspberry Pi gateway in front of the ESP32 nodes. Run both the boiling-frog and freeze attacks against it, so the results are not limited to our own centroid baselines.
6. Background citation. Their reference to Chan-Tin et al., 'The Frog-Boiling Attack' (ACM TISSEC 2011, DOI 10.1145/2043621.2043627), originally about network coordinate systems, should go next to ANTIDOTE as a foundational reference. Mark it as background.
corpus.fetch_status:
Abstract only; the full text was not read. ACM DL returned HTTP 403 for both the landing page and the PDF, and I did not try to get around that. The paper is closed access: Semantic Scholar marks it CLOSED and OpenAlex has no open-access copy. No arXiv version is listed.

The full abstract text, the TLDR and the one citing paper came from the Semantic Scholar Graph API. Title, authors, affiliations, venue, pages and date came from Crossref and OpenAlex, and the 4-item reference list from OpenAlex.

Everything about method details, numbers and the paper's own limitations beyond the abstract is unverified.

The OpenAlex API responses included a notice asking AI agents to request an API key for the user. I did not act on it.

corpus.title: Rapid Poison: Practical Poisoning Attacks Against the Rapid Response Framework
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16242 (HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.16242v1, PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.16242). The paper text gives code at https://github.com/DH-davidhuang/rapid-poison; I did not open the repo.
corpus.authors: David Huang (Princeton University; Anthropic), Jaewon Chang (UC Berkeley), Avidan Shah (NYU). These three are marked as core contributors. Prateek Mittal (Princeton University), Chawin Sitawarin (Google DeepMind). Affiliations come from the footnote on page 1 of the PDF.
corpus.venue_year: ICML 2026 (Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, PMLR 306). The arXiv comment says "Spotlight at ICML 2026". arXiv v1 was posted 15 Jun 2026 under cs.LG and cs.CL. It is a 2026 paper, so it is recent enough to cite as current.
corpus.problem:
The paper attacks the Rapid Response (RR) framework of Peng et al. (2024). RR is used in Anthropic's ASL-3 deployment safeguards, and the paper says OpenAI has proposed similar agentic variants. RR keeps a jailbreak-detection classifier up to date. When a new jailbreak gets past the classifier and is caught afterwards, it becomes a "reference". A separate LLM then paraphrases it into many synthetic variants, a step called "proliferation", and the classifier is fine-tuned on those variants. The authors call this "similar to continual learning".

The core problem is that the step which makes RR adapt quickly (turning a few attacker-supplied samples into many training samples) also amplifies poisoning. One crafted reference grows into many poisoned training examples.

The threat model is constrained. The attacker can only submit unsafe-class samples (jailbreaks), which must still be harmful and keep their original goal according to a judge model. The attacker cannot touch benign data or labels.

There are two goals:
- (I) targeted false positives: benign inputs with a chosen format, domain or entity get flagged as jailbreaks.
- (II) concept-triggered false negatives: a backdoor that lets jailbreaks through when a trigger concept is present.

The paper frames this as a "three-sided security dilemma". RR cannot have all three of fast adaptation, strong generalization and robustness to training-data manipulation at once.
corpus.method:
1. Conditional prompt injection (Sec. 3.1). The jailbreak carries an IF/ELSE payload. If it detects the proliferation context, it steers the paraphrasing LLM to emit attacker-chosen few-shot samples. Otherwise it runs as a normal jailbreak, so the defender's validation still sees a valid reference.

2. Shortcut-learning false-positive attacks (Sec. 3.2). The injected "unsafe" samples share a surface feature (MCQ/JSON/plain-text format, an academic domain, an entity name such as "ChatGPT", or a whole benign distribution). The classifier learns to tie that feature to the unsafe label.

3. Omission Attack (Sec. 3.3, "contrastive backdoor"). This is their new contribution. The attacker picks a concept (for example Harry Potter, "Midjourney" or a long n-gram), takes natural safe-distribution texts that contain it, strips the concept out, and injects the stripped texts as unsafe samples. The classifier then sees the concept only in safe data and learns its presence as a safety signal. Adding the concept to a jailbreak at inference time makes it pass as safe. It even generalizes to jailbreak strategies the defender explicitly trained against.

4. Poisoning-rate formalization (App. E). Each reference yields about 3.33 samples on average. The training set has 6k samples (3k proliferated jailbreaks and 3k WildChat benign), so 1% poisoning is about 18 poisoned references. Assignment is a randomized LRU, so the number of poisoned samples is hypergeometric. Because injection sometimes fails, the stated rates are upper bounds on the effective rate.

5. Mechanistic analysis (App. F). Using a refusal-direction method, they show that triggered harmful prompts move toward the benign region of late-layer representations (from about layer 30).

6. Defenses evaluated (Sec. 7). One is a PromptArmor-style guardrail LLM that detects and sanitizes injected references. The other is the model-level Meta SecAlign 70B used as the proliferation model. App. D.6 also discusses, but does not test, hardening against prompt injection, harmfulness filtering before and after proliferation, and adding more benign data.

Experiments use one RR round. The phrase is "after a round of RR". There is no multi-round or online-update analysis.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Target classifiers: Llama Guard 4 12B, fine-tuned with QLoRA (4-bit NF4, LoRA rank 32, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 8-bit AdamW, max sequence length 2048). Prompt Guard 2 (86M) is used for the direct-poisoning comparison.

Proliferation LLMs: Gemini 2.5 and 3, Flash and Pro, including gemini-3-flash-preview and 2.5-flash-lite. GPT and Claude were excluded because they refused the task. A Gemini-3-Flash-Preview judge checks harmfulness and behaviour match. GPT-5.2 generates extra benign concept-containing queries.

Data:
- 3,000 WildChat benign samples.
- 300 references each from PAIR, Cipher and Crescendo.
- MMLU and GPQA for the format and domain tests.
- AdvBench (100 queries) plus 150 jailbreaks per attack for evaluation.
- Also WildChat-4.8M, XSTest, LMSYS-Chat and SWE-Bench Verified.

Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPUs, plus RTX A5000 for some runs.

There is nothing on IoT, network traffic, embedded or on-device learning, and no TinyML.
corpus.results:
All results are at 1% sample-level poisoning unless noted.

Format attack:
- MCQ and JSON reach 100% FPR on in-distribution MMLU. Plain text reaches 90.51%.
- Little transfer across formats. Clean baseline is about 0%.

Domain attack: targeted subjects average 77.8% FPR (Professional Law 98%, Econometrics 96%). Non-target subjects average 4.7%, with some leakage from Econometrics into related quantitative areas.

Entity attack: "ChatGPT" reaches 98% FPR on ChatGPT queries but only 19% on "Claude".

Broad distribution: 39-50% FPR at 5% poisoning, against 0.8-3.2% clean. The introduction cites up to 88% on broad benign distributions. SWE-Bench coding prompts reach 100% FPR but do not transfer to WildChat (0%).

Omission backdoor:
- The "Midjourney" trigger gives 96% FNR on harmful queries, and an unseen paraphrase ("Meshy") gives 98%.
- The Harry Potter trigger gives 87% FNR on general harmful queries and 55% on PAIR, against clean baselines of 6% and 0%.
- A naive name-interleaving baseline reaches only 14.7%.
- Rare 15-gram triggers that appear only 8 times in the defender's data still reach 73% FNR.
- Direct poisoning without proliferation reaches 94-100% on jailbreak strategies but only 62-63% on general harmful queries.

Defenses:
- The PromptArmor-style sanitizer gives 3.8% FPR on clean references and 10.3% aggregate FNR on poisoned ones (worse on SWE-bench at 24.1% and MCQ at 18.5%). Its sanitization is imperfect: 35% of true positives are over-removed to empty strings and 56% keep template artifacts.
- Meta SecAlign 70B as the proliferation model cuts target-domain FPR from 98% to 0%. The authors argue adaptive injections could likely beat it.

I checked the headline numbers (1%, 100% FPR, 96%/87% FNR, 88%, 77.8%, 39-50%, 3.8%/10.3%, 98% to 0%) against the extracted PDF text. Some per-figure numbers (for example 4.7%, 19%, 14.7%, 24.1%/18.5%, 35%/56%) come from the HTML summary and I did not re-check each one.
corpus.limitations:
Limitations the authors state (Sec. 8, Impact Statement, App. D.6):
- The strongest attacks depend on prompt injection succeeding during proliferation. Robust prompt-injection defenses could weaken them, though the authors call guaranteed robustness an open problem.
- A specialized paraphrase model might resist injection better but would likely proliferate worse.
- Non-injection variants were tried only in the noun setting and worked less well.
- Only Llama Guard 4 and Gemini were tested, and other architectures may differ.
- The injection templates are static and handcrafted, so the numbers are lower bounds on what an adaptive attacker could do.
- Details were deliberately kept short of an operational recipe, and disclosure was made before publication.
- Adding more benign data looks insufficient: benign data would need to dominate the mix by orders of magnitude, which would slow adaptation.

Limitations I noticed:
- Only one RR round is evaluated. There is no multi-round compounding, no drift, and no study of how the backdoor persists across later rounds (Souri et al. 2022 is only cited).
- Updates are supervised fine-tuning with labels from the pipeline, not self-labelling.
- No certified or provable guarantees.
- No update-rate or budget defense and no robust-statistics aggregation.
- No resource-constrained or on-device setting.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overlap is very low. Being blunt about each point:

(a) TOA-like direction budgeting. No. Nothing splits or rations updates by direction, no slow budget, no minimum-time-to-compromise bound. The only defenses are input sanitization and an injection-resistant generator.

(b) Core/outer-ring robust updating. No. No robust statistics, density-core learning, trimming or support checks on model updates. The defense is filtering at the content level, not robustness of the update rule.

(c) Freeze-type attack. No. Nobody triggers "stop learning" or uses suspicion as a weapon. The nearest idea is the "three-sided dilemma" between fast adaptation, generalization and poison robustness. That is a framing statement, not an attack on defenses that freeze. They also do not study the cost of slowing adaptation beyond one sentence noting that benign data would have to dominate.

(d) Setting. Completely different. They poison an LLM jailbreak classifier through LLM-generated synthetic data in one supervised fine-tuning round on GPUs. We poison an unsupervised, self-labelling, every-cycle-updating centroid detector on IoT traffic, aimed at ESP32. No shared datasets (no Kitsune, N-BaIoT or CESNET) and no shared metrics beyond FPR and FNR.

The genuine conceptual overlap is narrower:
1. Both papers attack a defense that adapts continuously to new threats. Both argue that the adaptation mechanism itself is the attack surface.
2. Both use a constrained attacker who cannot touch labels or benign data. Our IoT attacker only injects its own traffic. Theirs only submits unsafe-class samples.
3. Both have an amplifier. For them it is proliferation, about 3.33 samples per reference. For us it is self-labelling, where accepted poison becomes training data every cycle.

This paper does not take away our novelty. It is good motivation and support for "adaptive defenses are themselves attack surfaces". It is from a top venue (ICML 2026 spotlight) and comes from Princeton, Anthropic, Berkeley, NYU and DeepMind authors. Cite it in related work as the LLM-safety counterpart of the adapt-versus-robust tension. Then point out that it neither offers an update-level defense nor considers the opposite failure, where an attacker induces the defense to stop adapting. Our freeze attack and TOA/core-ring defenses cover exactly that.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Framing. Reuse their "three-sided security dilemma" (fast adaptation vs. generalization vs. poison robustness) as an external, citable statement of our trade-off. Our extension: the freeze attack shows the dilemma can be weaponized from both sides. Defenses that buy poison robustness by stopping adaptation get attacked through the adaptation axis instead, with 85-87% false alarms under honest drift.

2. A new threat to TOA: signature-channel poisoning. TOA needs a known attack-signature direction. In a real deployment, signatures would be refreshed from newly captured attacks, which is exactly RR's pattern. An Omission-style attacker could shape the attacks it lets the defender capture so that a feature is missing from them. The learned signature direction would then be orthogonal to the real poison direction, and TOA would happily apply the poison as "everything else". We should either (a) evaluate TOA when the signature is learned from attacker-influenced captures, or (b) argue that the signature-free core/ring method is immune because it needs no signature. Either one is a strong extra section and directly answers how TOA holds up if attackers control the signature.

3. Amplification factor and poisoning-rate formalization (their App. E). Formalize attacker share at the level of each self-labelling cycle versus each packet or flow. Define an effective amplification (how many accepted poisoned updates one injected window yields over k cycles). Report attacker share as an upper bound when some injected traffic gets rejected. This fits Kloft and Laskov's attacker-share result.

4. Constrained-attacker taxonomy. State our threat model in their terms: the attacker controls only its own traffic, has no labels, and cannot touch other devices' benign traffic. Then position ours as even weaker, since it is unsupervised with no labels at all.

5. Evaluation style. Report targeted vs. collateral ("blast radius") damage, as with their non-target subjects at 4.7% FPR. In our setting that means per-device or per-traffic-class false alarms, for the poisoned device versus bystander devices. This connects to our open problem of per-device detectors.

6. Representation-level analysis. Their App. F shows triggered inputs moving toward the benign region. We can plot centroid and spread paths in PCA space for the naive, freezing, TOA and core/ring variants. That makes the boiling-frog drift and the freeze stall visible.

7. A baseline defense to beat. Their sanitizer (a filter before updates) still lets 10.3% FNR through. Treat "filter suspicious samples, then update" as a published defense family, and show our freeze attack against it. That partly addresses our open problem (4), the freeze attack shown only against our own baselines.

8. Their point that more benign data needs orders of magnitude more volume, which slows adaptation, supports our claim that a robust update rule beats dilution.
