corpus.title: Adversarial Attacks for Drift Detection
corpus.authors: Fabian Hinder, Valerie Vaquet, Barbara Hammer (Bielefeld University group; I did not separately check the affiliation)
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16591 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.16591v2 ; code: https://github.com/FabianHinder/Drift-Adversarials)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv v1 posted 25 Nov 2024, v2 posted 6 Feb 2025. The arXiv comments say "Accepted at ESANN 2025", and v2 calls itself an extended version of the ESANN paper. I could not check the ESANN 2025 proceedings page because the session's web-search budget ran out. ESANN is a European symposium, not an A/A* venue (I did not verify a CORE rank). Treat this as a 2025 paper that sits close to our work and supplies theory, not as a top-venue competitor.
corpus.problem: Unsupervised concept-drift detectors are used in monitoring (machine faults, network security, critical infrastructure). The paper asks whether a stream can drift in a real way while a standard two-window detector never raises an alarm. A two-window detector compares a reference window with a current window using a metric or statistical test such as MMD or KS. The authors call such undetected streams "drift adversarials". They want to characterise every adversarial for common windowing schemes and show the attacks work in practice. The framing is about how reliable monitoring is. There is no formal attacker model: capabilities and budget are never defined, and the adversary is simply assumed to control the mixing schedule of the stream.
corpus.method:
The stream is modelled as D_t = f(t)P + (1 - f(t))Q with P != Q. A detector A built on a windowing scheme W(n) (fixed reference, growing reference or sliding window; point-wise or chunk-wise updates) misses the drift exactly when the window means of D_t match for every compared window pair.

Theorem 1: A detects nothing if and only if t -> D_t(S) lies in Adv0(A) for every measurable set S. The set of undetectable drifts depends only on the windowing scheme, not on the test or metric, as long as d is a true metric. A detector catches every drift exactly when Adv(A) is empty. Combining detectors helps: Adv((A,B)) is a subset of Adv(A) ∩ Adv(B).

Propositions 1-3 give closed forms for each window type:
- Fixed reference: f is l-periodic after the reference period and keeps the reference-period mean.
- Sliding window: f = p(t) + t*q(t) with p and q l-periodic and q zero-mean over a period. The proper adversarials are the l-periodic functions, where l is the window length.
- Growing reference: f is arbitrary during the reference period and constant afterwards at the same mean.

Algorithm 2 is a finite-sample construction. Encode each window pair as a row of W_n (indicator of W1 minus indicator of W2), solve W_n v = 0 with v in [0,1]^n, then sample x_i from v_i P + (1 - v_i) Q. The authors suggest binary v or slow oscillation so the stream looks natural. They also note that feature-wise KS can be beaten through correlation-only drift (metric adversarials), that model-based detectors have known flaws, and that block-based detectors resist window adversarials.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Data, two parts:
(1) The synthetic "two-squares" drift dataset (drift intensity 5). Streams have 1,000 samples, the sliding window is 100, the initial reference windows are 100 or 150, the permutation-MMD test uses 2,500 permutations, and each setup is run 500 times.
(2) Real pressure measurements from water distribution networks, used for leak detection with the authors' Shape Drift Detector. This part illustrates designing a detector, not attacking one. The paper cites Vaquet et al., ICPRAM 2024 for this data; I did not confirm the exact benchmark name.

There is no network traffic, IoT or intrusion-detection data.

Hardware: none stated, and no runtimes are reported. The code is Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Matplotlib) with RunExperiments.py and Analyze.ipynb. The README says MIT licence but the repo lists Apache-2.0, so the licence is unclear. Nothing runs on embedded hardware.
corpus.results:
Table 2 reports the 90%/10% quantiles of the smallest p-value per stream. Every cell the theory predicts as adversarial stays clearly undetected. Examples:
- Periodic stream: fixed(100) 0.63/0.28 and sliding 0.39/0.27.
- Random-constant(100) stream: undetected under fixed(100), fixed(150), grow(100) and grow(150), with values from 0.39/0.27 to 0.59/0.31.
- Random-periodic(150): fixed(150) 0.65/0.22.
- Cells the theory says are not adversarial come out at 0.00/0.00.

The authors report a "(nearly) perfect alignment" with one exception they do not name. It is probably Rand.Per.(150) under grow(150) at 0.02/0.00, but that is my inference from the table.

Water network result: a 1-day window flags weekends, while a 1-week window (and a 6.5-day control) mostly flags the leak. The point is that you can choose the window so that expected cyclic drift becomes an adversarial, i.e. invisible, and only the anomaly gets flagged.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors:
- Adversarials "might be numerically unstable", and more analysis is left to future work.
- Boundary effects make the finite-sample adversarial set larger than the theoretical one.
- Chunk-based updates allow trivial hidden drift inside a chunk.
- Building detectors tailored to a problem from the theory is "promising but requires further research".

My own observations:
- There is no formal threat model, attacker budget or cost.
- Only two-window detectors are analysed. The theory treats the reference as fixed in advance and never reset or adapted after an alarm, so there is no feedback loop between the detector and a learner.
- Only small synthetic experiments (n = 1,000) plus one non-adversarial real case study.
- No defense is evaluated beyond the remark about combining detectors.
- No IoT, network or resource-constrained setting.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low overlap, and there is no conflict with our novelty.
- It does not do anything like TOA's direction budgeting: no decomposition of updates and no rationing of movement toward an attack direction.
- It does not do core/outer-ring robust updating. It has no learner at all, only a monitor.
- It does not describe a freeze attack. Its attack is the opposite: hiding drift so the alarm never fires. Our freeze attack deliberately causes suspicion so the defense stops adapting. Nothing in the paper covers poisoning, self-labelling, retraining, or detectors that stop or reset adaptation.

What it shares with us is the high-level idea that an adversary can shape a stream's time profile to defeat a window-based monitor. That is close to our boiling-frog attacker's goal.

Two technical consequences matter for us:
(a) By Propositions 1 and 3, a monotone boiling-frog ramp is NOT an adversarial for fixed or growing reference windows. A pinned, fixed-reference two-sample test would therefore catch our ANTIDOTE-style attacker, but it would also flag honest drift. That is exactly the freeze/false-alarm tension we measured.
(b) Against sliding-window monitors, an attacker whose poisoning is l-periodic with the window length, or any solution of W_n v = 0, is provably invisible. Any drift-gated defense that uses sliding-window tests, including drift-aware poisoning defenses like those we cite, is open to this.

For the paper we write: cite this as 2025 theory showing window-based drift monitors have provably blind attack schedules. It supports our claim that "detect drift, then decide whether to learn" defenses are fragile.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Formal language. Define the set of poisoning trajectories our defense cannot see, Adv(defense), in their style. Prove for TOA that any trajectory with a nonzero attack-direction component pays the slow budget, so it shows up as a minimum time to compromise. For the signature-free version, characterise its outer-ring check by its windowing scheme (Theorem 1 says only the windows matter, not the statistic). This gives a clean theorem section at A-venue standard.

2. A principled adaptive attacker for open problem 1. Use their Algorithm 2 (solve W_n v = 0 over our update and outer-ring windows) to build a poisoner that is provably invisible to our outer-ring/spread check, or l-periodic with our cycle length. That is stronger than a hand-made "hide in the core" attacker. Then show whether TOA's direction budget still bounds compromise time. The budget does not depend on windows, so it plausibly does, but this is untested.

3. Multi-timescale checking as a defense. Adv((A,B)) is a subset of Adv(A) ∩ Adv(B), so outer-ring checks over two or three non-commensurate window lengths (e.g. l and 1.37l) shrink the blind set. That is cheap enough for an ESP32.

4. Design for IoT diurnal cycles. Following their water-network trick, choose window lengths so that known benign periodicities (day/night device usage, polling cycles) are adversarials and so never raise suspicion. This directly reduces freeze-attack and false-alarm exposure under honest cyclic drift.

5. A new attack class to evaluate. "Detector-blind poisoning" with periodic or binary-v schedules. Evaluate it against published drift-gated defenses as well as our own baselines, which partly addresses open problem 4.

6. Their MMD permutation-test setup, 500 runs, p-value quantile reporting and Python code serve as a baseline drift monitor to compare against.

corpus.title: Online robust covariance matrix estimation and outlier detection
corpus.authors: Paul Guillot, Antoine Godichon-Baggioni, Stéphane Robin, Laure Sansonnet
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, stat.ME (Methodology), v1 submitted 7 January 2026; it is the only version listed. The arXiv comments field names no venue. I could not check whether it has since been accepted anywhere: the web search budget for this turn was used up, so I made no venue search. Treat it as an unrefereed 2026 preprint.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03957 (HTML full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.03957v1 ; PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.03957 ; DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2601.03957, CC BY 4.0)
corpus.problem: The goal is to estimate a robust location and covariance, and to flag outliers in real time, on a sequential stream without storing or recomputing past data. This matters most when the share of contaminated points is large or grows with dataset size. Outliers bias the estimates and mask one another, and the strong robust estimators (MCD/FastMCD, OGK, trimmed or shrinkage estimators, Comedian/MAD, projection-pursuit/PCA-type methods) all work offline. The authors say none of these methods has an online implementation.
corpus.method:
1) Location: the online geometric median by Robbins-Monro SGD with a normalized gradient, m_{n+1} = m_n + gamma_{n+1} (X_{n+1} - m_n)/||X_{n+1} - m_n||, plus a weighted-averaged iterate. Averaging weights are proportional to log(n+1)^omega.
2) Dispersion: the online Median Covariation Matrix (MCM), also by SGD, on the Frobenius-normalized difference (X - m_bar)(X - m_bar)^T - V_n, plus an averaged V_bar.
3) Eigenvalue correction: the MCM shares eigenvectors with Sigma but not its eigenvalues. A fixed-point relation (Kraus and Panaretos 2012) maps MCM eigenvalues delta to variance eigenvalues lambda. It is solved by an inner Robbins-Monro loop with n_MC Monte Carlo draws per step, and Sigma_hat = P diag(lambda) P^T.
4) Mahalanobis distance without matrix inversion: D_i = sum_j lambda_j^{-1} <X_i - m, P_j>^2. It is rescaled Maronna-Zamar style by chi2_d(0.5)/median(D), with the median of D also tracked online by a quantile SGD. A point is flagged when the scaled distance exceeds a predefined threshold c. The paper does not report c numerically; it mentions a nominal 5% level and the chi2_10 95% quantile in a figure.
5) Step size gamma_n = c_gamma (n+n0)^-gamma with gamma in (1/2,1); numeric settings are not reported. The first n_init = 100 points are handled by the offline method.
6) Variants: pure online (batch size 1); streaming mini-batch (s = 10 in the simulations, s = d in timing), which eigendecomposes once per batch and is about 10x faster; and a non-robust baseline, the online sample covariance with Sherman-Morrison updates.
Every point updates the estimators, including flagged ones. Robustness comes only from the bounded, normalized gradient steps, not from exclusion or gating. There are no new theorems: convergence rests on cited results (Godichon-Baggioni 2016; Cardot et al. 2013; Cardot and Godichon-Baggioni 2017), and the 50% breakdown point of the geometric median is cited from Gervini 2006. An appendix derives influence functions: the influence is unbounded for mean shift and for variance inflation, and bounded for a change in correlation. Complexity: O(N d^2) for V, O(N d^3) for eigendecompositions (O(N d^3/s) when streaming), O(N n_MC d^2) for the eigenvalue recursion.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Simulated data only; there is no real-data application. Inliers are drawn from N(0, Sigma0) with d = 10, Sigma0 = D0 T0 D0, variances 2i/(d+1) and Toeplitz correlation rho0 = 0.3. Contamination is an iid mixture (1-r)F0 + rF1 whose outlier component F1 combines a mean shift k, a variance scale l and a correlation change rho1. There are four scenarios with KL divergence 17.79 (A), 8.59 (B), 5.75 (C) and 1.68 (D). For example, A uses k = 4.29, l = 402, rho1 = 0.92 and D uses k = 0.86, l = 2.03, rho1 = 0.61. Contamination r is varied, with trajectories shown at 5/20/30/40%. Each run has n = 10,000 points, with 100 replicates per setting. Timing runs use (n,d) in {(1e4,10), (1e4,100), (1e5,10)}. Outliers are interleaved iid; there is no temporal structure, drift or adversarial ordering. Baselines are the online sample covariance and an oracle that knows the true mu0 and Sigma0; MCD/FastMCD are not compared. Implementation is R with Rcpp 1.0.9, code available on request. No hardware is specified, and nothing is embedded or on-device.
corpus.results: In scenario A the robust online and streaming estimators keep Frobenius error bounded at high contamination, while the sample covariance breaks down even at r = 5%. Detection in A is perfect up to about 30% contamination. In B, false negatives stay under about 10% up to about 35%; beyond 35% the robust methods start missing outliers, because early overestimation of distances inflates the scores. In D, where outliers sit close to the inliers, every method has high false negatives, and even the oracle misses over 50%. The robust methods do not reach the nominal 5% false-positive rate, because Sigma is overestimated, and the median rescaling does not fix this. Estimates stabilise after about 1,000-2,000 iterations. Streaming is about 10x faster than pure online. All numbers are from the HTML text; I could not view the figures, so per-panel values (e.g. the exact 40% trajectory) are not verified.
corpus.limitations:
Stated or evident in the paper:
- Cost is high when every step needs an eigendecomposition or orthonormalisation; streaming reduces this but does not remove it.
- Early estimates are poor, so the method suits long streams only.
- Detection is miscalibrated: false positives miss the nominal 5% and the rescaling does not help.
- Detection degrades above about 35% contamination and for outliers close to the inliers.
- There is no real data, and there are no comparisons with MCD/FastMCD or other online robust methods.
- There is no new theory for the combined online procedure and no breakdown analysis of the full pipeline.
- Influence is unbounded for mean shift and variance inflation, which is exactly the slow-poisoning direction.
Not addressed at all: drift or non-stationarity (no forgetting factor, so step sizes decay to zero and the estimator effectively freezes on long streams); adversarial or adaptive contamination (contamination is a fixed iid mixture); temporal ordering of outliers; resource-constrained hardware. Hyperparameter values (c_gamma, gamma, n0, omega, n_MC, threshold c) are not reported. The HTML version has no conclusion or future-work section.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low overlap. It is a statistics paper, not a security paper.
- TOA-like direction budgeting: no. There is no notion of a known attack direction, and updates are not split into components or rationed by a budget. Every point is applied through the same normalized SGD step.
- Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. Nothing gates centre shifts on outer-ring support or spread growth on outer-ring activity. Flagged points are not even excluded from updates; robustness comes only from bounded per-point influence (normalized gradient plus geometric median).
- Freeze attack: no. Nothing about adversaries, poisoning or deliberate tripping appears. The paper does share our failure mode passively: decreasing Robbins-Monro steps with no forgetting make the estimator converge and stop adapting, so under real drift it would raise false alarms. That is a freeze by design, not the attack we describe.
- Mahalanobis on a robust centre/spread online: yes, the same family as our centroid plus spread detector. It is a stronger and more principled version of our "centre + spread" (geometric median plus full median-based covariance instead of mean plus diagonal or scalar spread).
- 30-40% contamination regime: yes, partly. It tests 5-40%, comparable to our 40% attacker. But its contamination is iid, unordered and non-adaptive, unlike boiling-frog poisoning, which pushes in a consistent direction over time. The paper's own unbounded influence for mean shift and variance inflation suggests a slow directional poisoner would eventually move its estimator too.
Verdict: no novelty threat to TOA, the signature-free core/outer-ring method or the freeze attack. It is a natural, recent, strong baseline or substrate rather than a competitor.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1) A strong 2026 robust online baseline. Implement the streaming geometric median plus MCM detector, with averaged SGD and mini-batches of about 10, as an extra published defense. Then show (a) boiling-frog poisoning still moves it, as its own unbounded mean-shift and variance influence functions predict, and (b) adding a forgetting factor or constant step size, which drift needs, makes it far easier to poison. This also helps with open problem (4): the freeze/poison analysis would cover a defense we did not design.
2) Swap our mean-based centre for the online geometric median. Normalized-gradient updates give bounded per-sample influence and a 50% breakdown point (cited). TOA's direction split and budget can be applied to the normalized step, which could give a cleaner minimum-time-to-compromise bound, since each step's movement toward the attack direction is at most gamma_n.
3) Inversion-free Mahalanobis from eigen-pairs plus online median rescaling of distances (chi2_d(0.5)/med(D), median tracked by quantile SGD). This suits ESP32: no matrix inverse, a small d after PCA, and the streaming variant with eigendecomposition once per batch keeps cost near O(d^2) per point. Their own miscalibration finding (false positives off nominal) is a reason to calibrate thresholds empirically or with an online quantile.
4) Influence-function analysis (their Appendix B): the same mean-shift / variance-inflation / correlation-change decomposition is a clean way to state formally which update directions the attacker exploits and why gating the mean-shift and variance-inflation components (TOA, outer-ring checks) is what matters.
5) The KL-divergence-indexed contamination scenarios (A-D, KL 17.8 down to 1.7) as a principled sweep of poison subtlety. Scenario D, near-inlier outliers, is the analogue of our open problem (1), an attack hidden in drift.
6) Their metrics (Frobenius error, det(Sigma), false positives and false negatives against an oracle, convergence over iterations) as supplementary estimator-quality metrics alongside detection and false-alarm rates.

corpus.title: ACORN-IDS: Adaptive Continual Novelty Detection for Intrusion Detection Systems
corpus.authors: Sean Fuhrman, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing (Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering, UC San Diego, per the arXiv HTML full text). This is the same group that wrote CND-IDS (DAC 2025), which is already on our list.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.07291 [cs.CR], v1 submitted 7 Feb 2026. There is only v1, and no comments field, venue or page count is listed. I could not find any peer-reviewed venue: my one search for an acceptance failed because the session's web-search budget was used up. Treat it as an unrefereed 2026 preprint. The authors say code will be released on acceptance, so no code is public yet.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07291 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07291v1)
corpus.problem: Intrusion detectors have to keep up with changing benign traffic and new (zero-day) attacks without labelled attack data. The paper frames this as continual novelty detection (CND): the model learns only from normal data while using the structure of an unlabelled stream that mixes benign and malicious samples. It assumes a small clean, trusted set of normal samples is available for every task. It has no threat model for the learner itself: poisoning of the stream, manipulation of updates and attacks that stop learning are never treated. The only nod to adversaries is a general remark that attack distributions change in "adversarial settings".
corpus.method:
1) Continual Feature Extractor (CFE): an MLP autoencoder (hidden sizes 256/512/256, Adam, learning rate 1e-3). Its loss is reconstruction MSE plus a triplet-margin metric loss (margin 0.2, Euclidean distance).
2) Pseudo-labels: MiniBatchKMeans clusters the unlabelled stream, with K chosen by the elbow method (the chosen values are not reported). Any cluster with at least one clean normal sample is labelled normal; every other cluster is labelled attack. Each sample takes the label of its nearest cluster centre. These pseudo-labels drive the triplet loss.
3) Dual reservoir memories, each capped at 10K samples: a normal-data memory merged with each task's clean set, and a training memory that stores past samples with their pseudo-labels for replay. There is no explicit regulariser such as EWC or distillation.
4) Scoring: PCA is refit every task on the encoded clean normal data (95% of variance kept). The anomaly score is squared reconstruction error. The threshold is mean + 2 standard deviations of the errors on a 20% clean validation split, which they say gives roughly 2.3% false positives under a Gaussian assumption. Plain mean and standard deviation are used, not robust estimators.
5) Tasks are processed in sequence. The model is never frozen, and nothing caps how far one update can move it.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Datasets: X-IIoTID, WUSTL-IIoT, CICIDS2017, CICIDS2018 and UNSW-NB15. WUSTL-IIoT is split into 4 tasks with one attack type each; the others into 5 tasks with 2-4 attack types each, the attack classes split into roughly disjoint subsets.

Two scenarios:
- EA (evolving attacks).
- ENA (evolving normal and attack distributions). Here normal data is split into m groups by K-Means, and task i takes the normal samples nearest centre i, so the drift is synthetic.

Baselines:
- Unsupervised continual learning: ADCN, LwF.
- Continual novelty detection: VLAD.
- Novelty detection: SLAD, ICL, DIF, AE, PCA, OCSVM, IF, LOF.

Hardware: not stated. There is no on-device, edge or microcontroller deployment. The only cost figure is average inference time per sample: 0.005 ms for ACORN-IDS, 0.002 ms for plain PCA, 0.406 ms for ADCN. These are compared with a 27.77 ms median flow duration. No parameter count, model size, training time or memory footprint is given. The paper never mentions Kitsune, N-BaIoT, ESP32, microcontrollers or TinyML; "IoT" appears only in the IIoT dataset names and in a CITADEL citation.
corpus.results:
Headline (abstract and introduction): F1 is about 62% higher on average than ADCN, the best unsupervised continual-learning baseline, and zero-day detection (forward transfer) is about 58% higher. Forgetting is near zero and inference overhead is small.

EA scenario: AVG is about 43.5% above the best novelty detector (SLAD). Mean backward transfer (BWT) is -1.9%. Mean forward transfer (FWT) is 52.6% in Table II, but the text says 53.88%, an internal inconsistency.

ENA scenario: AVG is about 18.5% above the strongest baseline (ICL), with BWT -0.7% and FWT 57.2% (Table III).

PR-AUC (no threshold): highest on average in both scenarios; exact values are only in a figure.

Ablation (ENA, on CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15 and X-IIoTID): the metric loss, the reconstruction loss, the memories and stored pseudo-labels all help. Recomputing pseudo-labels at replay time instead of storing them causes severe degradation. Numbers are only in Fig. 7.

Memory policy comparison: reservoir sampling beats SSF (better forward transfer but worse forgetting) and PSA.
corpus.limitations:
Stated: there is no limitations section. Future work is limited to memory mechanisms that trade off forward transfer against forgetting, and releasing code.

Unstated limitations I observed:
(a) It is not truly self-labelling. Each task needs a fresh clean, trusted set of normal samples from that task's distribution, used for pseudo-labelling, PCA fitting and the threshold. Its size is only described as "a small clean subset", with no number.
(b) No adversary against the learner. Poisoning, a contaminated clean set and pseudo-label errors are not analysed.
(c) The pseudo-label rule is fragile. A cluster with even one clean sample is entirely labelled normal, so attack traffic placed near benign points gets labelled normal and then pulled toward normal by the triplet loss.
(d) The threshold uses non-robust mean and standard deviation.
(e) Tasks are discrete and the ENA drift is synthetic (K-Means split), not a real time-ordered stream.
(f) No hardware or on-device evaluation; only a timing figure on unspecified hardware.
(g) Minor reporting inconsistency (FWT 52.6% vs 53.88%), and ablation and PR-AUC numbers appear only in figures.
(h) Unrefereed preprint with no code.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overall: moderate on the setting, near zero on our contributions.

Where it overlaps:
- It is the closest recent work to our setting: unsupervised, normal-only, continually updated IDS, with PCA in the scoring path, a "new normal plus new attacks" stream, and low inference cost.
- Our PCA-plus-centroid detector looks like a stripped-down relative of its PCA reconstruction scorer.
- Reviewers will cite it, together with CND-IDS (same group, DAC 2025), as the state of the art in continual novelty detection IDS. We must position against it and ideally use it as a baseline.

Where it does not overlap:
- TOA-like direction budgeting: NO. There is no splitting of updates into an attack-direction component and the rest, no rationed budget, no per-update cap, no trust region, and no bound on time to compromise.
- Core / outer-ring robust updating: NO. There is no dense-core learning, no outer-ring corroboration of centre shifts, no gate on spread growth, and no robust statistics anywhere. Updates use all pseudo-labelled data plus reservoir replay, and the threshold uses plain mean and standard deviation. The nearest mechanisms are reservoir memories and replay, which fight forgetting, not adversaries.
- Freeze-type attack: NO. Poisoning and frog-boiling are not discussed, and nothing stops learning under suspicion. The model always updates, so it is exposed to slow poisoning rather than the freeze attack.
- Self-labelling: NO. It sidesteps the self-labelling danger we study by assuming a fresh clean, trusted normal set every task. That is a stronger, more privileged assumption than our fully self-labelling detector, and we should point this out.
- IoT / on-device: NO. No IoT-device datasets (no Kitsune, no N-BaIoT), no ESP32, no TinyML.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1) A strong baseline and an attack target. Its rule "any cluster with one clean sample becomes normal" is directly open to boiling-frog poisoning: attacker points placed near benign samples get labelled normal and then pulled toward normal by the triplet loss. Re-implement it (there is no code yet, but the description is enough: MLP autoencoder, triplet plus MSE loss, MiniBatchKMeans pseudo-labels, two 10K reservoirs, PCA at 95% variance, threshold mean + 2 SD). Then run our boiling-frog poisoner and the freeze attack against it. This fixes our open problem (4), that the freeze attack has only been shown against our own baselines. It turns a published 2026 continual novelty detector into a victim.
2) Show that our core/outer-ring and TOA mechanisms can wrap its update step: robust core-only pseudo-labelling, outer-ring corroboration before a cluster or PCA basis is accepted, and direction budgeting on the PCA subspace or encoder update.
3) Use its evaluation protocol and metrics: AVG, forward transfer (zero-day), backward transfer (forgetting) and PR-AUC with no threshold, plus EA/ENA-style scenarios. Also add our poisoned and frozen variants and real time-ordered drift (N-BaIoT / CESNET-TimeSeries24) in place of their synthetic K-Means drift split.
4) Use its per-sample inference timing as a reference point, and argue that we go further with real ESP32 latency, memory and energy measurements.
5) An argument for our side: ACORN-IDS needs a trusted clean set every task. Removing that need, or making it robust when the set is small or contaminated, is a clear distinction in our favour.
6) Its memory-policy comparison (reservoir vs SSF vs PSA) points to buffer choices worth testing for poison resistance, for example whether reservoir replay spreads poison further.

corpus.title: Navigating the Latent Manifold: Proactive Concept Drift Adaptation for Resilient NIDS (DriftXpert)
corpus.authors: Chao Zha, Zifeng Kang, Tian Liu, Dakun Shen, Ruyun Zhang (as listed on the arXiv abstract page). The paper cites "Zha et al. 2025 (A-NIDS, TIFS'25)" as a baseline, so this is probably the same group as A-NIDS. That link is my inference and I have not verified it.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08623 (HTML full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.08623v1 ; PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.08623 ; code: https://github.com/cc-sec-hub/DriftXpert, which I checked exists: public, 3 commits, no license shown, needs Python 3.8 + PyTorch/CUDA 11.7)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint (cs.CR), v1 submitted 8 Sep 2026. No venue is stated. The header still contains an unfilled ACM template placeholder ("Woodstock, NY, June 03-05, 2018"), so it has not been accepted anywhere yet, or the authors have not said where. Treat it as not peer-reviewed.
corpus.problem: ML-based NIDS models assume traffic is stationary. Under concept drift they lose detection and raise more false alarms. The paper separates local drift (a change confined to one subspace or attack type) from global drift (a change across the whole distribution, such as a new attack or a covariate shift). It assumes no historical data can be kept (storage and privacy) and that labels are costly, so drift detection has to be unsupervised. Threat model, Sec. 2.3: drift is natural, and adversarial drift is explicitly excluded ("excluding adversarial drift"). The same section then lists three threats: evasion via distribution shift, false-positive amplification from benign drift, and forgetting-induced vulnerability (updates erasing known attack patterns). It also says adversaries may "craft traffic patterns that mimic benign distribution changes". So the scope contradicts itself.
corpus.method: Two stages, both offline and batch. Stage 1 (Proactive Sensing, drift detection): freeze the historical encoder and run K-means on its latent vectors (K in [L, 3L] for L labels; K=5 used). A point's anomaly score is its squared distance to its cluster centre. The threshold is CI = mean historical distance + alpha * std. The drift statistic is the Outlier Ratio OR = (outlier fraction in the recent window) / (outlier fraction in the historical window), with the denominator set to 1 when it is zero. Drift is flagged when OR > T (T = 2.0 or 3.0). Detection runs periodically, not per packet. Stage 2 (Evolutionary Alignment, adaptation) runs only after drift is flagged. It keeps three models: current, previous-epoch and historical. (a) A model-contrastive loss (cosine similarity with temperature) pulls current latents toward the historical model's latents and pushes them away from the previous epoch's. (b) Weight aggregation interpolates W_his = beta*W_his + (1-beta)*W_cur, with beta 0.3 or 0.5. (c) Selective freezing keeps the first encoder layer fixed; the text says first layer, but the ablation D.X-EnFre freezes the whole encoder. Loss = cross-entropy on drifted data + gamma * contrastive loss (gamma 0.1 or 1.0). The model is a supervised MLP, encoder 50-96-96-64-32 plus a 32-2 classifier (benign/attack), 11,550 parameters in total. Adaptation needs labelled drifted samples: the authors propose manually labelling only the samples flagged as drifted, and in the enterprise data the labels came from an existing security system and were checked by experts. There is no streaming or online update mode. Appendices give a Gaussian-cluster analysis of alpha and a convergence argument for the contrastive loss.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Datasets: CICIDS-2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (CICFlowMeter features, 80 extracted and 50 kept, IPs and ports removed), with hand-built local and global drift splits. Also private traffic from the external-facing services of a large enterprise, collected month by month in early 2026 (attacks: command injection, directory traversal, SQL injection). There is an encrypted-traffic experiment whose dataset I could not identify. No IoT data (no N-BaIoT, Kitsune or IoT-23) and no IoT devices. Hardware: one PC (Intel i5-13500, 16 GB DDR5, Windows 11), scikit-learn for Stage 1 and PyTorch for Stage 2. Appendix H.5 reports about 46 KB of parameters, about 230 KB total training footprint (optimizer state and the three stored models), per-sample latency of 2.3 us or less, and throughput of 1.6 MQPS (encoder) and 16 MQPS (classifier). No MCU, ESP32 or embedded measurements. "Resource-constrained" here means a low-end PC. The Discussion calls it a "front-line scout residing at the high-speed network edge" and mentions "the power grid infrastructure evaluated in this study", but no power-grid evaluation appears anywhere I could see. That looks like a leftover from another paper.
corpus.results: The summarizer gave these numbers; check them against the PDF before citing. CICIDS-2017 local drift: drifted-set benign/malicious F1 = 99.79/97.96, historical set 99.79/97.90. CICIDS-2017 global drift: drifted 98.35/98.22, historical 87.20/84.90. CICIDS-2018 local drift: drifted 99.03/98.75, historical 92.47/91.07. CICIDS-2018 global drift: drifted 98.14/97.96, historical 88.49/88.97. Enterprise drifted set: F1 99.43 benign / 97.10 malicious, historical malicious recall 96.12. OWAD reportedly scores only 7.97 malicious F1 on this set. Encrypted traffic, drifted: ACC 0.85 / F1 0.89 / TPR 0.90, versus A-NIDS 0.71, SSF 0.54 and OWAD 0.32 ACC. The drift detector itself is weak: macro-recall 84.29 (local) and 81.77 (global), macro-precision only 50.07 (local, which they blame on class imbalance), accuracy 81.07 / 78.69. Enterprise month 2: OR = 20.4 at alpha around 3.5, with about 1,357 of 42,875 sampled flows shifted. FPR is never reported directly, only benign precision and recall. Baselines: MLP fine-tuning, MLP with the first layer frozen, OWAD (NDSS'23), A-NIDS (TIFS'25, CTGAN replay), SSF (INFOCOM'25).
corpus.limitations: The paper has no limitations or future-work section. Limitations stated or implied: (1) adaptation needs labelled drifted data, so it is not self-supervised; (2) drift-detection precision is low (50% for local drift); OR needs a minimum outlier count to be reliable, and K must be estimated from history; (3) appendix analysis assumes Gaussian clusters and uses approximations (Taylor expansion, Plackett's approximation); (4) latent distributions are only partly aligned after adaptation, which the authors argue is enough; (5) offline batch only, no streaming updates; (6) adversarial drift is excluded, yet the threat-model text mentions adversaries mimicking benign drift; (7) no FPR reported; (8) quality problems: an unfilled ACM template, the stray "power grid" claim, and freezing described as first-layer in the text but whole-encoder in the ablation; (9) no IoT data and no embedded hardware.
corpus.overlap_with_us: Low. The only real overlap is the drift-detection primitive. Their Stage 1 (cluster centre plus a mean + alpha*std distance threshold, then the ratio of recent to historical outlier fractions) is close to our centre + spread detector. Their OR statistic is essentially our signature-free test of whether the outer ring really gets busier. They use it as a trigger for supervised retraining, while we use it as an evidence gate on spread growth. Point by point: (a) TOA-like direction budgeting: no. There is no projection, no per-direction rationing, no budget on movement toward an attack signature, and no minimum time-to-compromise bound. Their beta weight interpolation and contrastive pull toward the historical model are an undirected stability anchor, closer to an EMA prior than to TOA. (b) Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. There is no trimming, no robust statistics, no core-only learning and no check that the outer ring backs a shift; they retrain on all labelled drifted samples. (c) Freeze-type attack: no. Their "selective freezing" means freezing encoder layers for stability, not halting learning under suspicion, and nobody attacks it. But their pipeline is exactly the kind of gated, stop-start adapter our freeze attack targets. Updates happen only when OR > T, so an attacker who keeps OR under T (blending in, or raising the historical outlier rate) stalls adaptation while honest drift piles up. Pushing OR over T on purpose triggers retraining on whatever the label oracle produces, and floods the labelling queue. (d) Poisoning: not in scope. It appears only as a criticism of baselines (generative replay "introduce[s] additional security risks, such as data poisoning", and pseudo-labelling "may induce self-poisoning"). Their own update path is never analysed under attack. (e) Setting: supervised, offline, enterprise/CICIDS, PC hardware. Ours is unsupervised, self-labelling, online every cycle, IoT (N-BaIoT/Kitsune) and aimed at ESP32. In short, DriftXpert does not take our novelty. It is a 2026 example of a drift-adaptive NIDS that names false-positive amplification and adversarial mimicry of benign drift as threats and then explicitly leaves them out of scope. That is the gap we fill.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow: 1) Framing and citation: quote their exclusion of adversarial drift and their own threat list (false-positive amplification from benign drift, forgetting-induced vulnerability) as evidence that recent drift-adaptive NIDS work names these threats but does not defend against them. Our freeze attack is deliberately induced false-positive amplification, and boiling-frog poisoning is induced forgetting of the attack boundary. 2) Their OR = recent outlier fraction / historical outlier fraction with a mean + alpha*std threshold is a cheap statistic that fits on an ESP32. Adopt or cite it as the formal version of our outer-ring-gets-busier test, and use their Appendix E Gaussian analysis of alpha to set our ring thresholds in a principled way. 3) A new published target for the freeze attack (open problem 4): code is public. Run our freeze attack and boiling-frog poisoner against their OR > T trigger with our modelled label oracle, for example by keeping OR just under T while benign drift builds, or by forcing triggers to swamp labelling. That moves us past attacking only our own baselines. Their baselines OWAD (NDSS'23), SSF (INFOCOM'25) and A-NIDS (TIFS'25) are further published adaptive NIDS to attack and compare against. 4) Their local vs global drift split gives us a way to state open problem 1 precisely: an attack hidden inside strong global drift beats the signature-free version. We could evaluate both regimes. 5) Their Appendix H.5 (parameter memory, training footprint, per-sample latency, throughput) is a ready template for our ESP32 results table. Their 11,550-parameter, about 46 KB MLP would fit in ESP32 SRAM, so a ported version could serve as a supervised on-device baseline. 6) Their beta weight-interpolation anchor is a natural ablation against TOA: show that undirected anchoring either slows honest adaptation or still gets poisoned, while direction-aware budgeting does neither.

Everything above came through a summarizer, so check exact numbers and quotes against the PDF before citing them. Not captured: the body of Related Work (Sec. 8, which came out truncated), the ablation results (Sec. 5.4), the alpha-sensitivity results (Sec. 5.6.1) and the encrypted-traffic dataset name. I did not open the PDF itself.

corpus.title: Shift Detection and Adaptation for Network Intrusion Detection (the system is called NetSight in v1 and on the arXiv abstract page; the v2 body text seems to say "our work" instead)
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15100 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2508.15100v1 and https://arxiv.org/html/2508.15100v2)
corpus.authors: Ehssan Mousavipour, Andrey Dimanchev, Majid Ghaderi. I did not check affiliations; Ghaderi is probably at the University of Calgary, but that is from memory.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, cs.CR cross-listed to cs.LG. v1 was posted 20 Aug 2025 (4.3 MB) and v2 on 17 May 2026 (235 KB, the current version). The abstract page lists no journal, conference or comments field. I could not check whether it has been accepted anywhere: the shared web-search budget ran out before I could run a venue search, so I relied only on the arXiv pages.
corpus.problem: Normality shift: the distribution of benign traffic changes over time and deep-learning NIDS degrade (more false positives and false negatives). The authors argue that supervised adaptation needs costly manual labels, that unsupervised adaptation (OWAD) needs clean normal data, and that every adaptation method risks catastrophic forgetting. Their goal is online shift detection and adaptation with no manual labelling. They assume benign traffic is more consistent than malicious traffic. There is no threat model: no adversary, attacker capability or adversarial goal is defined anywhere.
corpus.method:
The pipeline follows OWAD's detect, explain, adapt structure.
(1) Detector: an autoencoder whose encoder and decoder outputs are both used. It is trained with an InfoNCE contrastive loss (cosine similarity, temperature 0.02), with labelled normal samples as positives and abnormal ones as negatives. The initial model therefore needs labelled training data, which is why they call it supervised. The architecture and batch sizes follow OWAD.
(2) Pseudo-labelling ("distribution-level voting"): a prototype is the mean embedding of normal samples. For each component (encoder, decoder), one Gaussian per class is fitted by maximum likelihood to the similarity-to-prototype scores. Each component labels a sample by comparing class likelihoods. Whichever component had the larger KL divergence between its abnormal and normal Gaussians on the training data supplies the final label. There is no confidence gate and no check of pseudo-label quality before adaptation.
(3) Shift detection: similarity scores become P(normal | score) through Bayes' rule with training-set priors. Old and new posterior histograms (same bins) are compared with a permutation test, using KL divergence as the statistic and "no shift" as the null hypothesis. Window size, number of bins, number of permutations and significance level are not given. The paper also never says what happens when no shift is detected.
(4) Shift explanation: learnable masks over old and new samples, relaxed to [0,1] and then rounded (the rounding rule is not given). The objective is a histogram-reconstruction KL term, plus 10 x the L1 norm of the masks (to keep the selected set small), plus 1 x a binary-entropy term.
(5) Adaptation: the old model is cloned as a frozen teacher and the student is fine-tuned on the selected, pseudo-labelled samples. The loss is the contrastive loss plus 0.1 x a similarity-preserving (relational) knowledge-distillation loss on softmaxed pairwise similarities. Optimisers: Adam for 10 epochs at lr 1e-5 for initial training; SGD at lr 1e-4 for adaptation, 5 epochs on Kyoto and 10 on CIC.
In effect this is self-training on the model's own labels, gated by a drift test.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Data:
- Kyoto2006+, preprocessed via the AnoShift benchmark and OWAD's code (roughly 10 years, 2006 to 2015): train on 2007, adapt on the 2011 training portion, test on 2011 to 2014 (periods T1 to T4).
- CICIDS2017 for training (1,270,155 normal, 69.53%; 556,549 abnormal) and CICDDoS2019 for testing. Non-TCP traffic was removed from CICDDoS2019. It was originally 0.65% normal (26,745) against 4,279,618 abnormal, and was rebalanced with ADASYN, falling back to SMOTE, to 1,270,155 normal. Of those, 1,245,236 (about 98%) are synthetic. It is then split 80/20 for adaptation and test.
- The abstract says "three long-term datasets".
Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3080 Ti, 3.8 GHz Intel i7, 16 GB RAM, so GPU only. No latency, memory, model size or training time is reported, and there is nothing on edge, IoT or microcontroller deployment.
corpus.results:
Baselines: Retrain, OWAD (unsupervised, given a 5% manual-label budget and its best threshold), AOC-IDS (supervised periodic retraining) and SSF (buffer plus regularisation with shift-triggered updates; also given 5% labels). Metrics: F1, accuracy, balanced accuracy (BACC) and MCC.
Headline: F1 up to 11.72% better than OWAD and up to 7.42% better than SSF, using zero manual labels.
Kyoto F1 values given in the v1 text (the text does not say which baseline is which):
- T1: 0.9634 against 0.8932, 0.9476 and 0.9260.
- T2: 0.9540 against 0.9374, 0.9432 and 0.9001.
- T3: 0.9610 against 0.9560, 0.9591 and 0.9414.
At T4 (2014) every method collapses (BACC about 0.49 to 0.50, MCC about 0), so no method adapts there.
CIC: pre-adaptation F1 is 0.4183 and absolute performance stays low; Retrain's final MCC is about 0.416. The reading tool's summary of the CIC gains was muddled, so treat any CIC delta other than the headline 11.72% and 7.42% as unverified.
Ablation: distribution-level voting is compared with point-wise labelling only in figures. The text quotes a 78% true-negative rate for the point-wise version on CICDDoS2019.
All other per-period numbers are only in Figs. 2-13, which I could not read.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors (there is no limitations section): future work on more domain-aware shift explanation and more strategic distillation. They also note that all methods fail at Kyoto T4.
Unstated, from my reading:
- No threat model and no adversarial or poisoning evaluation, even though the system trains on its own pseudo-labels.
- Pseudo-label accuracy is never measured directly, and how label noise propagates into adaptation is not analysed.
- Key drift-test settings (window, bins, permutations, alpha) and the no-shift branch are not specified.
- About 98% of the CICDDoS2019 normal evaluation data is SMOTE/ADASYN-synthetic.
- Initial training needs labelled data.
- Baselines got different label budgets, and OWAD was run at its optimal threshold.
- There is an internal inconsistency: 69.53% is quoted as the CICDDoS2019 normal share, but that is the CICIDS2017 figure.
- GPU-only deep autoencoder with no cost numbers and no IoT, edge or on-device angle.
- v2 shrank from 4.3 MB to 235 KB and seems to drop the NetSight name from the body text; I am not certain about that.
- Not peer-reviewed as far as I could tell.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low. It is in the same area (self-labelling, drift-adaptive NIDS that updates online without humans) but does not touch our contributions.
- No TOA-like direction budgeting. The closest thing is the frozen-teacher distillation term (weight 0.1). It limits forgetting the same way in every direction, is not aware of attack directions, and gives no minimum time to compromise.
- No core/outer-ring robust updating, trimming or robust statistics. Its shift-explanation masks pick the smallest set of samples that best explains the histogram change. That is close to the opposite of robust trimming: if an attacker caused the change, the attacker's samples are exactly the ones that explain it best.
- No freeze-type attack and no freeze-under-suspicion defense. It adapts only when the permutation test flags a shift; the frozen teacher is for distillation, not a safeguard.
- The words poisoning, adversary and attacker manipulation do not appear in the paper.
So it does not pre-empt us. It is a realistic, recent, published-on-arXiv victim system of exactly the class our threat targets: deep, GPU-based, and with no IoT or on-device focus, which is our angle.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. A published external target for our attacks (open problem 4). Run our boiling-frog poisoner against NetSight, or at least its OWAD-style detect, explain, adapt loop, and show it can be poisoned. I did not check whether NetSight's code is public. I believe OWAD's is, but that is from memory and unchecked here.
Two new attack angles to test:
(a) Gate-evasion poisoning: keep each cycle's poison below the power of the permutation test, so no shift is flagged while the drift accumulates. Or trigger a shift on purpose so that adaptation runs on data the attacker chose.
(b) Explanation-concentration poisoning: the sample-selection masks should select attack samples first, because those samples explain the shift best. A short theorem or experiment showing that minimal-explanation selection amplifies poison share would be a neat, citable contribution.
2. A principled drift test to replace our heuristics. A permutation test with KL on binned posterior or score histograms could turn our "outer ring really busier" and "outer ring backs the centre shift" checks into p-value tests. It is cheap enough for an ESP32 if we use few bins and few permutations.
3. Real long-term drift data for open problem 1 (an attack hidden inside strong genuine drift): Kyoto2006+ through the AnoShift benchmark gives about 10 years of real drift with a year-split protocol. Train on 2007, adapt on 2011, test on 2011-2014, and hide poison inside the real 2007-to-2011 shift. AnoShift is NeurIPS 2022 Datasets and Benchmarks from memory; treat it as background, unchecked here.
4. Evaluation hygiene: report BACC and MCC alongside detection rate and false-alarm rate, and include a "no-adaptation / Retrain" reference, as they do.
5. Related-work positioning: cite it as evidence that the latest self-labelling drift-adaptation NIDS (2025-2026) still have no threat model for their own feedback loop. That is our motivation.
6. Possible minor ideas: relational distillation as an alternative anchor for a future neural student, and their "choose the most separable component" voting, for choosing which PCA components to trust.

corpus.title: On the Adversarial Risk of Test Time Adaptation: An Investigation into Realistic Test-Time Data Poisoning
corpus.authors: Yongyi Su, Yushu Li, Nanqing Liu, Kui Jia, Xulei Yang, Chuan-Sheng Foo, Xun Xu
corpus.venue_year: ICLR 2025. arXiv v1 7 Oct 2024, v3 28 Feb 2025. The arXiv comments field says "Accepted by ICLR 2025", and the official GitHub README says it was accepted on 2025-01-23. I could not check the OpenReview page myself because the shared web-search budget had run out.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04682 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.04682v3 ; code: https://github.com/Gorilla-Lab-SCUT/RTTDP)
corpus.problem: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model's weights on the unlabeled test stream it receives. That opens a hole: a malicious user can put poisoned samples into the stream and degrade the model's predictions on other users' benign samples. The authors argue that earlier TTA poisoning attacks (DIA, TePA) overstate this risk because they assume too much: white-box access to the live model, access to other users' benign samples in the same batch, or poisoning before adaptation starts. They propose a more realistic protocol called RTTDP. It has three rules. (1) Grey-box: the attacker knows only the architecture and initial weights, not the live weights, but can query the online model. (2) No access to benign data: the attacker sees only its own clean samples and the poisoned samples it makes from them. (3) Online order: poisoned samples are mixed into minibatches during adaptation, so each batch combines attacker and benign samples. Success is measured as the error on the benign part of each batch. The attacker's share of a batch is r, 50% by default, with 10% and 20% in the appendix. There are two timing modes: Uniform (poisoned batches spread through the stream) and Non-Uniform (a short, heavy burst).
corpus.method: Attack: (1) A grey-box surrogate. The attacker distils the online model into a local copy by matching its outputs on the attacker's own queries (symmetric KL loss; SGD, learning rate 0.1, 10 iterations per update). The paper reports this works about as well as white-box access. (2) An in-distribution poisoning objective. It is built from DIA's two-level formulation but no longer needs benign samples. It adds a feature-consistency regularizer that keeps the Gaussian statistics of the poisoned samples' pre-normalization features close to those of the attacker's clean samples, so the poisoned batch-norm statistics carry over to benign data. (3) Two objectives aimed at how TTA learns. NHE (Notch High Entropy) pushes predictions toward a uniform spread over the wrong classes; it exploits entropy-minimizing methods, which make larger updates on high-entropy inputs. BLE (Balanced Low Entropy) sends each class to a different confident wrong class, using a moving-average confusion matrix and a linear assignment; it avoids class collapse so it gets past diversity-based safeguards. Poisoned inputs come from a 40-step L-infinity PGD attack on the surrogate, with budget 0.3 and step size 0.01; returns flatten beyond 40 steps. Defenses studied, each added to a plain entropy-minimization baseline: entropy thresholding (rejecting high-entropy samples), CoTTA-style augmentation with a consistency constraint, an EMA (slowly averaged) teacher update, and stochastic resetting of parameters to the source model.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Image classification only: CIFAR10-C, CIFAR100-C and ImageNet-C at corruption severity 5, in a continual TTA setting where the corruption type changes along the stream. Models: WideResNet-28 (CIFAR10-C), ResNeXt-29 (CIFAR100-C), ResNet-50 (ImageNet-C), all supervised source models pre-trained from RobustBench or torchvision/timm. TTA methods attacked: TENT, RPL, EATA, TTAC, SAR, CoTTA, ROID on CIFAR, and TENT, SAR, CoTTA, ROID on ImageNet-C. Hardware: the paper text I read gives none. The GitHub README recommends an NVIDIA RTX A5000 (24 GB) with PyTorch 2.3 and CUDA 12.1. There is no edge or embedded evaluation, and no measurement of on-device cost. I could not find the batch size in what was surfaced (the appendix details section A.3 did not come through).
corpus.results: CIFAR10-C, Uniform timing, error on benign samples: clean average 18.28%; under attack BLE 35.61% and NHE 36.25% on average, against DIA 20.05%, TePA 21.73% and MaxCE 18.71%. Per method: TENT 19.72% → 73.86% (NHE) / 54.07% (BLE); RPL 21.00% → 72.40% / 51.99%; EATA 18.03% → 29.73% / 45.20%; CoTTA 16.46% → 17.54% / 19.06%; ROID 16.37% → 17.00% / 19.06%. Methods with EMA updates (CoTTA, ROID) are nearly immune. CIFAR100-C: clean average 37.77%, NHE 53.65%, BLE 48.69%, TENT up to 92.08%. ImageNet-C: clean average 60.30%, NHE 68.04%, BLE 63.96%, TENT 78.03%, SAR 72.58%. Non-Uniform (burst) attacks are generally stronger than Uniform ones (CIFAR10-C, TENT, NHE: 73.65%). Ablations: the surrogate performs about as well as the real model; feature consistency adds a lot; adding the surrogate and regularizer also strengthens older attacks (TePA on TENT 33.78% → 38.79%). Defenses (CIFAR10-C, entropy-minimization baseline): entropy thresholding cuts NHE error from 73.86% to 35.86%; augmentation brings it to about 20%; EMA is the strongest, about 20% under both attacks when combined; stochastic restoration alone gives 50.68% under NHE and adds nothing on top of the others. Headline conclusion: under realistic assumptions the adversarial risk of TTA "might be over estimated".
corpus.limitations: The paper has no limitations section; in what I read, the conclusion only says the risk may be overestimated and that the practices they identified should guide robust TTA design. Limitations I can see myself: (1) Images only. An L-infinity pixel perturbation of 0.3 has no direct counterpart in network traffic, where features are bound by protocol rules. (2) The attacks are short-horizon: each batch is perturbed on its own, uniformly or in one burst. There is no slow, boiling-frog campaign and no study of how far the model drifts over many cycles. (3) Only supervised classifiers with batch-norm and entropy-based adaptation. No unsupervised anomaly or novelty detectors. (4) No provable guarantees for any defense, such as a minimum time before compromise. (5) No look at what defenses cost under honest drift. EMA and entropy thresholding are judged only on attack robustness, not on whether they slow legitimate adaptation. (6) No attack that switches adaptation off; they never ask whether gating defenses can be tricked into rejecting benign data. (7) GPU-only setup, nothing on-device. Details I could not verify: batch size, the numbers for the r = 0.1 / 0.2 runs (appendix A.4.4 was not surfaced), and the exact GPU used for the paper's own runs (only the README's recommendation).
corpus.overlap_with_us: Low overlap. TOA-like direction budgeting: no. No defense separates an update into a threat-aligned part and the rest. Their closest idea is EMA, which slows every direction equally. So EMA also slows honest drift, which is exactly the trade-off TOA avoids, and the paper never measures that cost. Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. Entropy thresholding (dropping high-entropy samples) is the only sample-selection defense, and it is a gate on confidence, not a robust centre/spread estimate with an outer-ring check. Freeze-type attack: no. Neither "stop adapting" nor "trip the defense on purpose" is discussed, and model collapse as an attack goal is not mentioned. The nearest it comes is the observation that EATA/SAR-style reliable-sample filtering and EMA buy robustness; it does not consider that an attacker could exploit those gates to stall adaptation while the domain drifts. Boiling-frog / slow poisoning over drift: no. The stream is continual (corruption types change), but the poison is batch-level adversarial perturbation, not gradual centroid dragging. The one real conceptual overlap: their feature-consistency regularizer makes poisoned samples statistically look like clean data so they pass and transfer, which is the same idea as our adaptive attacker hiding poison inside the dense core. Their "attacker share r" sweep is the TTA version of our attacker-share axis (Kloft and Laskov). Overall it does not pre-empt TOA, the signature-free core/outer-ring method, or the freeze attack, and it is a different setting: supervised image TTA versus unsupervised on-device IoT anomaly detection.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow: (1) A realistic threat-model checklist. Write our attacker in the same three terms: grey-box (knows the algorithm, not the live centre/spread), no access to other devices' benign traffic, and online injection mixed with honest traffic. Cite RTTDP as precedent, so reviewers see our threat model follows the latest standard rather than an overpowered one. (2) A surrogate-by-querying attacker. An adaptive IoT poisoner could watch accept/alert decisions (for example whether its packets are dropped) and rebuild a surrogate centroid, then steer the poison. That gives a stronger, more believable adaptive attacker than one assumed to know the state. (3) Timing modes. Evaluate Uniform versus Non-Uniform (burst) poisoning on top of slow boiling-frog, and sweep the attacker share r in {0.1, 0.2, 0.5}, matching their grid. (4) The defense-ablation table format. Map their defenses onto our baselines (entropy thresholding ≈ suspicion gating/freezing, EMA ≈ uniform slow learning rate, stochastic restoration ≈ periodic reset to a clean snapshot). Then show TOA keeps the robustness of EMA without slowing honest drift. They only measure attack robustness, so a "robustness versus drift-tracking" Pareto plot is something we add beyond them. (5) A freeze attack on published gating defenses (our open problem 4). EATA and SAR filter by entropy or reliability, and the paper shows thresholding is a main source of robustness. A natural extension is to show that such filters can be tripped so honest drifted data gets rejected. It is cross-domain, but it would let us claim the freeze attack applies beyond our own baselines. (6) Their feature-consistency regularizer is a cited example of the "poison that looks like the core" adaptive attack. Use it to justify our core-hiding attacker and as an adaptive-attack design pattern (matching first and second moments of clean traffic). (7) Positioning line for related work: "Recent TTA poisoning work (Su et al., ICLR 2025) studies per-batch adversarial perturbations against supervised image classifiers and finds EMA and entropy filtering effective; it considers neither gradual drift-camouflaged poisoning, the cost of these defenses under honest drift, nor attacks that exploit the defenses' rejection behaviour."

corpus.title: Provably Safe Model Updates
corpus.authors: Leo Elmecker-Plakolm, Philip Sosnin, Calvin Tsay, Matthew Wicker (Department of Computing, Imperial College London); Pierre Fasterling (EPFL, School of Computer and Communication Sciences). Affiliations come from the arXiv HTML full text.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv:2512.01899. v1 submitted 1 Dec 2025, v2 revised 18 Mar 2026. The arXiv comments field says it was accepted at SaTML 2026 (IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning), with the final version due on IEEE Xplore. I could not check the acceptance against SaTML's own accepted-papers list because the shared web-search budget ran out, so it rests on the authors' arXiv note only. 12 pages, 9 figures, cs.LG / stat.ML.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01899 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2512.01899v2)
corpus.problem: Deployed models need regular updates. Even harmless updates can cause catastrophic forgetting or alignment drift, and heuristics like EWC, LwF, regularization or parameter isolation cannot certify that the updated model still meets its specification. The paper defines a "delta-safe update mechanism": for ANY new update dataset D', the expected specification loss phi (in the experiments, 1 minus accuracy) on the ORIGINAL task distribution stays at or below delta after the update. The definition says nothing about how well the model does on the new task, and doing nothing is trivially safe. The setting is sequential, batch-based continual learning and fine-tuning. It is not streaming, not anomaly detection, not IoT, and has no attacker model: the "worst case over D'" is a robustness quantifier, not a security threat model.
corpus.method: 1) Local Invariant Domain (LID): a connected region T of parameter space that contains the current parameters theta, such that every theta' in T satisfies the spec bound delta. The maximal LID is the one with the largest volume (Def. 3), which is intractable to compute exactly. 2) Relaxation: restrict T to a parametric abstract domain. In practice this is an orthotope (an interval box [theta_L, theta_U]); zonotopes are mentioned but the visible text gives no working detail for them. The expectation is replaced by an empirical mean, and the inner max over theta' by an Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) upper bound, which needs monotonic activations and costs at most about 4x a forward pass. The box volume is maximized under the constraint "IBP bound <= delta" with a Lagrangian, solved by gradient descent-ascent (Cooper library), training on soft accuracy and certifying on true accuracy afterwards. 3) Safe update: whatever optimizer proposes the update (SGD, SFT, DPO, ...), it is projected onto the LID. For a box this is just per-coordinate clamping. 4) Continual learning: the per-task LIDs are intersected, or a joint LID is optimized over a replay buffer. Algorithm 1 RETURNS EARLY, meaning updating stops, once the intersection is empty. The buffer variant recomputes the LID when target accuracy is not reached. 5) Extras: (a) several LIDs saved as checkpoints during optimization, with the projection choosing the nearest box or the one with the lowest batch loss; (b) "regularization-inspired" biases, where the top fraction of important weights (by Fisher information or synaptic intelligence) is frozen, or wide intervals on important weights are penalized; (c) a "lookahead buffer": a small sample from the FUTURE task used to estimate which weights must stay free to move, so the box is widened along them. 6) Finite-sample certificate: a Hoeffding margin sqrt((b-a)^2 log(1/beta)/(2N)) for bounded phi, or a Chebyshev margin; unbounded losses need clipping or a CLT approximation.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Continual learning: Split-MNIST (5 two-digit odd/even contexts, small CNN with 2 conv layers of 8 channels, 5x5 kernels, plus a dense layer; 100 runs without a buffer, 15 with one) and Split-CIFAR-10 (pretrained ResNet-18 backbone, LIDs computed only for the head; the main text says 5 tasks but the appendix lists 4 class pairs, an inconsistency inside the paper). Class-IL, Domain-IL and Task-IL scenarios. Baselines: SGD, EWC, LwF, InterContiNet (ICN), A-GEM. Buffer sizes 1k/5k/15k. Foundation-model fine-tuning: binary hate-speech classification with a linear head on frozen embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, MXBAI, M2-BERT-80M-2k-retrieval, GTE-Large, Voyage-3; Gemini also appears in the results). The head is trained on Jigsaw, then updated on Twitter Hate Speech, Civil Comments, Hatemoji, SBIC and HateCheck. Also multilingual 3-way sentiment on XLM-T (8 languages, English first). Hardware: 2x NVIDIA L40 GPUs, custom PyTorch. Appendix G (two Split-MNIST tasks, 50 runs): ours 43.18 +/- 2.19 s total, of which the LID takes 12.92 +/- 0.79 s; ICN 70.09 s (LID 51.81 s); SGD 16.08 s; EWC 15.17 s; A-GEM 20.29 s; LwF 14.96 s. Nothing on-device or embedded.
corpus.results: Split-MNIST: competitive in Class-IL with formal lower bounds on forgetting (shown as dashed lines in figures; the exact certificate numbers are only in the figures, which I could not read). Better first-task retention in Domain-IL. With the 15k buffer it beats A-GEM in Class-IL. ICN suffers "constraint collapse". Split-CIFAR-10: competitive overall, clearly better task-1 retention in Class-IL. In Domain-IL average accuracy is higher, but the worst-case certificates are BELOW the baselines' actual performance, so the certificates are conservative. Hate speech and multilingual sentiment: LID-constrained updates sometimes cost a little downstream accuracy and sometimes match or beat the EWC baseline, while certifying non-trivial lower bounds on Jigsaw macro accuracy; the authors call this the first formal forgetting guarantee in a real LLM-embedding NLP pipeline. Table I (Split-MNIST Class-IL, Task-2 accuracy, 15 seeds): unbiased LID 0.20; lookahead with synaptic intelligence peaks at 0.73 +/- 0.18 at 82.5% pruning; lookahead with Fisher 0.73 +/- 0.15 at 82.5%; without lookahead the best is only about 0.36-0.39, with high variance. In other words, a plain certified box leaves very little room to learn the new task, and most of the gain comes from knowing in advance where the future task needs to move.
corpus.limitations: Stated by the authors: IBP gets looser with depth and width, so early layers end up effectively frozen; activations must be monotonic; finite-sample guarantees need a bounded spec (otherwise clipping or an asymptotic CLT argument); gradient descent-ascent finds only local optima, so a post-hoc certificate is required; training uses a soft-accuracy surrogate while certification uses true accuracy; variance across seeds is high, especially for biasing without lookahead. Also visible but not stated as limitations: (1) the certificate only covers the OLD specification on i.i.d. samples from the old distribution, so under concept drift it certifies a stale target; (2) the paper never analyses plasticity once the LID is small or the intersection is empty; Algorithm 1 simply stops updating; (3) there is no adversary, no poisoning analysis and no streaming or online setting; (4) zonotopes are claimed in the abstract but not developed in the visible text; (5) the LID is computed once offline on GPUs, roughly 3x slower than SGD.
corpus.overlap_with_us: Overall overlap is low, and it is conceptual only. Blunt answers to the three questions: (1) TOA-style direction budgeting: NO. Both methods restrict proposed updates by projection, which is the shared idea, but theirs clamps each coordinate to a fixed box computed once around the starting parameters. There is no attack direction, no split into an attack-aligned and an orthogonal component, no slow budget, and no time-to-compromise bound. Their guarantee is a static region ("stay inside the box and the old task holds"); ours is a rate ("the attack-aligned movement accumulates no faster than the budget, so compromise takes at least T cycles"). (2) Core/outer-ring robust updating: NO. They never look at the update data at all; the method is deliberately independent of the data and the optimizer, and it has no robust statistics, density cores or support checks. (3) A freeze-type attack: NO. There is no attacker of any kind. Their method is, however, a FREEZING-CLASS defense in our sense. The do-nothing mechanism counts as safe; drift pushes parameters out of the fixed box and gets clamped (a per-coordinate freeze); important weights are frozen outright in the pruning variant; and Algorithm 1 stops learning once the intersected LID is empty. If transplanted to a self-labelling IDS whose spec includes "low false alarms on the old normal traffic", honest drift would be clamped and false alarms would climb, which is exactly the failure mode we measured. Recomputing the LID from a buffer, their fix, would rebuild it from self-labelled data that the poisoner can influence. Different domain (vision/NLP continual learning versus IoT network anomaly detection), no on-device side. So it neither pre-empts nor scoops TOA, the signature-free defense, or the freeze attack. It is, though, a 2025/2026 published, certified "safe update" defense that reviewers will expect us to cite and probably compare against.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow: 1) A formal definition: adapt their delta-safe update mechanism to our detector. For example: for any stream the attacker controls at share at most rho, the detection rate on held-out known-attack samples stays at least 1-delta for at least T cycles. That gives TOA's guarantee a crisp statement reviewers will recognise. 2) An exact, cheap LID for our detector: our parameters are only (centre c in R^k, spread s), so we can compute a certified safe box in closed form or by tiny LP-style bounds with no IBP looseness. Projection is k+1 clamps, trivial on an ESP32. Pitch: "certified safe-region projection, made exact and microcontroller-cheap for centroid detectors". 3) A published baseline for the freeze attack (our open problem 4): implement LID projection with box intersection and buffer recomputation on our detector, then show (a) that a box fixed around the start freezes under honest drift, giving high false alarms, and (b) that recomputing from self-labelled buffers is poisonable. That turns "shown only against our own baselines" into "shown against a SaTML 2026 certified defense". 4) A hybrid contribution: a certified box ALONG the attack direction only, with full freedom orthogonally, so TOA's rate bound plus a hard certificate. This answers their own Table-I lesson that unconstrained boxes kill plasticity. 5) Lookahead buffers, mapped to our open problem 2 (a new device joining): a small labelled sample of the new device's traffic tells us which directions to free up, similar to their 0.20 -> 0.73 gain. 6) The Hoeffding finite-sample margin for certifying detection on a finite set of attack-signature samples. 7) Multiple LIDs, as several candidate safe regions, the nearest one chosen per update; this could pair with per-device detectors.

The fetch tool returned model-written summaries rather than the raw text, so the details above are paraphrased, not quoted.
