corpus.title: When Normality Shifts: Risk-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Unsupervised Tabular Anomaly Detection (RTTAD)
corpus.authors: Wei Huang, Hezhe Qiao, Kailai Zhang, Zaisheng Ye, Yu-Ming Shang, Xiangling Fu (as listed on the arXiv abstract page; affiliations not checked)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, cs.LG / cs.AI, v1 submitted 11 May 2026 (13 pages, 6 figures). The arXiv page names no venue. I could not check whether it has been accepted anywhere because this turn's web-search budget ran out, so treat it as an unrefereed 2026 preprint.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10242 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.10242v1)
corpus.problem: "Normality shift" in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection. The training data is small and not very varied, so it covers only part of the normal manifold. At test time, valid but unseen normal samples get flagged and false alarms rise. Naive test-time adaptation (TTA) on the unlabeled test set can absorb anomalies, which the paper calls "anomaly contamination". The paper wants to fix the shift without being contaminated. Contamination is treated as a passive property of the test data. No attacker is involved.
corpus.method:
Two stages.
(1) Training: a masked-autoencoder backbone in the MCM style. A mask generator makes several sigmoid masks that share one encoder. The main task reconstructs the input from the masked embedding. The auxiliary task uses an MLP to predict the embedding of the unmasked input. A diversity loss stops the masks from being redundant. Total loss = main + lambda*aux + gamma*diversity, with lambda = min(1, 1/L_m).
(2) Test-time contrastive learning (TTCL), run in rounds over the whole test set:
- Each sample's loss is min-max normalised to [0,1] and used as an anomaly probability.
- A GMM "adaptively" sets confidence thresholds, giving a high-confidence normal set and a high-confidence abnormal set. The paper does not say what the GMM is fitted on, how many components it has, or how the threshold is derived.
- Update loss: for each selected sample, the sign is +1 if pseudo-normal (lower its reconstruction/aux error) and -1 if pseudo-anomalous (push its error up). Added to this is a kNN contrastive term (k = 3) toward a growing pool O of known-normal embeddings, with the same +/-1 sign.
- After each round, the new pseudo-normals join O. Rounds stop when "no sufficient samples remain" (undefined).
- Final labels: the top alpha-percentile of scores, which needs the contamination rate.
"Risk-aware" is never defined or computed as a quantity. It just means updating only on confident samples. There is no anchor to the source model, no EMA teacher, no frozen layers, no per-update budget, and no bound on the negated (-1) loss term. Optimiser: Adam, batch 512, 200 epochs, weight decay 1e-5.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
15 ODDS/ADBench tabular datasets: Arrhythmia, BreastW, Cardio, Cardiotocography, Glass, Ionosphere, Mammography, Optdigits, Pendigits, Pima, Satellite, Satimage-2, Thyroid, WBC, Wine. None are network-intrusion or IoT data (no KDD, NSL-KDD, UNSW, CIC, Kitsune or N-BaIoT).
The shift is synthetic. K-Means is run on the normal samples, the largest cluster is split between train and test, and the other normal clusters plus all anomalies go to test. The gap is checked with t-SNE, Jeffreys divergence and OTDD. There is no temporal stream and no real drift.
Hardware: one NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, PyTorch. No runtime, memory or energy figures. Nothing on edge or microcontroller hardware.
corpus.results:
Averages over the 15 datasets, 3 runs, against 15 baselines (IForest, LOF, OCSVM, DeepSVDD, ECOD, GOAD, NeuTraL AD, ICL, DIF, SLAD, LUNAR, MCM, DRL, TTAD, EPHAD):
- AUC-PR: 0.6388 vs 0.6073 for LUNAR
- AUC-ROC: 0.8408 vs 0.8071 for EPHAD
- F1: 0.5953 vs 0.5290 for DIF
- Wilcoxon tests: significant against 11 of the 15 baselines.
Ablation (AUC-ROC): full 0.8408; without TTCL 0.7827; without the adaptation term 0.6590; without the contrastive term 0.6434; without the aux task 0.6800. Taking out either guard leaves the model worse than not adapting at all, which the authors read as "unguarded adaptation is harmful".
Other findings: pseudo-label accuracy goes up and down over rounds instead of falling steadily. A co-teaching variant did best with a 40% forget rate. Sensitivity to k and to the loss weights is mostly flat.
corpus.limitations:
Stated: there is no limitations section. The only future work named is "more reliable pseudo-label refinement and dynamic risk estimation".
Our own reading:
- The adaptation is transductive and batch over the whole test set, not online or streaming.
- The shift is synthetic (K-Means splits), not temporal drift.
- It claims to need no contamination prior, yet the final labelling needs alpha.
- The GMM threshold and the stopping rule are underspecified.
- The negated loss on pseudo-anomalies is unbounded.
- There is no adversary: no crafted anomalies and no varied contamination rate.
- No security or IoT data, no resource-constrained hardware, no runtime cost reported.
- The model can drift without limit, since nothing anchors it to the source model.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low overlap. It shares the problem framing, not the mechanisms.
What overlaps: the core tension is the same as ours, adapting to a shifted normal without absorbing anomalies, and so is the main tool, updating only on samples judged confidently normal. That is essentially our naive self-labelling baseline, made stronger with a GMM threshold and a kNN normal pool. Their ablation finding (unguarded TTA is worse than no TTA) matches our "naive gets poisoned" result in a non-adversarial setting.
What it does NOT do:
- No TOA-like direction budgeting. It never splits an update into a component toward a known attack direction and an orthogonal component, has no rationed budget, and gives no minimum-time-to-compromise bound.
- No core/outer-ring robust updating. It selects by score threshold, not by a dense core, and it does not check centre moves against the outer ring or gate spread growth on outer-ring density.
- No freeze-type attack. Adversaries, poisoning and deliberately stalling adaptation never come up. Its only "stop" is running out of selectable samples, and it never considers that an attacker could exploit stopping or over-cautious selection.
- No streaming, no IoT or intrusion data, no on-device angle, no adaptive attacker.
Verdict: this paper does not take away any of our novelty claims. It is a useful 2026 citation showing the ML community sees contamination during TTA as a problem, but only for non-adversarial, offline settings. That supports our gap statement: no existing work handles adversarial, streaming, on-device test-time adaptation.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Related-work positioning: cite RTTAD, plus the TTAD (Cohen et al., Information Sciences 2023) and EPHAD (Patra and Taieb, NeurIPS 2025) baselines it cites, and Kim, Park and Choo, "When model meets new normals" (AAAI 2024), as the non-adversarial test-time-adaptation and contamination line. Our addition is a deliberate attacker, streaming updates, an MCU budget, and the freeze attack. These three citations come from RTTAD's reference list. I did not check them independently.
2. A stronger self-labelling baseline: fit a 2-component GMM on normalised scores to pick confident-normal and confident-anomalous samples, instead of a fixed threshold. Running our boiling-frog and freeze attacks against an "RTTAD-style selective TTA" baseline would partly close open problem (4), that the freeze attack has only been shown against our own baselines. The freeze attack could also target their stopping rule ("adapt until no sufficient samples remain"): an attacker who inflates scores could stop selection on purpose.
3. A kNN normal-memory pool: a small ring buffer of recent accepted embeddings, used as k = 3 anchors for a consistency check. This is cheap enough for ESP32 and fits alongside our core/outer-ring test.
4. Negative feedback from confident anomalies (push away, not just ignore). If we use it, it must be bounded or clipped, which their method lacks. A bounded version could be a small extra contribution.
5. Evaluation tools: their K-Means normality-shift protocol, and measuring the shift with Jeffreys divergence or OTDD, could give a controlled "drift magnitude" axis for open problem (1), attack hidden inside strong drift. We can also report Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across devices or seeds as they do.
6. Ablation style: their "guard removed is worse than no adaptation" table is a good template for showing that each part of TOA and the signature-free method is needed.

corpus.title: Empirical Analysis of Evasion and Poisoning Against Malware Data Drift Detection
corpus.authors: Mingyue Yang, David Lie, Nicolas Papernot (University of Toronto / Vector Institute, according to the HTML full text; the abs page does not list affiliations)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, cs.CR, 2026 (v1 4 Aug 2026, v2 6 Aug, v3 12 Aug 2026). I found no venue or acceptance note on the abs page or in the paper. Treat it as non-peer-reviewed.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03642 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03642v3; PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.03642)
corpus.problem: Malware classifiers lose accuracy under concept drift, so ML drift detectors (CADE, Transcend/Transcendent) flag the most-drifted samples for an analyst to label, and those samples are then used to retrain. Prior work attacks classifiers, not drift detectors or the classifier-plus-detector pipeline. The paper asks how evasion and clean-label poisoning behave when the attacker has to fool both at once: malware must be classified benign AND stay outside the top-k most-drifted list that the analyst reviews.
corpus.method:
This is an attack-only empirical study. No defense is proposed.
- Victim: an MLP classifier (100-100) paired with either CADE or Transcendent.
  - CADE uses a contrastive autoencoder (CAE). Its score is distance to class centroids in the embedding, normalised by the median training distance: |d - d_med| / (b*d_med).
  - Transcendent uses conformal p-values (credibility, confidence) from distance to an SVM hyperplane, built on either the CAE embedding or the MLP's last hidden layer.
  - CAE sizes tested: 512-384-256-128 and 512-128-32-8.
- Analyst: labels only the top-k drifted samples (k=500, sometimes 200). Labels are always correct (manual triage). There is no self-labelling.
- Attacker: gray-box. Has 10% of the training data, trains surrogate models (MLP with cross-entropy toward benign, or CAE with MSE toward the benign centroid), and transfers attacks to the victim.
  - Optimises one universal additive perturbation with RAdam. Features can only increase, are clipped to [0,1], and have a magnitude limit.
- Evasion: add the perturbation to malware at test time.
- Poisoning: a clean-label backdoor. The same perturbation is used as a trigger on benignware. The most-drifted poisoned samples are inserted in a single retraining round, and models are retrained from scratch on the initial balanced set plus the inserted samples.
- Metric: overall ASR, the fraction of malware that is classified benign AND falls outside the top-k. Results are averaged over 30 runs.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Data:
- AndroZoo (Android): binary features, 16,978 total, reduced to the 200 or 1000 most significant by RFE with logistic regression. Train 2019-01 to 2019-12; future set 2020-02.
- BODMAS (Windows PE): numeric features, 2,381 total, of which 17 are modifiable. Train 2007-01 to 2019-09; future set 2019-11.
- No IoT, network intrusion or anomaly-detection datasets. No Drebin, APIGraph or EMBER.
- Poison counts: BODMAS 100/200(250)/500/1000; AndroZoo 500/1000/2000/4000.
- Perturbation limits: BODMAS 0.25/0.5/0.75/1; AndroZoo 50/100 (200 features) and 200/500 (1000 features).

Hardware, runtime and code release: none reported, and I found no code link. No embedded or on-device component.
corpus.results:
- Classifier-only evasion (Table 2): ASR against the MLP rises from about 78% to 100% (BODMAS) and from about 72% to 99% (AndroZoo) as the perturbation limit grows. Examples: BODMAS limit 0.5, MLP 97.6%; AndroZoo limit 200, MLP 98.3%.
- Classifier-only backdoor poisoning (Tables 3-4): near 100% ASR on MLP victims in most settings, e.g. BODMAS with 1000 inserted gives 100%, 100% and 91.3% across the three architectures.
- Main finding (from figures only; no overall-ASR numbers are tabled): CAE-based drift detectors behave counter-intuitively.
  - Against CADE, overall evasion ASR can FALL as the perturbation grows. Large feature values look like unseen patterns and push samples away from the benign centroid, so they get flagged.
  - Against CADE and Transcendent+CAE, poisoning ASR can FALL as more poison is inserted (Tables 5-6). The authors' explanation: the reconstruction term crowds the space near the benign centroid, which pushes triggered samples outward.
  - Transcendent+MLP is much easier to attack and less sensitive to the choice of surrogate, because it relies on decision-boundary distance.
- Conclusion: the surrogate and its loss have to match the detector's embedding geometry.
corpus.limitations:
The paper has no limitations, threats-to-validity or future-work section. Limitations I inferred from the text:
- It is one retraining round with retraining from scratch, not online or continual learning, even though the introduction motivates continuous training.
- It assumes every inserted sample is poison and that no further data balancing is done (the authors' own simplifications).
- Analyst labels are perfect, so there is no self-labelling or pseudo-labelling path.
- The main focus is a universal perturbation; the authors say per-sample and future-set-perturbation results are similar but leave them out.
- There are no headline numbers for overall ASR against the detectors, only plots.
- No defense, no compute cost, no code, and malware domain only.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
LOW. Bluntly:
- TOA-like direction budgeting: NO. There is no constraint on how far or in which direction an update may move.
- Core/outer-ring robust updating: NO. There is no trimmed or robust update rule at all; the victim retrains from scratch.
- A freeze-type attack: NO. The attacker's goal is the opposite: keep malware UNflagged. The paper never studies inducing false drift alarms, stopping retraining, or exploiting a defense that halts learning.
- Boiling-frog (gradual multi-round) poisoning: NO. The poisoning is a single insertion round.
- Self-labelling: NO. Labels come from a perfect human analyst; ours are self-labelled by the detector.
- Domain: none of IoT, network IDS, unsupervised one-class detection, drift-aware online updating, or on-device constraints.

Where it does touch us:
1. It is the first work (as it claims) to attack the drift-detection component rather than the classifier. That makes it related work for our claim that the adaptation and drift mechanism is itself an attack surface.
2. It uses centroid-distance drift scores normalised by median training distance (CADE), close to our centre-plus-spread detector.
3. Its finding that crowding near the benign centroid pushes poison outward is a geometric observation adjacent to our dense-core vs outer-ring reasoning, though they draw no defense from it.

It does not pre-empt any of our contributions.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Related-work positioning: cite it as the most recent (Aug 2026) example showing that drift detectors change attack dynamics. Then state the gap it leaves: one-shot clean-label insertion with perfect labels, no multi-round boiling-frog attack on a self-labelling online detector, no freeze attack, no defense, nothing on IoT or devices.
2. A joint success metric: require the attack to beat BOTH the classifier and the drift flag (their overall ASR). We could define a joint metric too, e.g. compromise = poisoned AND not tripping drift or suspicion alarms, which would make our adaptive-attacker results stricter.
3. A gray-box surrogate threat model (10% of data, surrogate trained to transfer). We could add a transfer-attack setting where the adaptive poisoner only has a surrogate of our centroid/PCA detector, instead of white-box knowledge.
4. Realistic feature constraints for the attacker (features only increase, clipped, magnitude limits). The network analogue: the poisoner can add packets or traffic but cannot remove legitimate traffic. This makes the poison model more credible.
5. Their geometric insight, that more poison can push itself outward because the core is crowded, motivates explicitly testing whether our outer-ring evidence test can be gamed by an attacker who crowds the core. This connects to our open problem of attacks hidden in genuine drift.
6. A reproducibility bar: 30 averaged runs over a sweep of poison budgets and perturbation sizes. Reviewers will expect similar sweeps of attacker share and drift rate from us.

Checked the arXiv abs page (metadata, abstract, versions v1-v3) and read the full HTML of v3 (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03642v3) in two passes: one for a section-by-section summary, one for exact poison counts, perturbation limits, table values, normalisation, venue, code and hardware. The affiliations (Toronto/Vector) come from the HTML extraction and are not on the abs page.

corpus.title: Adaptive Intrusion Detection System using Transformer-Based Neural Networks and Continual Learning Approach with Adversarial Investigation
corpus.authors: Azizi Ariffin, Afif Haris, Faiz Zaki, Hazim Hanif, Nor Badrul Anuar (corresponding, badrul@um.edu.my). Affiliations: Universiti Malaya (Centre of Research for Cyber Security and Network, CSNET; Faculty of Computer Science and IT; Dept. of Software Engineering), Universiti Teknologi MARA (Shah Alam), and the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (Network Security Research Dept.). The paper does not say which author belongs to which affiliation.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04602 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2608.04602v1; code: https://github.com/um-csnet/ReplayIDS, MIT licence)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, cs.CR, v1 submitted 5 Aug 2026 (only version). The arXiv page lists no venue or comments field. The repo has a folder named results/eaai-reported/, which suggests a submission to Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier). That is my inference and is not confirmed. Treat it as a non-peer-reviewed 2026 preprint.
corpus.problem: A network IDS trained on a fixed snapshot gets worse after deployment as traffic and threats shift. Fine-tuning on new attacks causes catastrophic forgetting, and retraining on the full history is too costly. The authors name two gaps: (1) continual-learning IDS benchmarks show benign traffic only in the first experience, which overstates robustness; (2) the replay buffer that the best continual-learning methods depend on has never been studied as an attack surface.
corpus.method:
A supervised, labelled, multi-class continual-learning IDS:
- Model: a tabular transformer. Categorical features get 32-dimensional embeddings and are joined with layer-normalised numeric features, then pass through 6 transformer blocks with 10 heads. An MLP head with GELU outputs a softmax over the classes seen so far.
- Head expansion: output units are added when new classes appear; existing weights are copied over unchanged.
- Experience replay: class-balanced reservoir sampling with a per-class budget b of 1%, 5% or 10% of each class's flows. The buffer is rebuilt after each experience and always keeps benign ("benign anchoring"). Each experience trains on current data plus the buffer with cross-entropy (AdamW, lr 5e-4, batch 256, early stopping).
- New evaluation scenario, CII (class-instance incremental): benign appears in every one of 4 experiences, alongside that experience's new attacks: E0 GoldenEye; E1 Hulk and Slowhttptest; E2 slowloris and FTP-Patator; E3 Heartbleed and SSH-Patator.
- Adversarial investigation: two attacks on the replay buffer only.
  - Label flipping: every stored exemplar gets a random wrong label.
  - Backdoor: a fixed perturbation of inter-arrival-time (IAT) features, with poisoned exemplars labelled benign. The authors say it could be done on live traffic by pacing packets.
  - The attacker has write access to the exemplar store or its labelling pipeline, but no access to gradients or parameters.
- No defense is proposed or evaluated.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Data: CICIDS2017 only, 1,138,612 flows in 8 classes after preprocessing, split 60/20/20. About 77% is benign, and Heartbleed has only 11 flows. A separate cross-architecture benchmark (MLP, SGM-CNN, FT-Transformer) is reported as trend-comparable only. Hardware: one NVIDIA RTX A5000 (24 GB). No IoT data, no edge or microcontroller deployment, and no figures for training time, memory, parameter count or latency. "Campus edge" appears only once, as motivation.
corpus.results:
CI, final experience: experience replay (ER) with a 10% budget reaches 0.9994 accuracy and 0.9953 macro-F1, against a joint oracle at 0.9997 / 0.9979. Naive fine-tuning gets 0.0052, EWC 0.0324, LwF 0.0699, iCaRL (2,000 exemplars) 0.8770 accuracy / 0.5448 macro-F1. ER with a 1% budget gets 0.9949 / 0.9352.

CII, checkpoint mean: ER-Balanced 10% gets 0.9989 / 0.9962. Naive gets 0.87 / 0.63 and iCaRL 0.95 / 0.83. CII, final experience: naive 0.77 / 0.35, ER 0.9989 / 0.9960. With ER-10%, forgetting is about 0.0003 (accuracy).

Label flipping at 1–10%: accuracy collapses to about 0.005 and macro-F1 to about 0.21.

Backdoor at 1/5/10%: overall accuracy stays high (0.9992 / 0.9982 / 0.9776) while attack success rate is about 95–100%. Three ASR cells exceed 100% (150%, 220%, 199%). The authors blame their estimator (subtracting a baseline, small injections, test sets reused across experiences), which weakens the ASR numbers.

Headline claim: buffer integrity is a strict operational requirement. Caveat: all numbers came through a summarising fetch tool and should be checked against the PDF tables before we quote them.
corpus.limitations:
What the authors state:
- Only one 2017-era benchmark, with possible labelling errors.
- The transformer's contribution is not separated from a well-tuned MLP.
- Only 4 experiences.
- Attacks are tested only in CI, not CII.
- No adaptive triggers that survive standardisation.
- No defenses evaluated.
- Clean labels assumed at training time.
- The ASR estimator is invalid in some cells.

Their future work: UNSW-NB15, CSE-CIC-IDS2018 and AnoShift; 10+ experiences with importance-weighted eviction; an architecture ablation; adaptive attacks under CII; defenses (buffer auditing, a timing-trigger detector, label revalidation); semi-supervised learning with about 20% of the stream labelled.

Our additional observations:
- The threat model is very strong and unrealistic: direct write access to the buffer, with 100% of stored exemplars poisoned. That is not an attacker who controls only a share of traffic.
- It is fully supervised, so label flipping does not apply to an unsupervised self-labelling detector.
- Drift is only motivation. It is never modelled or measured, and the experiences are new attack classes, not drifting benign traffic.
- The backdoor trigger values are not given, and there is an unresolved clean-label vs relabelled-to-benign inconsistency.
- No compute or cost reporting.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low. Blunt answers:
- TOA-like direction budgeting: NO. Updates are plain cross-entropy steps on current data plus buffer, with no limit on direction or magnitude.
- Core/outer-ring robust updating: NO. No trimmed, robust, quarantining or density-based update rule of any kind. Defenses are only recommended in prose (buffer integrity protection, anomaly auditing, periodic revalidation).
- Freeze-type attack: NO. No defense in the paper stops learning, so no one could exploit it. The closest point is a one-line remark in Sec. 7 that an attacker could craft flows that evict useful exemplars from the reservoir. False alarms or denial of service caused by a defense are never analysed.
- Other gaps relative to our work:
  - Supervised multi-class transformer, not an unsupervised online centroid detector.
  - CICIDS2017, not Kitsune/N-BaIoT IoT traffic.
  - GPU, not ESP32.
  - Not boiling-frog: it is a one-shot, total buffer compromise. ANTIDOTE, Kloft and Laskov, Kitsune and N-BaIoT are never cited.
  - No attacker-share analysis and no provable time-to-compromise.
  - No drift modelling.
- Real overlap is limited to the framing: (1) the memory or self-update path of an adaptive IDS is an attack surface; (2) benign traffic must be present in every update, which the CII scenario mirrors and our continual self-learning setting already assumes.
- It does not anticipate any of our methods or our freeze finding. If anything, it strengthens our novelty: an Aug 2026 paper explicitly lists poisoning defenses for continual IDS as open future work.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Metrics: report forgetting and intransigence (the Chaudhry-style metrics they use) alongside detection and false alarms.
   - The freeze attack is in effect an attack that forces intransigence: the model can no longer adapt, so honest drift turns into false alarms.
   - Boiling-frog poisoning is induced forgetting of the attack region.
   - Putting both on these axes lets reviewers from continual learning see TOA's trade-off directly (bounded forgetting, near-zero intransigence).
2. Their CII argument (benign only in the first experience overstates robustness) supports our setting, where benign traffic arrives every cycle. Cite it to justify our evaluation protocol.
3. Adaptive-attacker idea: a timing-only (IAT) poison or trigger made by pacing packets, leaving volume and flags unchanged. Kitsune features include jitter/IAT statistics, so we can test a poisoner that pushes only timing dimensions. That is a hard case for the signature-free outer-ring check and for TOA when the signature has no strong timing component.
4. Eviction attack (their Sec. 7 remark): an attacker floods traffic to push useful normal samples out of memory. This is related to our core-hiding adaptive attacker and to the freeze attack, and it is worth an experiment or a paragraph positioning it.
5. Positioning: cite them as recent (2026) evidence that continual IDS work assumes clean memory and evaluates no defenses. Our contribution is the defense plus the attack that breaks naive defenses.
6. Reproducibility template: their repo (uv lockfile, experiment manifests, pytest/ruff, a reported-results folder) is a good model for our artifact.
7. Metric hygiene: their ASR estimator gives values above 100%. Define time-to-compromise and false-alarm rate on held-out, non-reused windows, so we avoid the same reviewer criticism.
8. Related-work leads from their bibliography. Titles were cut off in the HTML, so look them up before citing:
   - Umer, Dawson and Polikar 2020, on targeted forgetting and false memory in continual learners via backdoors.
   - Guo et al. 2024, on backdoors that persist across continual-learning tasks.
   - Guo et al. 2025, on IAT trigger construction.
   - Amalapuram et al. 2024 (SPIDER), on buffer auditing.
   - Apruzzese et al. 2021, on poisoning and evasion of deep NIDS.

corpus.title: The Boiling Frog Threshold: Criticality and Blindness in World Model-Based Anomaly Detection Under Gradual Drift
corpus.authors: Zhe Hong, the only author (National University of Singapore, per the HTML full text; no email shown).
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint, 2026. v1 was submitted 9 Mar 2026 (arXiv:2603.08455, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2603.08455), filed under cs.AI with cs.LG. The comments field says 10 pages, 5 figures. No venue or journal reference is listed, so it is not peer-reviewed as far as I can verify. SOTAVerified lists it as not yet independently reproduced.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08455 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2603.08455v1)
corpus.problem: An RL agent can monitor itself using its own world model's prediction error (PE). The question is at what rate gradual corruption of the agent's observations becomes detectable, and what sets that boundary. The motivation is that real sensor degradation (fogging, calibration drift) is gradual, not abrupt. The paper extends Domberg and Schildbach (2025), which used world-model detection for abrupt changes; I did not verify that reference myself. Adversaries get only one passing remark: perturbations may accumulate incrementally, and zero-cumulative-drift perturbations could evade PE monitors.
corpus.method:
Agents are PPO (Stable-Baselines3) trained for 1e6 steps on four MuJoCo-v5 tasks. The world model is a 3-layer MLP forward model f(s_t, a_t) -> s_{t+1}, trained by MSE on policy transitions, with hidden sizes 128, 512 (default) and 1024. PE is e_t = ||f(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}||^2.

Drift is synthetic, additive and axis-aligned, applied to velocity dimensions: s~_t = s_t + g(eps, t - t0)*d, with d a unit vector. The linear form is g = eps*t; the sinusoidal form is g = eps*sin(2*pi*0.01*t), which is zero-mean. Episodes run 1000 steps and drift starts at step 300. There are 16 intensities from 1e-4 to 0.5.

Three detectors are tested, all against a FIXED pre-drift baseline:
(a) Doubt Index: an EMA of PE, z-scored against the baseline, firing after W consecutive steps above z. Sweeps cover z in 2 to 4 and W in {1, 3, 5, 10, 20}. The EMA constant and exact formulas are not given.
(b) Variance detector: 50-step windowed PE variance, firing when it exceeds k baseline SDs for 5 windows, k in {2, 3, 5}.
(c) Percentile detector: PE above the 95th or 99th baseline percentile within a 5-step window, with no smoothing.
CUSUM is mentioned as a comparison.

The threshold eps* is the midpoint of a sigmoid fitted to detection probability vs. eps, with Wilson 95% CIs. A power law, log eps* = a + alpha*log z + beta*log W, is fitted per environment.

Nothing in the paper updates online. I found no self-labeling, no model retraining during deployment, and no adaptive baseline.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
The data is simulation only: four MuJoCo-v5 locomotion environments, HalfCheetah (obs 17), Hopper (11), Walker2d (17) and Ant (105). There is no real-world data, no network or IoT traffic, and no vision. Each condition uses 10 seeds x 8 episodes = 80 episodes.
- Experiment A (full DI ablation): 576 conditions, about 46,080 episodes.
- Experiment B: sinusoidal drift.
- Experiment B1: percentile-detector control.
- Experiment C: capacity ablation.
No hardware, GPU/CPU or runtime is reported. No code is released ("code will be made available upon publication"); supplementary JSON files are mentioned without a URL.
corpus.results:
1. Threshold: every configuration shows a sharp sigmoid detection threshold, from about 0% to 100% detection. Its position moves with detector settings; within the Doubt Index it spans about 10x, roughly 0.0003 to 0.004 in HalfCheetah. Table 1 ranges for eps* are HalfCheetah 0.0003-0.004, Hopper 0.007-0.012, Walker2d 0.0003-0.003 and Ant 0.0001-0.001.
2. Sinusoidal blindness: all detectors give near-zero detection even at eps = 0.5. In HalfCheetah at eps = 0.01, linear drift raises PE power 201.6x over baseline; sinusoidal drift gives 0.8x. The paper attributes this to the world model, not the detector.
3. Power law per environment:

| Environment | R^2 | alpha (z) | beta (W) |
|---|---|---|---|
| HalfCheetah | 0.97 | 0.43 | 0.23 |
| Hopper | 0.95 | 0.44 | 0.45 |
| Ant | 0.89 | 1.35 | 0.46 |
| Walker2d | 0.78 | 0.61 | 1.00 |

   A single global fit across environments reaches only R^2 = 0.45, which the paper attributes to environment dynamics (dPE/d eps). Baseline MSE does not predict the rank order of eps*: Hopper has the lowest MSE but the highest eps*.
4. Collapse Before Awareness (CBA): in Hopper at eps = 0.05, the agent collapses in about 25 steps, while detectors need about 50 post-drift steps, so no detector fires. The paper names four regimes: sub-threshold, detectable, CBA and overwhelming. CBA is strong in Hopper, weaker in Walker2d, and absent in HalfCheetah and Ant.
5. Model capacity: larger models lower the MSE (HalfCheetah 0.254 -> 0.145) but leave eps* essentially unchanged, which the paper credits to z-score normalisation.
6. Walker2d has a baseline false-positive rate of 12-44%. After correcting for it, eps* converges to about 0.002.
7. CUSUM produces more than 95% false positives even with no drift.
These numbers come from a summarising read of the HTML text and match its tables as reported; I did not check every figure.
corpus.limitations:
Limitations the paper states:
- Only proprioceptive locomotion with MLP world models; no vision, RSSM or transformer models, and no non-locomotion tasks.
- Drift is synthetic, additive and axis-aligned.
- It detects that something changed, not what changed; causal attribution is not studied.
- Future work: multi-agent settings where corrupted perception spreads, and vision world models.

Further limitations I noticed:
- It is a single-author preprint with no peer review and no code.
- The detector baseline and world model are frozen, so the paper does not cover the self-updating case at all.
- There is no adversary model and no attack is implemented.
- The only mitigation offered is external monitoring.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Overlap is low; this paper does not take away our novelty. It shares the "boiling frog" metaphor and the gradual-drift-vs-detector framing, and that is about all.

Point by point:
(1) TOA-like direction budgeting: no. Nothing is updated online, so there is no update to split or ration and no minimum-time-to-compromise bound.
(2) Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. There is no robust update rule of any kind.
(3) Freeze attack: no. Freezing and pausing adaptation are never discussed. In fact its detectors are permanently frozen against a pre-drift baseline. That is the opposite of our setting: honest drift there would produce false alarms (compare its Walker2d false-positive rate of 12-44%), but the paper never studies drift being absorbed into the model.
(4) Poisoning or self-labeling: absent. The paper never mentions ANTIDOTE, Kloft and Laskov, intrusion detection, IoT or data poisoning.
(5) Domain: RL robotics in MuJoCo, not network IDS, and no embedded hardware.

What the "absorbed" sub-threshold drift means here is passive: the drift stays under the noise floor. It is not the active poisoning of a learner, which is our threat. The one conceptual point that touches our open problem (1), an attack hidden inside strong genuine drift, is its sinusoidal or zero-cumulative drift result. Oscillating perturbations stay invisible to prediction-error monitors, and the paper itself suggests adversaries could exploit that.

Heads-up from the search: a citing paper is much closer to us than this one. It is "The Price of Self-Calibration: Exact Evidence Budgets and Manufactured Blind Sets in Adaptive Monitoring" (Abdou-Raouf Atarmla, arXiv:2609.23254, submitted 19 Sep 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23254). It analyses self-calibrating threshold trackers under drift. Its claims include that the tracker's gain sets which drift-speed class it absorbs, and that declaring absorbed drift normal "manufactures" a blind set. Per its abstract it has no explicit adversary and no IDS or IoT setting, but it sits right next to our budget, rate-limit and minimum-time-to-compromise arguments. It should be read in full and cited.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Evaluation protocol: sweep poison or drift rate eps on a log grid and plot P(detection) against eps with Wilson 95% CIs over many seeds. Report the sigmoid midpoint eps* for each defense: naive, freezing baselines, TOA, signature-free. This gives a clean "boiling frog threshold" figure, and a defense can show it raises eps* or removes the sub-threshold regime.
2. Power-law fits of eps* against detector hyperparameters, e.g. our budget rate or ring quantile, in the form log eps* = a + alpha*log(param). This turns tuning knobs into a predictive law, which reviewers like.
3. Sinusoidal or zero-mean poisoning as a new adaptive attacker: an oscillating poison whose net displacement sums to near zero but which ratchets the spread upward. Test whether TOA's direction budget and the signature-free outer-ring spread check catch it. This connects directly to our open problem (1).
4. A Collapse Before Awareness analogue: compare time-to-compromise with time-to-detection, and name regimes (sub-threshold, detectable, compromised-before-detection, overwhelming). This frames our provable minimum time to compromise as a guarantee that the compromise-before-detection regime is empty.
5. Report false-positive-corrected thresholds, as the paper does for Walker2d. Also note that baseline reconstruction error does not predict detectability, so we should measure dScore/d eps per device or dataset rather than rely on fit quality.
6. Related-work positioning: cite it as gradual-drift detectability for frozen detectors, then contrast with our self-updating detector under adversarial drift. Also cite and contrast arXiv:2609.23254 on self-calibration blind sets.
corpus.fetch_status:
I read the full paper. That covers the arXiv abstract page and the complete HTML v1 (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.08455v1), through two targeted fetches. All content passed through the fetch tool's summariser, so numbers and quotes were not compared line by line against the PDF.

Not stated in the paper, so not verified:
- the exact Doubt Index and EMA formulas and the smoothing constant
- hardware and runtime
- a code link (none exists)
- any venue acceptance (none found)

The citing paper arXiv:2609.23254 was checked at the abstract and metadata level only.

corpus.title: Mean-Shift PCA by Knockoff Mean
corpus.authors: Mengda Li (School of Data Science, CUHK-Shenzhen), Zeng Li (Dept. of Statistics and Data Science, SUSTech), Jianfeng Yao (School of Data Science, CUHK-Shenzhen)
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25460 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25460)
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint (stat.ML, cross-listed cs.LG), v1 submitted 25 May 2026. The arXiv comment field says "ICML 2026". I did not check this against the ICML 2026 proceedings, so treat it as the authors' own claim.
corpus.problem: Standard PCA is sensitive to shifts in the sample mean. If a fraction of samples comes from a sub-population whose mean is shifted, the leading principal components get distorted. The data model is X~ = X + A, where A = sum_i m_i * gamma_i^T: k outlier sub-populations, each with a mean shift m_i and a mixture weight pi_i. The authors argue that classical Robust PCA (sparse outliers, e.g. principal component pursuit or alternating projections) handles this kind of contamination poorly in high dimensions, because it is dense and low-rank rather than sparse. The goal is to recover the clean covariance eigenspace from the contaminated data. It is a batch, offline statistics problem. Nothing in it is about security, streaming, IoT or anomaly detection.
corpus.method:
The theory uses random matrix theory with d/n -> c in (0, inf), i.i.d. entries with a finite 4th moment, and a spiked covariance Sigma = I + P with finite rank (generalised to any compactly supported spectral limit). The shift directions are assumed uniform on the sphere, or i.i.d. with a log-Sobolev property, and independent of the clean data and of the memberships.
- Theorem 3.5: the top eigenvalues of the contaminated covariance split into two separable sets, one from covariance spikes (l_i) and one from mean-shift spikes (theta_j^2). A spike only appears above a BBP-type threshold sqrt(c). Everything else sticks to the Marchenko-Pastur edge.
- Theorem 3.11: clean eigenvectors stay approximate eigenvectors of the contaminated matrix, with residual O_p(n^-1/2), whatever the mixture weight.
- Corollary 3.7: adding a deliberately injected, strong enough "knockoff" mean shift leaves the covariance spikes in place and moves the mean-shift spikes.
Algorithm (MS-PCA, two stages):
1. Run PCA on the contaminated data.
2. Inject a random knockoff mean m' (uniform on the sphere) with membership weight pi' (e.g. 0.5 or 1).
3. Run PCA again.
4. Keep an eigenpair only if its eigenvalue stays within eps = C*n^-1/2. Eigenvalues that move are treated as contamination and dropped.
Parameters (Algorithm 2): theta'^2 = 2*g^-1(lambda_1), ||m'||^2 = theta'^2/pi', and C = 1 for large d or 1/c for small aspect ratio. The cost is two truncated PCAs, O(K*n*d).
corpus.data_and_hardware: Synthetic data only: two-component Gaussian mixtures with one population spike at l1 = 2*sqrt(c) and a mean-shift vector in a random direction, plus a variant that adds a covariance shift. Dimensions were d = 900/1000 up to 10000 and 50000, mostly with n = d or c = 0.1. There are no real datasets. Runs were on CPU only, on an AMD EPYC 9755 server (256 cores, dual socket, no GPU). One read of the page said code is released on GitHub, but a second targeted read found no repository URL in the HTML, so code availability is unconfirmed.
corpus.results:
- Eigenvector residuals: at d = 1000, 10000 and 50000 (c = 1), they shrink roughly as n^-1/2 for every outlier proportion pi1 from 0.1% to 100% (Table 1).
- Against RPCA via accelerated alternating projections (Cai et al. 2019), the main comparison: MS-PCA reaches perfect top-PC alignment at c = 0.1 when pi1 >= 25%, while RPCA's alignment collapses towards zero in high dimensions.
- Against the other robust estimators (Tyler M, Huber M, l1-PCA, winsorized PCA, centred PCA): at d = 900, n = 1000 over 200 trials, MS-PCA stays above 95% alignment and the others stay near random.
- With mean shift plus covariance shift (mixture weights 5-20%, covariance spikes 2-16): MS-PCA stays above 95%, the others below 17%.
- Runtime at d = 900, n = 1000: about 14 ms for one PC and 19 ms for nine, versus about 79 ms for RPCA-AAP. The speedup grows from about 5.4x to 12.6x as d goes from 1000 to 10000.
- Two baselines (median-of-means PCA and robust sub-Gaussian PCA) were left out because no public Python code exists.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors:
- The theory only covers homoscedastic mixtures. The general case where sub-populations differ in mean, covariance and higher moments is left open.
- The results are asymptotic. The threshold constant C needs tuning when the aspect ratio is small.
- The method needs the mixture weight (shift strength) to be large enough to create a detectable spike. Shifts below the BBP threshold leave no spike.
Not stated, but important for us:
- No real data, no streaming or online version, no drift, and no adversary. The contamination is random, and the theory assumes the shift direction is random and independent of the data. A poisoner chooses the direction, so the guarantees do not cover us.
- It needs two eigendecompositions per fit, and it was tested on a 256-core server. I found no edge or embedded evaluation.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Very low. It is not a competitor and does not anticipate any of our contributions.
- It has no direction budgeting like TOA: nothing splits updates into an attack-aligned part and the rest, there is no rationed budget, and there is no minimum time to compromise.
- It has no core/outer-ring robust updating. It works on a whole batch at once and has no notion of accepting a centre shift only when the outer ring confirms it.
- It describes no freeze-type attack, nor any attacker at all. There is no online self-labelling, no detector, no false-alarm metric, and nothing on IoT, intrusion detection or N-BaIoT/Kitsune.
The only conceptual link is a general idea. Telling contamination apart by perturbing the data and checking which statistics stay stable is loosely similar to our signature-free rule of accepting only changes that the robust part of the cloud supports. It touches our pipeline in one place: the PCA compression step. A poison cluster, or a newly joined device, is exactly a "mean-shift sub-population" that could tilt our PCA axes if we refit them online.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. A guard on the PCA step. If our PCA basis is ever refit online, a poison cluster could rotate it, so each refit could run the knockoff test: inject a random mean shift, recompute the top eigenvalues, and drop any axis whose eigenvalue moves. That gives a cheap, signature-free way to stop a contaminating sub-population from taking over the compressed space. If the basis is frozen after a clean warm-up, we should say so, and cite this paper for why refitting would be risky.
2. Theory for the boiling-frog argument. The BBP threshold says a shift with pi*||m||^2 below roughly sqrt(c) leaves no spectral trace. We can cite this to formalise why slow, low-share poisoning is invisible to spectrum-based checks. It also helps explain open problem (1), poison hidden inside genuine drift. One caveat: our d (about 115 Kitsune/N-BaIoT features) and window sizes put us far from the asymptotic regime.
3. The new-device problem (open problem 2). A device that joins shows up as a new mean-shift spike. The test that separates "moved" from "stable" spikes could flag "new sub-population appeared" and trigger a per-device detector, instead of letting one shared detector absorb it.
4. Evaluation idea. Their contamination sweep (pi from 0.1% to 100%, with subspace alignment as the metric) is a clean template for a robustness curve of our PCA stage against attacker share.
Caveats before using any of this: the guarantees assume random, independent shift directions (an adaptive poisoner breaks this), the theory is high-dimensional and asymptotic, C needs tuning at small aspect ratio, and two eigendecompositions per cycle on an ESP32 still needs to be costed. Cite it as a related robust-statistics tool, not as prior work on our threat model.
corpus.fetch_status: I read the full text. I checked the arXiv abstract page (title, authors, date, categories, "ICML 2026" comment) and read the whole arXiv HTML v1 (about 120k characters) in two passes, plus a third targeted pass for affiliations, contributions, related work and keywords. corpus.title: Data Poisoning Attack against Neural Network-Based On-Device Learning Anomaly Detector by Physical Attacks on Sensors
corpus.authors: Takahito Ino, Kota Yoshida, Hiroki Matsutani, Takeshi Fujino (Ritsumeikan University and Keio University, Japan). The corresponding author for data is K. Yoshida.
corpus.venue_year: MDPI Sensors, vol. 24, no. 19, article 6416, published 3 Oct 2024 (received 20 Aug 2024, accepted 1 Oct 2024). DOI 10.3390/s24196416. Open access. An earlier short version is Ino et al., "A Feasibility Study of Data Poisoning against On-device Learning Edge AI by Physical Attack against Sensors", Journal of Signal Processing 28(4):107-110, 2024, doi:10.2299/jsp.28.107 (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsp/28/4/28_107/_article). There is also an IPSJ 2024 conference version (https://ipsj.ixsq.nii.ac.jp/records/240912). This is a 2024 paper, so treat it as recent related work rather than core 2025/26 literature. I did not check the journal's quartile.
corpus.url: https://doi.org/10.3390/s24196416 (redirects to https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/19/6416, which returned HTTP 403 to me). Full text read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11479347/
corpus.problem: Edge AI devices that learn on-device sit in physically reachable places. That makes their training data a target, and most poisoning defenses assume cloud or batch training, which does not fit low-latency on-device learning. The authors do a risk assessment of an on-device-learning vibration anomaly detector for factory machines. The question is whether an attacker with only physical proximity can tamper with the sensor so that the detector learns a real fault state as "normal". The victim watches only the normal/abnormal output, never the raw sensor data or the training status. This extends their earlier single-model feasibility study to a more realistic detector that has concept drift detection and several model instances.
corpus.method:
Victim detector: ONLAD, an autoencoder built on an extreme learning machine and trained online with OS-ELM.
- Input weights are fixed. Only the output weights are updated, sequentially, without storing past data.
- Input is an 800-point FFT spectrum (800 input/output nodes, 10 hidden nodes, sigmoid).
- Anomaly score is reconstruction RMSE against a threshold theta_error, set manually (4.25e-10).
- Multi-instance: several small ELMs, each learning one normal pattern. The instance with the lowest error on an input makes the decision and gets the update.

Concept drift detector (Yamada and Matsutani, IPDPSW 2023):
- It keeps running centroids of training data and of test data.
- Drift rate = distance between the two centroids, normalised so that the distance from the training centroid to the last training sample is 1.0.
- When drift rate passes theta_drift (2.0 in the experiments), the system creates a new instance and trains it on the latest data.

Attack: acoustic injection into the MEMS accelerometer.
1. Characterise how the sensor responds to tones: an audible sweep of 2.7-3.2 kHz, an ultrasonic sweep of 25.3-25.8 kHz, and a 3 kHz tone at 2-10 V. The tone shows up as an extra spectral peak whose amplitude scales with voltage. The sensor responds more strongly in the audible range.
2. Tune a tone (2806.6 Hz at 9.91 V) so that the spectrum of the healthy machine looks like the faulty one (unbalanced fan blade).
3. Play the tone while the machine is healthy. Drift rate climbs past theta_drift and the detector spawns a "poison" instance trained on the fake fault spectrum.
4. Switch the speaker off. The real fault now matches the poison instance and is classified as normal.

The attack is a single abrupt one, with the speaker on at a fixed setting. It is not a gradual boiling-frog schedule.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Sensor:
- ADXL345 3-axis MEMS accelerometer, x-axis only, 100 Hz sampling, connected over I2C.
- Read by a Raspberry Pi Pico (characterisation experiments) or a Raspberry Pi 4B (poisoning experiments).
- The paper says FFT and anomaly detection ran on a PC. Nothing in it shows training or inference on the microcontroller.

Attack equipment:
- P800K full-range speaker and CUSA-T601 ultrasonic transmitter.
- PMA-600NE amplifier, MFG-2260MRA and FG-281 signal generators, P4K-80L power supply.

Target machine:
- Two Ainex CFZ-120F cooling fans glued together. A weight on one blade of the top fan gives the "abnormal" state.

Data:
- Their own lab recordings: 1,000 samples for injection characterisation and 100 baseline samples with the fans stopped.
- Training and test sample counts for the poisoning run are not given.
- No public dataset and no code release. Derived data are available on request.
- No network or IDS data of any kind.
corpus.results:
The results are qualitative only, shown as spectra and time-series plots. There are no accuracy, precision, recall, false-alarm or time-to-compromise numbers.
- Baseline noise with the fans off stays below 0.015 amplitude outside DC.
- Audible injection gives a clear extra peak that tracks the tone frequency. Ultrasonic injection gives a weaker one. Peak amplitude grows with drive voltage while peak frequency barely moves.
- Without attack, normal-state error stays below theta_error and the fault is flagged correctly.
- With the attack, drift rate rises gradually after poisoning starts, crosses 2.0, and a poison instance is created. Afterwards both normal and fault inputs score below threshold and are both labelled normal, so the fault goes undetected.
- Not reported: how long the poisoning took, how many samples it used, and any attacker-share or budget analysis.
- One oddity, flagged by the extraction tool rather than by me after reading the figures: the paper does not seem to explain how a roughly 2.8 kHz tone appears as a low-frequency peak at 100 Hz sampling (presumably aliasing or resonance). I have not verified this.
corpus.limitations:
Limitations the authors state or that follow directly from the setup:
- Only one normal and one abnormal condition were tested. They claim the attack works with several normal states but did not test it.
- theta_error was set by hand. A real system would need it set automatically.
- One machine (fans), one fault type (mass imbalance), one accelerometer model.
- Only ELM autoencoders were tested. Other networks are suggested to be vulnerable but not tested.
- No countermeasure is proposed or evaluated. The authors say defenses for on-device learning are needed and leave this to future work.

Further gaps from my reading:
- Detection ran on a PC, not on-device.
- No quantitative metrics.
- No gradual or stealth-optimised attack, and no budget or attacker-share study.
- Concept drift is only something the attacker exploits. Honest drift is not modelled together with the attack.
- No adaptive defender.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low overlap, and none at all on our methods. Being blunt:
- **TOA-like direction budgeting:** No. There is no defense, no decomposition of updates and no rate limit.
- **Core/outer-ring robust updating:** No. Updates are plain OS-ELM plus running centroids, with no robust statistics or trimming.
- **Freeze-type attack:** No. Freezing or disabling learning is not discussed. Their attack is the opposite: a hijack that spawns a new model instance to absorb the fault.
- **Domain:** Different. They work on physical-sensor (vibration) anomaly detection, not network intrusion detection. No Kitsune or N-BaIoT, no Mirai.
- **Poisoning style:** Abrupt sensor spoofing, not boiling-frog poisoning of self-labelled traffic.

What it shares with us at the concept level:
- The target is an unsupervised, self-updating, on-device anomaly detector.
- The attack surface is the drift-adaptation mechanism itself. Their drift trigger is centroid-based (normalised distance between running centroids), which is close in spirit to our centre-plus-spread detector.
- It shows that adaptation built for honest drift can be turned against the detector. That supports our framing, but it is a different attack from ours.

Novelty risk to us: essentially none. It is a citable 2024 example that poisoning on-device learners in practice is a recognised threat with no defense. That strengthens our "nobody defends this" gap rather than closing it.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. **Motivation citation.** A peer-reviewed 2024 demonstration that a real on-device-learning anomaly detector with drift adaptation can be poisoned by an attacker who never touches the software, and that the authors explicitly call for on-device countermeasures. We can open the paper with it.
2. **Threat-model wording.** The victim sees only normal/abnormal outputs, not training status or raw data. That backs a stealth requirement: poisoning and freeze attacks must not raise visible alarms while they run.
3. **A warning for our open problem 2 (per-device or multi-instance detectors).** Their multi-instance design creates a new model whenever centroid drift passes a threshold, and that creation step is exactly what the attack hijacks. If we move to per-device detectors to handle a new device joining (34% false alarms), the step that creates or admits an instance becomes a new poisoning vector. We should guard it, for example by:
   - requiring device identity or provenance before a new instance is created,
   - rate-limiting new instances,
   - applying the outer-ring support test or the signature-direction budget to a new instance's initial centre.
   That would be a clear extension that answers this paper.
4. **A published adaptation mechanism to attack.** Their centroid drift detector (Yamada and Matsutani, IPDPSW 2023, ref. 10) and ONLAD/OS-ELM are published adaptation mechanisms. We could reimplement them on our N-BaIoT features as a non-own baseline. That partly answers open problem 4 (freeze or poison attacks shown only against our own baselines). We could show that naive ONLAD-style instance spawning is poisoned, and check whether TOA or the signature-free rule blocks the spawned poison instance.
5. **Scope for an ESP32 demo.** OS-ELM with 10 hidden nodes is tiny and suits the ESP32. We could run their learner and ours side by side on-device, which they themselves did not do (their detection ran on a PC).
6. **Possible extra threat class for the discussion section.** Physical or sensor-side injection on ESP32 sensor nodes, in addition to network-side poisoning. This is optional and out of scope for the network IDS core.

I found no 2025/26 follow-up from this group proposing a defense. A quick search turned up none; this is not exhaustive.
corpus.fetch_status: Full text read through the PubMed Central copy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11479347/) in two WebFetch passes: (1) abstract, method, hardware, results and limitations; (2) references 6-10 and 32-34, the conclusion, and checks for timing, budget, freeze, robust-update and code/data release. The MDPI page (https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/19/6416) returned HTTP 403. WebFetch returns a model-written summary, not the raw text, so I did not inspect figures or equations directly. The numbers above (thresholds, frequencies, voltages, network size) are as extracted, and the low-frequency peak value and the aliasing point are unverified. Bibliographic details (authors, venue, volume, issue, article number, date, DOI) were confirmed by both the search results and PMC.

corpus.title: What changes after deployment? A survey on On-device Learning in TinyML
corpus.authors: Massimo Pavan, Luca Pezzarossa, Xenofon Fafoutis (Technical University of Denmark, DTU); Fabrizio Pittorino, Manuel Roveri (Politecnico di Milano). The affiliations come from the arXiv HTML full text.
corpus.venue_year: arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.31226, v1 submitted 29 May 2026 (cs.LG primary, cs.AI; ACM class I.2.6; CC BY 4.0). No journal or conference reference is listed, so it is not yet peer-reviewed as far as I can verify. URL found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31226 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.31226v1).
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31226
corpus.problem: Earlier surveys of on-device learning (ODL) on microcontrollers grouped together methods that solve different problems. This survey argues the right organizing question is what kind of distribution change happens after deployment. It reviews about 70 MCU-class ODL works and sorts them into three regimes. (a) Single-change: the distribution shifts once at deployment and then stays put (e.g. wake-word enrollment). (b) Concept drift: the distribution changes repeatedly, and the learner must adapt fast by "discarding or downweighting" old knowledge (e.g. pressure-sensor calibration). (c) Continual learning: formally the same as (b), but changes are rarer and bring new concepts, so the goal is to avoid catastrophic forgetting (e.g. an EEG brain-machine interface). It then compares works through three lenses: application, hardware and solution. It also points to a gap between method benchmarks and real deployments.
corpus.method: This is a literature survey with no new algorithm and no experiments. Search: Google Scholar as the main source, plus IEEE Xplore, ACM DL and arXiv, using keyword groups such as "On-Device Learning", "Continual Learning" and "Learning in the presence of concept drift", each combined with "tiny", "MCU" or "IoT", then snowballing through references. Inclusion rules: MCU-class hardware or smaller (about MB-scale RAM, under 500 MHz, under 500 mW); the learning phase itself, not just inference; and learning that runs, or is designed to run, on the device. Formal frame: a data-generating process P gives (x^t, y^t) from p^t, which is stationary before deployment time T. S0 is pre-deployment data and S is the post-deployment stream. Every solution is split into four parts: R = dimensionality-reduction block (latent delta^t); B = data-management buffer (Delta^t, with a trigger condition); f = the ML model; L = the learning mechanism. Solutions are then labelled batch learning (L runs once, which by construction only fits the single-change regime) or incremental learning (L runs whenever a trigger fires, for the device's whole life). Evaluation protocol per regime: single-change uses a final test set; concept drift uses prequential evaluation (Gama et al. 2013; each sample is used first for inference, then for an update, scored by running average); continual learning uses a test set per distribution re-checked after later ones, measuring forgetting and forward transfer.
corpus.data_and_hardware: The survey has no data of its own; these are the datasets and hardware of the works it reviews. Datasets: image (CIFAR-10/100, MNIST, CORe50, MiniImageNet, ImageNet, CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, SHIFT, plus Flowers, Food, Cars, CUB, Pets); audio (Google Speech Commands, DCASE2020); IMU/HAR (UCI-HAR, PAMAP2, SHL, CWRU, Opportunity, Skoda, MHEALTH, WISDM, EuRoC MAV); biosignal (MIT-BIH, HYSER, UniBo-20-Session); tabular (Iris, Heart Disease, Cancer); and stream-mining sets (the DataStream suite: NOAA, ELEC, RIALTO and others). Many application works use private datasets. There is no network-traffic or IDS dataset: no Kitsune, N-BaIoT, CIC or TON_IoT. Hardware tables: ultra-constrained (Cortex-M0 / RP2040-class, ST ISPU in-sensor processor), standard MCUs (Cortex-M4, M7, STM32, e.g. STM32H7 at 480 MHz) and PULP chips (GAP8, GAP9, VEGA, Mr. Wolf). Cortex-M55/Ethos-U55 NPUs are noted as missing from the literature. ESP32 does not appear anywhere in the text (I checked by keyword scan), and neither do nRF or Arduino Nano 33 in what I saw.
corpus.results: These are synthesis findings, not experiments. (1) Method-oriented and application-oriented works barely overlap; keyword spotting and IMU-based HAR are the only shared tasks. (2) Many real TinyML domains, including biosignals, sensor calibration and anomaly detection, have no standard benchmark. (3) Application papers rarely state power or latency requirements, so hardware and algorithm are picked one after the other instead of together. (4) Hardware capability tracks regime difficulty: ultra-constrained chips mostly appear in single-change work, PULP dominates continual learning, and standard MCUs cover all three regimes but are thin in continual learning. (5) Batch-learning solutions can only handle single-change. Full-network on-device training appears only in method papers. Frozen pretrained CNNs are the usual R, and fully online |Delta|=1 is the usual B for single-change and concept-drift work. (6) Instance- and prototype-based methods grow in memory over time, which makes them poorly suited to indefinite adaptation. (7) Latency and energy are normalized inconsistently, concept-drift works rarely report energy, and method papers often leave out the buffer's memory cost. On the anomaly-detection side, normality "cannot be defined a priori" and must be learned on the device. Examples: Pereira et al. 2023 (IEEE Micro), an extreme-value-theory Weibull model fitted by EM, in batch, on a Cortex-M0 with 264 kB RAM; Ren et al. 2021 (TinyOL), an autoencoder adapted to a fan's normal operation on a Cortex-M4; Silva et al. 2023 (MetroAutomotive), unsupervised online clustering for driver behaviour. Concept-drift MCU work they cite: Disabato and Roveri 2024 (audio/GSC, prequential evaluation, Cortex-M7; I could not capture the exact reference title) and Ma et al. 2025, "On-demand Test-time Adaptation for Edge Devices" (arXiv; CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, SHIFT). Their stated pattern for concept-drift works is that learning is switched on only when "an explicit change detection mechanism signals a distribution shift". Future directions: (i) a solution-oriented benchmark with fixed worst-case RAM and compute, several stream lengths and full memory accounting including B; (ii) a hardware-oriented benchmark that fixes the solution and reports latency, energy per learning event and peak power; (iii) a co-design benchmark with explicit latency and power budgets; (iv) organizing benchmarks by regime and building label-efficient streams that mix labelled and unlabelled data; (v) end-to-end tools that optimize R, B, f and L jointly; (vi) ODL-specific hardware for scarce labels, no on-device validation and tight power.
corpus.limitations: The paper has no explicit limitations section in the full text. Limitations I observed: it is not peer-reviewed (arXiv v1 only). It covers no security at all: my keyword scans of the whole text found no "secur", "attack", "adversar", "poison", "malicious" or "intrusion". The only "robust" is a reference title about corruption robustness, and "privacy" appears once as a general TinyML benefit. It never discusses label noise, self-training error build-up or confirmation bias, even though it describes self-supervised pseudo-labelling (e.g. Rusci et al. 2025 on audio streams; Cereda et al. using a drone flight controller as the label source). It does not name or compare drift detectors (no ADWIN, CUSUM or ICI). It covers no network-traffic or IDS domain and no ESP32. It treats the trigger condition purely as a design choice, never as an attack surface. "Freezing" only means a frozen pretrained backbone or bias/head-only updates, not stopping learning in response to suspicion. "Budgets" only means RAM, compute, latency and power, never limits on how far or how fast the model may move.
corpus.overlap_with_us: There is almost no overlap with our contribution. The survey does not do TOA-like direction budgeting: there is no splitting of updates into components and no rationing of movement toward any direction or signature. It does not do core/outer-ring robust updating: no trimmed, density-based or robust updates appear, and "robust" never occurs in the body. It does not describe a freeze-type attack, or any attack: poisoning, adversaries and malicious data are absent, and the change-detection trigger that gates learning is never considered as something an attacker could fire or suppress on purpose. It covers no intrusion detection, no network traffic and no ESP32. The overlap that does exist is about framing. (a) Our setting fits squarely in their concept-drift regime: an unlabelled stream, self-labelled updates and prequential-style evaluation. (b) Our detector fits their R/B/f/L decomposition: R = PCA, B = online |Delta|=1 with an accept-if-judged-normal trigger, f = the centroid with centre and spread, L = the gated update. (c) They survey the same family of target systems, on-device unsupervised normality learners for anomaly detection (Pereira 2023 EVT, TinyOL autoencoder, Silva 2023 clustering), and leave them completely undefended. Net: it does not threaten our novelty, and it is useful as evidence that the 2026 TinyML ODL literature leaves the security of the self-learning loop unaddressed.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. A gap statement with a citation. A May 2026 survey of about 70 MCU on-device-learning works covers no poisoning, no adversarial triggering of drift adaptation and no IDS or network domain. Cite it in the intro and related work as "ODL surveys cover how to adapt, not whether the adaptation can be hijacked".
2. Its taxonomy and notation. Present our detector as a concept-drift-regime ODL solution in their R/B/f/L terms, and frame our threat as an attack on L (poisoning) and on the trigger condition (the freeze attack). This places us inside an established TinyML vocabulary that reviewers from that community will recognize.
3. Its evaluation protocol. Report prequential results (inference then update, running-average detection and false alarms) alongside our per-cycle curves, as their concept-drift protocol prescribes.
4. Its hardware reporting checklist for the ESP32 work (open problem 3): peak RAM including the buffer, latency per learning event, energy per learning event and peak power, plus clock and RAM specs in the same format as their Tables 4-6. They note concept-drift papers rarely report energy, so measuring it on the ESP32 is a cheap way to stand out. ESP32 never appears in the survey, so an ESP32 (Xtensa/RISC-V) deployment is itself new. My own assessment, not the survey's: ESP32 roughly meets their MCU-class inclusion limits of under 500 MHz and MB-scale RAM, but Wi-Fi transmit power can exceed their 500 mW figure, so report compute-only power separately.
5. Constant memory as a selling point. They flag that instance- and prototype-based learners grow in memory, which makes them poorly suited to indefinite adaptation; our centroid detector and its update rules use fixed memory, which we should state explicitly.
6. Attack targets for open problem 4. The on-device anomaly learners they list (Pereira et al. 2023 EVT/Weibull, IEEE Micro; Ren et al. 2021 TinyOL; Silva et al. 2023 unsupervised clustering), and the change-detection-gated adaptation pattern (Disabato and Roveri 2024; Ma et al. 2025, On-demand Test-time Adaptation), are published on-device learners we could subject to boiling-frog poisoning and the freeze attack. One caveat: these are adaptation schemes, not published poisoning defences, so they only partly close that gap. Pereira's extreme-value tail model is also a natural point of comparison for our outer-ring rule.
7. Their future direction (iv), label-efficient benchmarks mixing labelled and unlabelled data, is a hook for positioning our signature-free variant.
