corpus.title: Strategic Games and Zero Shot Attacks on Heavy-Hitter Network Flow Monitoring
corpus.authors: Francesco Da Dalt and Adrian Perrig (both ETH Zurich). Verified from the NDSS landing page and the paper's first page.
corpus.venue_year: NDSS Symposium 2026 (Network and Distributed System Security Symposium, 23-27 Feb 2026, San Diego). DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.241301 (printed in the PDF footer). This is a 2026 paper, so it fits our recency preference. It sits in an adjacent area (in-network DDoS/rate-limiting monitors), not IoT anomaly detection.
corpus.url: Landing page: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/strategic-games-and-zero-shot-attacks-on-heavy-hitter-network-flow-monitoring/ | PDF: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2026-f1301-paper.pdf | Slides: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/f1301-dadalt-slides.pdf | Video: https://youtu.be/vv1xcudyhQU | Code (cited as ref [22] in the paper; I confirmed the repo exists): https://github.com/FrancescoDaDalt/HHNFM
corpus.problem: Heavy-hitter detectors (HHDs) feed token-bucket rate limiters for DDoS and fair-share enforcement. They come with probabilistic accuracy guarantees, but they are benchmarked only on static traces. The paper asks how far an adaptive sender can exceed its bandwidth cap by shaping packet timing and size, given limited HHD memory, LRU eviction from a small pool of token buckets, and refresh or decay timing. It also asks whether adversarial co-training can harden HHDs, and whether one attacker trained against a flexible surrogate can beat HHDs it has never seen ("zero-shot"). Threat model: the attacker is an ordinary flow. It cannot spoof, it chooses packet sizes from 0.01 to 1 MTU at any rate, and it optionally sees ACKs. Its goal is evasion and throughput overuse. It does not poison any learned model.
corpus.method: (1) Simulated data plane: ingress queue, then an HHD, then 10 token buckets with LRU eviction (refill 2u, capacity 4u), with HHD memory capped at n/10 cells. Nine HHDs are tested: ElasticSketch, HeavyKeeper, Misra-Gries, Space-Saving, CountMin-Heap, CountBayes-Heap, ALBUS, Count-Heap and HashPipe. (2) PPO tunes each HHD's hyperparameters (threshold, refresh time, decay rate) with a defender reward: -s for each packet it marks heavy, +2s for each packet the rate limiter drops. The tuned "policy" is a constant (a 1-layer network with zero-dimensional input). The deployed defender therefore has fixed parameters and does no online learning. (3) Neural Traffic Agent (NTA): a PPO attacker built on a time-series transformer (2 layers, 4 heads, 16-d input). It reads a 20x6 history of its past actions and ACKs, and outputs wait time, packet count and packet size. Reward is +s per delivered packet and -s per dropped packet. (4) Hardening uses Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO): attacker and defender populations grow over 9 iterations, and Nash equilibria of the meta-game are solved by mixed-integer LP in MOSEK. The defender becomes the Nash-weighted mix of its population. (5) Zero-shot attack: they build a Neural Monitor Agent (NMA), a flexible transformer-managed counter structure used only as a training opponent. The NTA is co-trained against it with PSRO, and the Nash mix of NTA policies (0.34/0.66) is then run blind against all 9 real HHDs.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Everything runs in simulation. There is no switch hardware, no P4 or Tofino, and no embedded device. Synthetic traffic: flow durations exponential with mean 1 s, per-flow rate Weibull with mean 20 MTU/s, up to n = 1000 concurrent flows (100 when training the NMA), packet sizes uniform from 0.01 to 1 MTU, rate cap 40 MTU/s, link latencies 100/200/100 ms. All training uses synthetic traffic only. For real background traffic in evaluation they use one MAWI samplepoint-G capture (2020-03-18 14:00): 10,000 TCP/UDP flows, with packet sizes scaled down by 0.22. Compute: a single desktop with an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, an RTX 4070 SUPER (12 GB) and 32 GB DDR5. Software: C++ (gcc 13.3), libtorch 2.7.0, OpenMP and MOSEK 10.2. Wall-clock training time: about 5.3k s for an HHD, 19.7k s for the NTA and 14.5k s for the NMA. Defender results average 320 runs; training uses 32 parallel 6 s simulations, and evaluation uses 60 s runs. Repo: C++/CMake with Docker. Its README currently states a temporary pre-publication artifact-evaluation licence, becoming MIT on release, while the GitHub sidebar already shows MIT. The two disagree, so check before reusing code.
corpus.results:
- Attacks: the learned NTA beat the 40 MTU/s cap against all 9 HHDs whenever the ACK setting matched between training and evaluation. Overuse ranged from 10% to 299% on synthetic background traffic and from 78% to 671% on real MAWI background (for example, 308.2 RpS against ElasticSketch).
- Learned strategy: an on/off pattern. Against ES it sends about 360 MTU/s while unmonitored and drops to about 53 MTU/s while rate-limited. It deliberately stays above the cap while limited, accepting some loss as a probe to detect the earliest eviction. It ramps up in steps of about 400 ms, one round-trip each, waiting for ACKs to confirm eviction.
- Pre-attack HHD quality does not predict robustness. The best tuned HHDs (ALBUS, HashPipe) are, if anything, more exploitable, which the authors put down to over-specialisation. The pre-attack correlation was not significant; post-attack NTA-vs-HHD linear correlation was 0.44 (p = 0.022).
- PSRO hardening: ES exploitability fell from 299% to 139% (2.2x), and ES rate-limiting reward rose from 60.8 to 102.4 RpS (1.7x). ALBUS went from 85% to 64% (1.3x).
- Zero-shot attack: overuse on 8 of 9 HHDs with synthetic background (it fails only against HeavyKeeper, at 31.8 RpS) and on 9 of 9 with real background. Picking the best of the 25 learned NTA policies per target beat the dedicated per-target attacks in 8 of 9 cases.
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors:
- Co-training is computationally expensive on both CPU and GPU, and they say orders of magnitude more compute would be needed for attackers that generalise to arbitrary real systems.
- There is a sim-to-real gap; the trained models need further engineering before running in a live system.
- The zero-shot attack fails against HeavyKeeper because the NMA cannot mimic decay-based counters.
- The NMA was trained in a smaller environment (100 flows, 4 environments) than the evaluation, a mismatch they acknowledge.
- Generalisation is hard to quantify. The attacker benefits from noisy real background traffic and would do worse if it were the only flow.
- Future work: other attacker objectives (for example, raising other users' latency or jitter) and multiple communicating attackers and defenders.

My own observations (not stated by the authors):
- Pure simulation with a synthetic traffic generator and a single attacker flow. Real data is one MAWI hour with rescaled packets.
- Defenders are static hyperparameter vectors, so no online learning, drift or poisoning is studied.
- The final PSRO equilibria came out pure, so the "mixed defender" benefit was not actually exercised in the reported result.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low overlap, and none on our core contributions.
- TOA-like direction budgeting: no. Nothing splits updates into attack-aligned and orthogonal parts, nothing caps attacker-induced movement, and there is no provable minimum time to compromise. Their defence is game-theoretic co-training of a few fixed hyperparameters (threshold, refresh, decay).
- Core / outer-ring robust updating: no. They use no robust statistics, no dense-core learning and no support checks for centre or spread updates.
- Freeze-type attack: no. There is no self-learning detector to freeze; the deployed HHD is a constant hyperparameter set. The only loose analogue is that the NTA exploits the monitor's own state machine. It probes to detect eviction from the token bucket and times its bursts to refresh and decay windows. That is attacking a defender's reaction logic, as our freeze attack does, but it is evasion of a counter or rate limiter, not manipulation of a learning or suspicion mode, and nothing drives false alarms on honest traffic afterwards.
- Poisoning, drift and IoT: absent. No poisoning (ANTIDOTE / Kloft-Laskov style), no concept drift, no IoT, no on-device or embedded deployment, no anomaly detector.

Shared themes we can cite: guarantees and benchmark scores on static traces do not survive adaptive adversaries; high-accuracy, specialised monitors can be more exploitable; feedback-driven probing of a stateful monitor. Our work stays clearly distinct. Cite it in related work as adaptive-adversary evaluation of in-network monitors (evasion of fixed-parameter monitors) and contrast it with our setting (poisoning and freezing of self-learning, drift-tracking detectors).
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. A learned worst-case attacker in place of a hand-made poison ramp. Train a PPO attacker (a small transformer or MLP over a history of its actions and observed accept/alarm feedback) that picks per-cycle poison share, direction and magnitude. Rewards: speed to compromise for poisoning, or false alarms after leaving for the freeze attack. Use it to stress-test TOA's minimum-time-to-compromise claim and the signature-free core/outer-ring rule. This directly answers the reviewer objection that the attacker is only modelled.
2. Probe for budget-refill timing attacks. Their NTA learned on/off pulsing tuned to eviction and refresh timescales. The analogous threat to us is an attacker that pulses poison each time TOA's slow budget refills, or times poison to the outer-ring support window. Test explicitly that our bound holds against this.
3. Report exploitability as a metric: the best-response attacker's gain (worst-case FPR, or worst-case cycles to compromise) for each defence, plus the reduction factor, in the style of their 299%-to-139% figure.
4. A transfer attack against published defences, which addresses our open problem 4. Train freeze and poison attackers against a flexible surrogate (an NMA-style learner) or our own baselines, then run them zero-shot on AOC-IDS, CND-IDS and others. That shows the freeze attack is not an artefact of our baselines.
5. Attacker-observability ablation. They train and evaluate with and without ACK feedback. We should do the same: an attacker that sees alarms or blocks versus a blind one, since a freeze attack needs some way to sense the suspicion state.
6. Synthetic training with real-background evaluation, and their observation that attackers hide behind extreme real background flows. This mirrors our open problem 1 (poison hidden inside strong genuine drift); cite it as independent evidence that realistic background noise favours the attacker.
7. Optionally, PSRO-style co-training, or randomising TOA budget and ring thresholds as a mixed defender, to harden the hyperparameters. Note that their gains come at roughly 4-5 GPU-hours per agent, which is fine offline. Only the resulting fixed parameters would ship to the ESP32.
8. Presentation habits worth copying: phase-space plots of attacker strategies, compute-cost tables, and released code and checkpoints for artifact evaluation.

corpus.title: Provably Reliable Conformal Prediction Sets in the Presence of Data Poisoning (method name: Reliable Prediction Sets, RPS)
corpus.authors: Yan Scholten, Stephan Günnemann (Technical University of Munich, DAML group)
corpus.venue_year: ICLR 2025 (Spotlight). arXiv v1 posted 13 Oct 2024, current v4 dated 16 Mar 2025. The arXiv comments say "Accepted at ICLR 2025 (Spotlight)". The ICLR 2025 virtual poster page (iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/28340) and the TUM project page also list it. OpenReview id ofuLWn8DFZ comes from the TUM BibTeX as reported by search results; I did not open that page.
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09878 (full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.09878v4; project/code page: https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/daml/reliable-conformal-prediction/; ICLR page: https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/28340)
corpus.problem: Split conformal prediction promises that the prediction set contains the true label with probability 1-alpha. That promise breaks when an attacker poisons the training data, the calibration data, or both: they can insert, delete or relabel points, and a feature change counts as one deletion plus one insertion. The paper asks for prediction sets with provable reliability under a poisoning budget (r_t training points, r_c calibration points). It wants two separate guarantees. Coverage reliability means the attacker cannot remove a class from the set. Size reliability means the attacker cannot add a class to the set. Both are required together, so a defense cannot look reliable just by returning empty or full sets. Setting: static, offline, i.i.d. (exchangeable), supervised image classification.
corpus.method:
Two aggregation tricks, each limiting how much any one poisoned point can change the result.
(1) Training poisoning: a smoothed score function. A deterministic hash splits the training set into k_t disjoint partitions (for images, sum of pixel values mod k_t). One classifier is trained deterministically on each partition. The score for class y is a softmax over the fraction of the k_t classifiers that vote y. One poisoned point can change only one classifier's vote, so the score moves by at most 1/k_t per poisoned point. Lemma 1 shows this is still a valid conformal score.
(2) Calibration poisoning: a majority prediction set. The calibration set is hashed into k_c partitions, each partition gets its own conformal threshold and set C_i, and a class is kept only if it appears in more than tau_hat(alpha) of the k_c sets. tau_hat comes from the inverse CDF of Binomial(k_c, 1-alpha). Theorem 2 shows marginal coverage still holds on clean data, and k_c = 1 is ordinary split conformal.
Certificates (Theorems 3-6) are simple counting inequalities.
- Calibration only: coverage-reliable if (minimum vote count among in-set classes) - r_c > tau_hat; size-reliable if (maximum vote count among out-of-set classes) + r_c <= tau_hat.
- Training: a greedy worst case shifts 1/k_t of vote mass per poisoned point to get upper and lower score bounds.
- Joint: beta_y is the number of partitions guaranteed to contain y and gamma_y the number guaranteed to exclude it; the conditions are beta_y - r_c > tau_hat and k_c - gamma_y + r_c <= tau_hat.
- Side condition: the smallest calibration partition must satisfy |P_min| - r_c >= 1/alpha - 1. Otherwise an attacker can delete points until a threshold cannot be computed at all.
corpus.data_and_hardware: Datasets: SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 (32x32 RGB). Models: ResNet-18 (default), ResNet-50, ResNet-101. 1,000 test images are used for calibration and 9,000 for testing; results average 5 model seeds x 5 calibration splits. Training: SGD (lr 0.01, momentum 0.9, weight decay 5e-4), up to 400 epochs with early stopping, cosine schedule, batch size 128. Hardware: ResNet-18 trained on an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti; ResNet-50/101 on an A100 40GB; inference on the 1080 Ti; certificates on a Xeon E5-2630 v4 CPU. Cost: about 1-1.5 min per partition model, so roughly 1.6-2.4 h for 100 partition models. Building the sets takes at most 0.5 s. Certificates take under 1 s (calibration only) or about 1 min (training plus calibration). No embedded or IoT hardware, no network or intrusion data.
corpus.results:
All figures are CIFAR-10 at alpha = 0.1, as given by the full-text extraction.
- Calibration poisoning only (k_c = 22): empirical coverage 90.2%, average set size 0.94. More than 93% of sets are certified coverage-reliable at r_c = 4, and more than 87% size-reliable at r_c = 15.
- Training poisoning (k_t = 100): coverage 90.7%, average set size 3.18, and only about 34% of sets coverage-reliable at r_t = 4.
- Joint (k_t = 100, k_c = 40): coverage 92%, set size 3.41, about 31% of sets coverage-reliable at r_t = r_c = 3.
- CIFAR-100 with 100 training partitions: set size balloons to about 43 (about 18 with ImageNet fine-tuning), because each partition classifier reaches only about 30% accuracy versus 70% or more on the full data.
- Ablation: the softmax smoothing prevents oversized sets and over-coverage.
Takeaway: robustness to calibration poisoning is cheap and strong. Robustness to training poisoning is costly, and the certified radii are small (single-digit point counts).
corpus.limitations:
Stated by the authors:
- Partitioned training costs accuracy on harder or larger datasets (CIFAR-100, ImageNet), which they call an open challenge.
- With only 2-3 partition classifiers the score is unstable (4 are said to be enough to avoid huge sets).
- Calibration partitions cannot get too small, both because of the finite-sample correction and because an attacker can delete points to block set construction.
- Exchangeability may fail when the attacker knows the calibration set during training, which is why they rely on pointwise certificates.
- Future work: better partition classifiers, poisoning during fine-tuning, reproducible randomized scores.
Not stated, but important for us:
- Purely batch and offline, with i.i.d. data assumed throughout. No streaming, online updating, self-labeling, concept drift, or temporal or boiling-frog poisoning.
- Distribution shift appears only in related work (Cauchois et al. 2020).
- No anomaly detection. No adaptive or iterative attacker beyond the worst case inside the budget ball.
- No abstain or freeze mechanism, and no attack that exploits one.
- Certified radii count points and do not scale with an attacker's share of a stream.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Low; it does not anticipate our methods.
- TOA-like direction budgeting: no. It has no notion of an update direction, no projection onto an attack direction, and no slow per-direction budget. Its only budget is a count of poisoned points in a fixed dataset. The loose parallel is that both give a provable bound on attacker effort: certified radius r for RPS, minimum time to compromise for TOA. The mechanisms are unrelated, since RPS bounds influence by partitioning and voting and TOA by rationing one direction.
- Core/outer-ring robust updating: no. It has no density core, no outer-ring corroboration of centre or spread changes, and no geometry of the accepted cloud. Its robustness is purely combinatorial (hash partitions plus majority vote).
- Freeze attack: no. It does not describe an attack that trips a defense into stopping learning. The closest material is two small points. First, an attacker who deletes calibration points could make a partition too small to compute a threshold, a denial of service on set construction that they rule out with |P| - r_c >= 1/alpha - 1. Second, they insist on two-sided reliability so that empty or full sets cannot count as robust. That second point is conceptually close to our argument that freezing defenses look safe on detection but fail on false alarms, though in a static setting.
- Problem setting: it does not overlap with on-device, drifting, unsupervised, self-learning IoT intrusion detection. It is supervised image classification with heavy GPU ensembles.
Bottom line: cite it as related work on certified poisoning robustness. It does not threaten our novelty claims for TOA, the signature-free core/ring method, or the freeze attack.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Two-sided reliability definition. Restate our goal as (a) detection reliability: the attacker cannot get attack traffic accepted as normal, the analogue of coverage reliability; and (b) false-alarm reliability: the attacker cannot get honest traffic flagged, the analogue of size reliability. Then argue formally that freezing defenses meet (a) trivially and violate (b) under drift, the same way RPS rules out empty or full sets as trivial solutions. This gives the freeze attack a clean theory hook and a citation.
2. Hash-partitioned ensemble of tiny detectors with a majority vote. Run k centroid detectors, each updated only on windows hashed to it, and flag on a majority vote. One poisoned window can move only one sub-detector, so flipping a decision provably needs more than about k/2 corrupted sub-detectors. This is cheap on an ESP32: k centroid plus spread vectors in PCA space. Hashing on device ID or MAC also ties directly to our open problem 2 (per-device detectors when a new device joins). It could be combined with TOA as a second, orthogonal layer of certified robustness.
3. Conformal thresholds instead of a centre + k*spread cutoff. Use split-conformal p-values over recent accepted scores for the anomaly threshold, plus a majority-of-calibration-subsets threshold that resists calibration poisoning. Their condition |P_min| - r >= 1/alpha - 1 gives a principled minimum window or buffer size per partition, which also yields an ESP32 memory budget.
4. Evaluation metrics: report the fraction of decisions certified robust at each poisoning radius, plus the rates of trivial outcomes (always alarm, never alarm). This is a good template for an A-level evaluation table.
5. Gap they leave open: they assume exchangeability and note it breaks. That supports our claim that robust conformal or certified methods do not cover drifting streams. Any borrowed conformal threshold would need a drift-aware variant (adaptive or weighted conformal), which we would have to find and cite separately.

corpus.title: Anomaly Detection in the Open World: Normality Shift Detection, Explanation, and Adaptation (OWAD)
corpus.authors: Dongqi Han, Zhiliang Wang (corresponding), Wenqi Chen, Kai Wang, Rui Yu, Su Wang, Han Zhang, Jiahai Yang, Xingang Shi, Xia Yin (Tsinghua University / Zhongguancun Lab / Quan Cheng Lab); Zhihua Wang, Minghui Jin (State Grid Shanghai Municipal Electric Power Company).
corpus.venue_year: NDSS Symposium 2023 (27 Feb - 3 Mar 2023, San Diego). DOI 10.14722/ndss.2023.24830. It is older than our 2024 cut-off, so treat it as BACKGROUND. It is still a direct foundation and the most likely published defense a reviewer will tell us to compare against.
corpus.url: Paper page: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/anomaly-detection-in-the-open-world-normality-shift-detection-explanation-and-adaptation/ . PDF: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2023-830-paper.pdf . Code (checked, it exists; MIT licence, PyTorch, has KitNET-on-Kyoto and DeepLog-on-BGL demos): https://github.com/dongtsi/OWAD . Video: https://youtu.be/WSiqla03HLo
corpus.problem: The problem is "normality shift": the distribution of NORMAL data changes over time under zero-positive (normal-only) deep anomaly detectors used in security. New patches, devices, protocols or user behaviour cause the shift, and if it is not handled it produces large numbers of false positives and false negatives. Older drift work (CADE, Transcend/TRANSCENDENT, INSOMNIA) is either supervised or works sample by sample, and mostly detects drift instead of adapting to it. The authors name three challenges: (1) detecting the shift without any knowledge of anomalies, (2) picking few samples for a human to label, since normal drift and real anomalies look the same to a zero-positive model, and (3) adapting without catastrophic forgetting of old knowledge that is still valid, while still generalising to the new normality. There is NO adversary in the problem statement. Shift is treated as benign and natural throughout.
corpus.method:
OWAD wraps any deep zero-positive detector and runs periodically (once per collection round, not per packet) in four steps.
(1) Calibrator: isotonic regression fits a monotone piecewise-linear function that maps raw detector outputs to calibrated confidence, defined without labels. For normal-confidence models the target is the false-positive rate you would get if that output were the threshold; for reconstruction models it is the true-negative rate. It is fitted on the control (already-trusted) set.
(2) Shift detection: build K-bin histograms of calibrated outputs for the control set (old, trusted) and the treatment set (new, unlabelled, may contain anomalies). A permutation test uses KL divergence as the statistic (Np=1000, K=5, shift declared at p<0.05).
(3) Explainer: gradient descent on relaxed masks m_c and m_t in [0,1]. The loss has three parts: KL between the treatment histogram and a histogram rebuilt from the masked control+treatment samples (M=100 bins), a labelling-cost term that favours keeping many control samples and few treatment samples, and an entropy term that pushes masks towards 0/1. Treatment samples whose outputs fall outside the control range are always added. The selected treatment samples go to a HUMAN, who removes anomalies. Control samples with low masks count as normality that has expired.
(4) Adaptation: fine-tune the detector on the selected samples with a regulariser that penalises parameter changes, L' = L + λ3 Σ Ω_i (θ*_i − θ_i)² (in the style of EWC / Memory Aware Synapses). Ω_i is the squared gradient of the output norm, weighted by the control masks. Parameters important to old normality that is still valid are held back; unimportant ones move freely. The kept samples become the next control set.
corpus.data_and_hardware:
Datasets (all public except SCADA):
(a) Network intrusion detection: Kyoto 2006+ honeypot flow features using the AnoShift (NeurIPS 2022 D&B) split. Train on 2007 (50K normal flows for KitNET from Kitsune); test points are one per year, 2011-2015.
(b) Log anomaly detection: BGL BlueGene/L logs (214 days, about 7 months), DeepLog LSTM, sampled 10 times every 2-3 weeks.
(c) APT / lateral movement: LANL-CMSCSE login events (58 days), GLGV with an autoencoder head, sampled weekly.
(d) Real deployment: State Grid SCADA security-monitoring logs from more than 20 devices over 18 weeks (19 Oct 2021 - 20 Feb 2022), tens of millions of logs, one DeepLog per device. Shift was checked at weeks 9 and 18. This data is not released.
Each collection round is split 1:1 into validation (used for adaptation) and test sets.
Hardware: NOT stated anywhere in the paper. I searched the full text for GPU, CPU and hardware and found nothing. The only cost figure is a mean of 116 s per adaptation round on 10^5 validation samples, against 975 s for CADE and 1,449 s for TRANS. There is no embedded, edge or IoT-device evaluation, and none of the data is IoT device traffic.
corpus.results:
Single adaptation with a fixed 30% labelling budget (Fig. 4a-c): OWAD scores best at the adaptation point and degrades least later (most visible at T4). Adapting early helps more than adapting late.
LogAD, Table III: F-score at T1/T2/T3 is 0.82/0.72/0.65 for OWAD, against 0.74/0.66/0.42 for No-Update. False positives at T1 are 1,491 against 2,404. OWAD is the only method that cuts false positives and false negatives together. UNLEARN cuts false negatives but raises false positives.
Labelling needed: about 10% for network detection (about 5,000 flows once a year), 30% for LogAD and 5% for APT. Some baselines do worse than No-Update when labels are scarce.
Ablations:
- Calibration: the piecewise-linear isotonic fit is the only calibrator that gets shift vs no-shift right on both NID and LogAD (Table IV).
- Explainer: its sample selection beats CADE, TRANS and uncertainty sampling (Table V).
- Full OWAD: NID AUC 0.88 at T1 and 0.75 at T3; LogAD F1 0.89 and 0.65; APT AUC 0.79 and 0.81 (Table VI).
- The regulariser adds about 2% F-score.
Multiple adaptations (T1-T10, Fig. 4g-h): OWAD is mostly better than the baselines with far fewer labels. Retrain is slightly better on APT but needs dozens of times more labels.
SCADA (Table VII): device A had no shift (p=0.999, then 0.257). Devices B and C shifted (p=0.000). False positives at week 18 after adapting at week 9 were 154 for device B (1,678 without adaptation) and 98 for device C (3,103 without). Labelling device A took about 200 logs, roughly half an hour of operator time.
Hyperparameters are insensitive over wide ranges: K from 4 to 30, λ3 from 1e-3 to 1e1.
corpus.limitations:
Limitations the authors state (Sec. VII and Sec. V-D):
(1) Explaining a shift needs domain knowledge, and finding root causes automatically is left as future work.
(2) The SCADA deployment is only a first trial.
(3) Robustness of OWAD itself, against adversarial attacks or noisy labels, is explicitly left to future work.
(4) Data is collected periodically; when to test for shift and how to collect treatment data are left open.
(5) Default hyperparameter ranges are not checked on other applications.
(6) OWAD is better at removing false positives than false negatives.
Limitations they do not state (my reading):
- A human labels the selected treatment samples every round. Without that human, nothing removes poison.
- It works in batch rounds (yearly or weekly), not as an online per-cycle self-learner.
- The control set is assumed clean.
- It needs a deep model and a gradient-based mask optimisation, which is not realistic on an MCU.
- There is no IoT data, no attacker model, and no time-to-compromise guarantee.
- It cannot tell malicious drift from benign drift. Any shift that passes the permutation test and survives human labelling gets learned.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Bluntly, the overlap is low on our core contributions and high on the framing.
- TOA-style direction budgeting: NO. OWAD has no attack signature, no attack direction, no slow budget and no provable minimum time to compromise. The one loose relative: its λ3·Ω_i regulariser splits the update by PARAMETER axis. It slows parameters that matter to valid old normality and frees the rest. That is the same "restrict some directions, update the rest fully" pattern, but it is chosen to prevent FORGETTING, not to resist an ATTACKER. A reviewer may raise it, so we should say plainly that TOA is threat-aware consolidation and OWAD is forgetting-aware consolidation.
- Core / outer-ring robust updating: NO. The Explainer picks samples that best rebuild the new score histogram, and it FORCES out-of-range treatment samples into the set a human must label. It is a labelling-efficiency tool, not a robust estimator. Removing poison is left entirely to a human.
- Freeze-type attack: NO. There is no adversary anywhere, and robustness to adversarial attacks or noisy labels is listed as future work.
- Where it does overlap: the same problem framing (zero-positive detectors broken by drift in normal traffic), KitNET from Kitsune as a base detector, per-device detectors in a real deployment (which matches our open problem 2), and a strong focus on false positives caused by drift.
Implication: OWAD does not anticipate our threat model or our defenses. It is the most natural "published defense" to attack for our open problem 4.
My inference, not tested: in self-labelling mode (no human), OWAD would take in boiling-frog poison directly. With a human in the loop, an attacker could either keep each round's KL shift under the p<0.05 test, or deliberately set off shift alarms to blow up the labelling budget, which is a cost-based cousin of our freeze attack. The paper does not say whether the control set is refreshed in rounds where no shift is detected, so I could not verify whether small poison accumulates through the control set.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Use OWAD as the published-defense target for our freeze and boiling-frog attacks (open problem 4). The MIT code already ships a KitNET-on-Kyoto demo. Run it in two modes: human-gated (simulate a perfect or a noisy labeller) and self-labelled. Report the share of rounds poisoned and the false alarms after the attacker leaves, next to our naive, freezing, TOA and signature-free numbers.
2. The unsupervised calibrator. Isotonic regression maps our centroid distance to an FPR-calibrated score in [0,1]. That makes the inner core and outer ring definable in calibrated units that mean the same thing across devices. It helps per-device detectors (open problem 2) and makes thresholds easier to defend in a paper.
3. The permutation test with KL on K=5-bin histograms of calibrated scores (Np=1000) as a principled, p-valued replacement for our ad-hoc check that "the outer ring really got busier". The histograms are cheap. Np=1000 permutations may need to run on the gateway rather than the ESP32, but small windows on the ESP32 are plausible (not verified).
4. The evaluation protocol reviewers now expect: the AnoShift Kyoto 2006+ yearly split (train 2007, test 2011-2015) for long-term real benign drift, which is exactly the hard case behind our open problem 1. Also borrow their single-adaptation vs multiple-adaptation tests, AUC rather than single-threshold rates, and their baseline set (No-Update, Retrain, UNLEARN from CCS 2019, CADE from USENIX Security 2021, TRANSCENDENT from S&P 2022).
5. Their SCADA per-device deployment (Table VII) is prior evidence that per-device detectors are the practical unit, which supports our new-device-joining result.
6. Optionally pair TOA with OWAD-style importance weighting (budget along the threat direction, consolidation weighted by importance elsewhere) to show the two are complementary.
Two related 2025 papers surfaced in search but I did NOT read them: "Shift Detection and Adaptation for Network Intrusion Detection" (arXiv 2508.15100, uses OWAD's Kyoto split and OWAD as a baseline) and CAShift (arXiv 2504.09115, benchmarks normality shift in cloud logs). I found no published paper that attacks OWAD's adaptation with poisoning.

corpus.title: Network Intrusion Datasets: A Survey, Limitations, and Recommendations
corpus.authors: Patrik Goldschmidt (Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies (KInIT), Bratislava; a Brno address is also listed, and Brno University of Technology FIT has the paper in its publication records) and Daniela Chudá (KInIT, and Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava).
corpus.url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06688 (full text read at https://arxiv.org/html/2502.06688v3; journal DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cose.2025.104510; authors' notebooks at https://github.com/xGoldy/nid-datasets)
corpus.venue_year: Computers & Security (Elsevier), vol. 156, article 104510, 2025. arXiv v1 10 Feb 2025, v3 (the accepted version) 22 May 2025. 42 pages. Computers & Security is generally ranked Q1, but I did not check the ranking for this exact year.
corpus.problem: Network intrusion detection (NID) research depends on datasets, but the authors argue the main problem is no longer a lack of data. In their words, "datasets exist, but the community is largely unaware of their existence," and people do not know best practices. The last full survey (Ring et al., 2019) is out of date. They tie the slow uptake of ML in real NIDS to features of the field: high cost of errors, non-stationary traffic (data drift and concept drift together cause "model drift"), the fact that "Every network is unique," label shift, and biased evaluation (e.g., random splits that ignore time).
corpus.method: This is a systematic literature review, not a detection method. Search: network (intrusion OR anomaly OR outlier OR attack OR threat) (dataset OR data set), matched on titles or keywords, publications up to 2023. Sources: SCOPUS (656 hits), ACM DL (42), IEEE Xplore (179), Google Scholar (600), plus 302 datasets taken from earlier surveys and forward/backward citation search. This gave 113 relevant objects, 138 after the reference search, and 89 public datasets after quality checks. Each was downloaded and analysed by hand; the supervisor validated a random 10%. Each dataset is described by 13 properties in 5 groups: general (year, focus, normal traffic, attack), nature of data (format, number of features, anonymised), volume (size, duration), network (network type, complete capture), evaluation (split, labels). Duration ignores gaps longer than 1% of the dataset's time span, and each dataset is rated continuous, discontinuous or periodic. A popularity study covered 45 NID papers from 2020-2023 at CORE A*/A security venues. The paper ends with a 10-step, 4-phase guide for building datasets, plus advice on choosing and using them.
corpus.data_and_hardware: No experiments, no models, no hardware. The 'data' is the 89 surveyed datasets. IoT ones covered include N-BaIoT, IoT-23, MedBIoT, the IoT network intrusion dataset/IoTID, Bot-IoT, TON_IoT, the Kitsune Network Attack Dataset (IP camera plus a Mirai scenario), CCD-INID-V1, CIC IoT 2022, CICIoT2023 (105 devices, 33 attacks), WUSTL-IIoT-2018/2021, X-IIoTID and Edge-IIoTset. CESNET datasets (including CESNET-TimeSeries24) are not mentioned anywhere in the text I read; they fall after the 2023 cut-off. ENIDrift and UGR'16 are discussed as drift and long-term examples. Nothing on ESP32, microcontrollers or edge deployment beyond citing TON_IoT and Edge-IIoTset.
corpus.results:
Survey findings:
- 51 of the 89 datasets were published since 2020.
- Since 2016, 83% of new datasets are special-purpose. IoT accounts for about 15% (about 20% with IIoT), botnets 10%, DoS 9%.
- Only 17% have purely real normal traffic, 71% use emulation (84% since 2020), and only 19% contain real attacks (13.7% since 2020).
- 60% are flow-based (76.5% since 2020); 31% of flow datasets use CICFlowMeter features.
- 60% model networks under 100 hosts, 43% are discontinuous (55% since 2020), and only 23% ship a predefined train/test split.
- Popularity: most top-venue papers use custom, unshared data. CIC-IDS2017 is the most used public dataset, but in only 29% of papers and mostly in its original flawed version. CTU-13, Kitsune and UNSW-NB15 each have more than 5 uses.
- The authors say they are "not aware of any public dataset for NID in an environment with concept drift." ENIDrift contains drift but is undocumented.

Recommendations:
- Train data must strictly precede test data in time; cross-validation risks "temporal data snooping."
- Remove shortcut features such as IP, port, TTL, timestamps and flow IDs; one cited study reached 70-100% accuracy from the destination port alone.
- Start with simple models.
- Report precision/recall, PR/ROC, AUC and false-alarm rates, not accuracy.
- Run repeated experiments with t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests.
- Evaluate on several datasets, and avoid mixing sources (if you must, use similar time periods and networks).

Future directions: continual real-world capture with automated labelling, long-term datasets with cyclostationary patterns, window and packet-level features, and formal ways to check dataset quality.
corpus.limitations:
Limitations the paper states itself:
- It covers datasets only up to 2023.
- It covers network traces only; host and sensor-only IoT/ICS data are excluded.
- Well-known sets such as LBNL and ADFA, and dozens of non-public sets, were left out (the exclusions are listed on GitHub).
- It explicitly does not judge dataset quality or recommend specific datasets.
- The popularity sample is only 45 papers from selected venues.
- Some dataset documentation was thin, so some extracted properties may be wrong.
- The authors disclose using GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Flash for editing.
- No formal threats-to-validity section was found.

Gaps I see:
- No coverage of adversarial ML beyond a passing mention of evasion by perturbation and obfuscation, plus two cited adversarial-ML references.
- Data poisoning is not discussed at all.
- Online or self-training learners are not evaluated.
- Nothing on resource-limited or on-device deployment.
corpus.overlap_with_us:
Bluntly, there is essentially no method overlap. This is a dataset survey, not a detector paper.
- It has nothing like TOA, i.e. no splitting of updates by direction and no budget on movement toward an attack signature.
- It has no core/outer-ring robust updating and no robust statistics for self-learning.
- It describes no freeze-type attack, and no poisoning, boiling-frog or attacker-share analysis.
- It runs no experiments on N-BaIoT/Kitsune and builds no anomaly detector.

The only overlap is in motivation and evaluation practice:
- It names drift ("model drift") and non-stationarity as major obstacles.
- It says real traffic "cannot be declared benign with absolute confidence, as undetected attacks might be present." That is the same assumption a self-labelling learner breaks, but the paper does not draw the poisoning conclusion.
- It suggests incremental, lifelong and active learning for drift, but only in passing.
- It stresses inter-network variability.

It does not compete with our novelty claims. It is a citation to support them.
corpus.what_we_can_borrow:
1. Motivation citations:
   - The "model drift" framing.
   - The point that real traffic cannot be assumed benign, which justifies a threat model where self-labelled updates can be contaminated.
   - "Every network is unique" (inter-network variability), which supports our per-device detector direction (open problem 2).
   - The statement that no well-documented public concept-drift NID dataset existed through 2023. This justifies our synthetic drift sim and using CESNET-TimeSeries24 (2025, after their window) as a real long-term dataset.
2. An evaluation checklist reviewers will expect, which we should follow explicitly:
   - Strict train-before-test ordering in time, no cross-validation.
   - No IP/port/TTL/timestamp shortcut features. Check that our PCA inputs from Kitsune/N-BaIoT do not encode identifiers.
   - Report false-alarm rate, PR-AUC and ROC-AUC, not accuracy.
   - Repeated seeds with Mann-Whitney U tests.
   - Evaluate on more than one dataset.
   - Keep the simple-model baseline (our centroid detector fits their advice to start simple).
3. Their warning about mixing datasets applies to our N-BaIoT experiments that splice benign traffic, Mirai traffic and a modelled poisoner. We should state that benign and attack traffic come from the same device capture, and explain how we build a continuous timeline. My unverified inference is that N-BaIoT is a set of separate captures, which is the 'discontinuous' problem they flag for time-dependent detectors.
4. Their 13-property scheme and the GitHub notebooks (xGoldy/nid-datasets) can help us pick a second dataset that is continuous, long-duration, real-traffic IoT (e.g., CICIoT2023, IoT-23, MedBIoT, or UGR'16 for long-term periodicity). Use it to justify our choice in a short table.
5. Their call for continual real-world capture and window-based features matches recording live ESP32/home traffic as a small new continuous dataset, which could be a minor extra contribution.
